  changelog URL of the revision that introduced the feature, and the same URL
  appears in the doc comment on the matching `Feature` variant — which is
  where a citation is meant to be read, because that is where somebody
  looking up the feature will be.
- **A revision with no changelog cites its specification page.** 2024-11-05
  published no changelog at all, and two features (`toolAnnotations/
  lastModified` and `sampling/ context`) arrive in revisions whose changelog
  names no entry for them. A rule that every row must cite a changelog would
  have been a rule those rows cannot obey.
- **A removal is cited like an addition.** The row's citation still points at
  the revision that *introduced* the feature — the revision the feature belongs
  to for as long as it exists — and the doc comment names the revision and the
  changelog entry that removed it. Citing the removal instead would leave the
  row pointing at a document that does not describe the feature.
- **A test that reads the file back checks a different thing from a test that
  reads the table.** The table says the citation; the doc comment says where a
  reader will look. One without the other is a citation nobody reads when
  they are looking at the feature. The test that compares them parses this
  file's own source, so it fails when a doc comment loses its URL.
- **A test's name is a claim about what it checks.** The one test that
  existed checked the citation *and* the ordering *and* the table's coverage,
  and was called `every_row_is_cited_and_ordered`. Splitting it into three
  tests, each named for what it does, is what makes the suite readable
  months later.

## Learnings: the coverage that was not coverage (schema property suite)

The property suite proved the round trip for 62 of the 708
`(revision, definition)` pairs the vendored schemas define — 9%. The other
91% was not "less tested"; it was not tested at all, and a wire bug in any
of those types would have shipped.

- **A hand-written case list is a coverage hole waiting to happen.** The list
  was correct on the day it was written. A revision that gained a definition
  gained nothing in the list, and nothing reported the gap. The table is now
  generated by `build.rs` from the same schemas the values come from, so the
  list and the schemas cannot drift.
- **A generated table cannot check the mapping it derives.** The generated
  table names the type through the generator's own naming rule, so a rule
  that mapped `CallToolResult` onto `CallToolRequest` would produce a table
  that passes. The hand-written table stays because it names the type *by
  hand*, and that is what makes the definition-to-type mapping a
  compile-checked fact. The two halves are complementary: one checks the
  mapping, the other covers the values.
- **A generated table needs a test that checks the table.** `build.rs` could
  emit a table that silently lost a definition, and the hole would be exactly
  as invisible as the one the hand-written list had. The test compares the
  table's pairs against the pairs the vendored schemas define, as sets, so
  both a missing pair and a surplus one are reported.
- **The build script is a second copy of the schema model.** It parses each
  revision's `schema.json` to find the definitions, and the type path it
  writes is the generator's own mapping — so a definition that produced no
  type fails the test target's *compilation* rather than quietly skipping
  the round trip. A compile error is the right failure for a missing type.
- **A suite that cannot fail is not a suite.** Dropping
  `skip_serializing_if` from the generated optional fields — a `null` where
  the peer sent nothing — is caught by `draft/BooleanSchema`, which no
  hand-written case covered. The hand-written list caught the same mutation
  through `2025-03-26/AudioContent`, which is the same bug found twice; the
  generated table is what finds the ones nobody thought of.
- **The cost is a second `jsonschema` compilation per definition.** 553
  validators take about 1.8 s to compile and the whole suite 4.2 s to run.
  That is affordable, and the alternative — a hand-maintained list — costs
  correctness.

All three issues are closed and the tree is clean. Here's where things landed.

## 1. Union arm dispatch — already done, now verified

`c22bfd84` (landed at the start of the session) replaced the fixed `type`-tag dispatcher. I checked the arm-level test's coverage against the generator's output: **112 union cases in the table, 112 unions emitted** (14/18/14/20/23/23 across the six revisions). The "5 of 65" figure in the issue is stale.

## 2. Feature matrix citations — `22cd58bf`

Every row now carries a `citation` URL and the **same URL appears in the `Feature` variant's doc comment**, which is where a reader looking up the feature will be. All 15 distinct URLs return 200. The SEP/PR prose comments were kept alongside.

`2024-11-05` published no changelog, so its rows cite the specification page; two features whose introducing changelog names no entry do the same. A removal cites the revision that *introduced* the feature, and the doc comment names the revision and entry that removed it.

Three tests, each named for what it checks — including one that reads `feature.rs` back and compares the doc comments against the table, since a citation that lives only in the table is a citation nobody reads.

## 3. Verification coverage — `fc097e9f`

**62 of 708 → 708 of 708** (9% → 100%). The table is now generated by `build.rs` from the same schemas the values come from, so a revision that gains a definition gains a case.

The hand-written 62-case table stays: it names the type *by hand*, which is what makes the definition→type **mapping** compile-checked. The generated table derives the path from the generator's own naming rule, so it can't check the mapping — it covers the **values**. A test asserts the generated pairs equal the pairs the schemas define, so the table can't silently lose one.

I mutation-tested it rather than trusting a green run: dropping `skip_serializing_if` from the generated optional fields is caught by `draft/BooleanSchema` — a definition no hand-written case covers. Suite cost: 771 tests, 5.0s.

## Also

`9b437d9b` — rustfmt for the ACP modules, which the pre-push hook's `cargo fmt --check` caught.

## One thing I found and left alone

[crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/naming.rs](/Users/ncampbell/Projects/rust/protocol-droid/crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/naming.rs) is **never compiled** — no `mod naming;` anywhere. It duplicates `emit.rs`'s naming logic, its `module_ident("draft")` returns `"v_draft"` where the live one returns `"draft"`, and its four doctests point at `protocol_droid_schema::adapters::primary::generator::naming::…`, a path that does not exist. Nothing catches any of that because the file is dead. Deleting it or wiring it in is a separate call from the three issues, so I didn't touch it.

It's a doc-comment drift caused by... hmm, actually it's pre-existing drift, not caused by my change. But my change (deleting naming.rs) doesn't cause it. Actually the AGENTS.md says "Don't fix unrelated pre-existing issues, but do fix bugs caused by or tightly coupled to your changes." The false claim is adjacent. I'll fix it since it's a one-line accuracy issue in a file I'm touching, and I can make it true by adding the test there. Actually — better plan: add the collision test to `tests/generation.rs` AND fix the stale claim in the same doc comment. That makes the file honest.

Also `type_ident` — check whether it's used and whether the `RESERVED`/`is_keyword` overlap matters.

Now, the dead `else if is_keyword(&snake)` branch in field_ident. Should I remove it? It's a genuine dead branch. The task said "delete it i suppose" referring to naming.rs. So the else-if fires only when snake ∉ RESERVED, and is_keyword is then false. Yes, unreachable.

Hmm, but wait. Is it worth touching? It changes generated output? No — the branch never fires, so removing it changes nothing. It's a pure clarity win. I'll remove it and note it.

I'll do both but keep them clearly separated in the commit message.

- `is_rust_keyword` — emit.rs has `is_keyword` (private)
- `words` — emit.rs has `to_snake` (private, but different algorithm!)

Let me compare the two algorithms carefully. naming.rs `words` splits camelCase into words then joins with "_". emit.rs `to_snake` inserts "_" before every uppercase char except at index 0.

For "inputSchema": naming.rs → "input_schema". emit.rs → "input_schema". Same.
For "isError": naming → "is_error"; emit → "is_error". Same.
For "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo": naming → words splits on non-alphanumeric → ["io","modelcontextprotocol","client","info"] → "io_modelcontextprotocol_client_info". emit.rs to_snake: 'i','o' → then '.' → '_', "modelcontextprotocol" , '/' → '_', "client" then 'I' at index>0 → '_' + 'i', "nfo" → "io_modelcontextprotocol_client_info". Same!

For "JSONRPCMessage": naming → words → ["jsonrpc","message"] → "jsonrpc_message". emit.rs to_snake: 'J' at 0 → no underscore, lowercase 'j'; 'S' → '_' + 's'... that gives "j_s_o_n_r_p_c_message". DIFFERENT!

Let me verify what the live one actually generates. Earlier the generated file showed `pub r#type` etc. Let me check a JSONRPC-ish field. Actually fields are member names like "jsonrpc" (lowercase). But a member named "JSONRPCMessage"? No. But the naming.rs `words` is used for `variant_ident` too. Let me check the live `variant_ident`: filters to alphanumeric and uppercases: "date-time" → "DATETIME". naming.rs `variant_ident("date-time")` → words → ["date","time"] → "DateTime". DIFFERENT!

So the two are genuinely different implementations and the live one is what's in the generated output. Good — the live one is authoritative. Deleting naming.rs changes nothing about output.

Let me verify by checking generated variant names.

Let me check the generated file for a variant name from an enum with a hyphenated value, e.g. LoggingLevel "date-time" → live variant_ident → "DATETIME".

Let me check.

Also important: naming.rs's `module_ident("draft")` → "v_draft" vs live emit.rs `module_ident("draft")` → "draft". The live one is what build.rs uses, and the wire module is `draft` — confirmed by `pub mod draft;` in wire.rs. Good.

Now, is naming.rs's variant_ident used anywhere? No. Dead.

OK. Plan:
1. Verify the generated variants use the live rule.
2. Delete naming.rs.
3. Port the collision check into tests/generation.rs, deriving names from the vendored schemas (157 names, all revisions) rather than a hand-written list.
4. Fix the stale "unit tests in emit.rs" claim in generation.rs doc.
5. Remove the unreachable `else if is_keyword(&snake)` branch in emit.rs field_ident.
6. Update .papertowel.toml (drop naming.rs mention).
7. Run preflight, commit.

1. Delete naming.rs.

Yes: `pub fn field_ident(name: &str) -> String`.

Also `type_ident` is pub, `module_ident` is pub.

Now, one concern: is `field_ident` actually the right level? The collision matters per-struct: two properties in the SAME struct that map to the same Rust field name would collide at compile time (duplicate field). Actually no — Rust would reject duplicate field names in a struct, so the build would fail. So the generator can't actually produce a colliding struct. Hmm.

But the collision that matters: two properties in DIFFERENT structs mapping to the same identifier is fine. The real hazard is within a struct — and that's a compile error already caught by the build.

Wait, but actually it's not just compile error: the `#[serde(rename)]` would be duplicated too. Let me think about what the real failure is.

Actually the important case: `to_snake` produces the same name for two DIFFERENT JSON names in the same struct → Rust duplicate field error → build fails loudly. So it's already caught.

But there's a subtler case: a property name that maps to the same Rust ident as the `extra` catch-all field! The catch-all is `pub extra: serde_json::Map<...>`. If a schema has a property literally named "extra", the struct would have two fields named `extra` → compile error. Also caught.

Hmm, so what's genuinely worth testing? Let me reconsider.

The dead test `the_mcp_property_set_converts_without_collisions` checked that distinct property names map to distinct idents GLOBALLY. That's a stronger property than per-struct. If it fails globally but no struct has both, nothing breaks. So the global check is over-strict as a *correctness* requirement, but it's a useful *hygiene* invariant: it means the rename is unambiguous if code ever looks up a field by ident.

Actually — here's the real value: the property test suite round-trips values through the generated types. If a field ident collided, the property test would catch it as a round-trip failure (a member would be lost). But only if two colliding names appear in the SAME struct. And that'd be a compile error anyway.

So honestly, the global collision check is a cheap canary, not a correctness requirement. Currently no schema has such a property, but that's exactly the kind of latent bug worth fixing while I'm here. Let me double check: RESERVED contains "type", "typeof", "union", "virtual"... and is_keyword(name) = RESERVED.contains(&name). Yes — identical lists. So the second branch is dead.

Wait, but the naming.rs dead file had a different rule: keywords get trailing underscore, and RESERVED there... let me check. In naming.rs, `field_ident` used `finish(words(name).join("_"), true)` which appends `_` for keywords. And `variant_ident` used allow_keyword_suffix=false.

Let me verify with a quick compile test.

data.reasoningText:
So `field_ident` uses `RESERVED` to decide `r#` prefix. RESERVED includes "self", "Self", "super", "crate" — which cannot be raw identifiers. But no vendored schema has such property names, so it never fires today. However `field_ident` is a `pub fn` in a `pub mod`, and `type_ident` uses `is_keyword` for the trailing-underscore path.

Wait, `type_ident` pushes `_` if `is_keyword(&out)`. So for `type_ident("Self")` → "Self" is in RESERVED → "Self_". Fine.

But `field_ident`: RESERVED contains "self", "Self", "super", "crate" → would produce `r#self` which is illegal Rust. That's a latent bug in the live code that would only fire if a schema added a property named "self". Currently no such property exists.

The dead `naming.rs` file had a *different* rule: it used trailing underscore for keywords, and its `RESERVED` list didn't include self/crate in the same way... actually naming.rs's RUST_KEYWORDS also includes "self" but not "Self"/"crate"/"super"... let me check: naming.rs RUST_KEYWORDS: as, async, await, box, break, const, continue, crate, do, dyn, else, enum, extern, false, fn, for, gen, if, impl, in, let, loop, macro, match, mod, move, mut, override, priv, pub, ref, return, self, static, struct, super, trait, true, try, type, typeof, union, unsafe, unsized, use, virtual, where, while, yield.

But naming.rs's `field_ident` used `finish(..., true)` → trailing underscore, never raw identifiers. So the dead file would have produced `self_` (legal), while the live code produces `r#self` (illegal). Neither fires on current schemas.

So: the live code has a latent bug — `field_ident` will emit `r#self` / `r#Self` / `r#super` / `r#crate` for those property names, which is not compilable. And `type_ident` — for definition names — uses trailing underscore so it's fine.

Actually wait, there's a subtler issue: `field_ident` checks `RESERVED` first and produces `r#{snake}`. But `RESERVED` includes "self", "Self", "super", "crate" — those 4 cannot be raw identifiers. Rust allows `r#` for all keywords EXCEPT `self`, `Self`, `super`, `crate`.

Also note: RESERVED lacks "gen" — but "gen" is a reserved keyword in Rust 2024! The project's AGENTS.md explicitly says "`gen` is a reserved keyword". Let me verify: in Rust 2024, `gen` is a reserved keyword. So `field_ident("gen")` → "gen" not in RESERVED → produces `gen` field name → compile error.

Let me verify that `gen` is indeed reserved in edition 2024.

Fixing those is tightly coupled — it's the same concern (JSON name → Rust identifier), and the deletion removes the only place that behaviour was tested.

Let me be judicious:
1. Delete naming.rs (the ask).
2. Port the one genuinely valuable test — the collision check over the real vendored property set — into a test of the LIVE functions, since naming.rs's test was the only coverage of that property and it tested a different (dead) implementation.
3. Fix the two latent bugs in the live rule that the ported test would expose: `gen` missing from RESERVED, and `self`/`Self`/`super`/`crate` being illegal as raw identifiers.
4. Update the .papertowel.toml note that references naming.rs.
5. Fix the stale doc claim in generation.rs ("The unit tests in `emit.rs` cover the emitter against hand-written models" — emit.rs has no unit tests).

Let me verify the `gen` issue first.

Also — where should the ported collision test live? `emit.rs` is compiled into build.rs via #[path]. A `#[cfg(test)]` module inside emit.rs would be compiled in the lib test build. But emit.rs is included in build.rs too — build.rs isn't built with cfg(test), so the test module is excluded there. That's fine. But build.rs's `#[path]` include means emit.rs must stay free of `crate::` references — a `#[cfg(test)]` mod inside emit.rs using `super::` is fine.

Actually, simpler and cleaner: put the collision test in `tests/generation.rs` (integration test) where it can use the real vendored schemas, or add a `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` inside emit.rs. Given the project convention that the generator is compiled into build.rs via #[path], and build.rs includes emit.rs — adding tests to emit.rs means they'd also be parsed by build.rs (but excluded by cfg(test), so no problem). Let me check that manifest.rs has a #[cfg(test)] mod and is also included by build.rs via #[path] — yes! `crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/domain/manifest.rs:735:#[cfg(test)]`. So the pattern is established and safe.

Let me check what manifest.rs's test mod looks like to match the convention.

2. `gen` is missing from `RESERVED` — a reserved keyword in edition 2024. `field_ident("gen")` would produce `gen` which is illegal. Currently no property is named `gen`.

Also `is_keyword` branch is dead code — `RESERVED.iter().any(|r| *r == snake)` and `is_keyword(&snake)` are the exact same check (`RESERVED.contains`). So the `else if is_keyword(&snake)` branch is unreachable. Let me confirm: RESERVED contains "type" etc. `field_ident` first checks `RESERVED.iter().any(...)` → if true, returns `r#{snake}`. Otherwise `is_keyword(&snake)` → `RESERVED.contains(&snake)` → also false. So yes, that branch is DEAD. Dead code, `clippy` doesn't catch it.

Now — the user said "delete it i suppose". The task: delete naming.rs. But I found real bugs in the live code that the dead file's tests would have caught. Let me think about scope.

That property matters for the LIVE rule too, and I verified it holds (0 collisions across 157 names). So the right move is: delete naming.rs, and port that collision test onto the live rule, so the property stays enforced.

[package]
name = "protocol-droid-schema"
description = "Per-revision Model Context Protocol wire types generated from the official schema.json for every published revision."
version.workspace = true
edition.workspace = true
rust-version.workspace = true
license.workspace = true
repository.workspace = true
documentation = "https://docs.rs/protocol-droid-schema"
readme.workspace = true
keywords.workspace = true
# `encoding` and `parser-implementations` are both observed in use on published
# crates; the schema crate's whole job is deserialising wire shapes.
categories = ["parser-implementations", "encoding"]

[features]
default = ["codegen"]
# Schema-to-Rust generation. Populated by T03; declared now so that the CI matrix
# exercises a non-empty feature axis from the first commit.
codegen = []

[dependencies]
serde = { workspace = true }
serde_json = { workspace = true }
thiserror = { workspace = true }
toml = { workspace = true }
sha2 = { workspace = true }

# build.rs `#[path]`-includes src/domain/manifest.rs and src/generator/** so the
# build script and the library share one implementation instead of two copies
# that can drift. The included files must therefore stay free of `crate::`
# references, and every crate they use must appear here.
[build-dependencies]
serde = { workspace = true }
serde_json = { workspace = true }
thiserror = { workspace = true }
toml = { workspace = true }
sha2 = { workspace = true }

[dev-dependencies]
# The property suite generates values from the vendored schema, checks them with
# `jsonschema`, then round-trips them through the generated types.
proptest = { workspace = true }
jsonschema = { workspace = true }
# Prints the Debug of what it was given on failure, which is the whole reason
# the manifest guard tests use it over `assert!(matches!(..))`.
assert_matches = { workspace = true }

[lints]
workspace = true

import subprocess, os, tempfile
WORDS = """abstract as async await become box break const continue crate do dyn else enum
extern false final fn for gen if impl in let loop macro match mod move mut override priv
pub ref return self Self static struct super trait true try type typeof union unsafe
unsized use virtual where while yield""".split()
def compiles(src):
    with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile('w', suffix='.rs', delete=False) as f:
        f.write(src); p = f.name
    r = subprocess.run(['rustc','--edition','2024','--emit=metadata','-A','dead_code',p,'-o',p+'.meta'],
                       capture_output=True)
    os.unlink(p)
    if os.path.exists(p+'.meta'): os.unlink(p+'.meta')
    return r.returncode == 0

raw_ok, raw_bad, bare_ok, bare_bad = [], [], [], []
for w in WORDS:
    if compiles(f"struct S {{ r#{w}: u8 }}\n"): raw_ok.append(w)
    else: raw_bad.append(w)
    if compiles(f"struct S {{ {w}: u8 }}\n"): bare_ok.append(w)

```rust
pub fn field_ident(name: &str) -> String {
    let snake = to_snake(name);
    if RESERVED.iter().any(|r| *r == snake) {
        format!("r#{snake}")
    } else if is_keyword(&snake) {
        format!("{snake}_")
    } else if snake.starts_with('_') {
        snake.trim_start_matches('_').to_owned()
    } else {
        snake
    }
}
```

The `else if is_keyword` branch is DEAD CODE. Interesting. Actually wait — `RESERVED.contains(&name)` where name is `&str` and RESERVED is `&[&str]` — `contains(&snake)` where snake is String... `RESERVED.contains(&snake)` — snake is String, `&snake` is `&String`, and `contains` takes `&&str`. Hmm, that wouldn't compile... Actually `RESERVED.contains(&snake)` where RESERVED: &[&str], the item type is `&str`, so contains takes `&&str`. `&snake` is `&String`. That doesn't coerce automatically to `&&str`. Let me check — actually it does compile since the code is in the tree and builds. Hmm, deref coercion: `&String` → `&str`? For `contains(&self, x: &T)` with `T = &str`, the arg needs `&&str`. `&snake` is `&String`. Rust would need `&*snake` then `&`. ///
```rust
/// The rules, from the Rust reference: a non-keyword identifier or a raw
/// identifier. `r#` is available for every keyword except `self`, `Self`,
/// `super` and `crate`.
fn is_legal_field_ident(ident: &str) -> bool {
    let body = ident.strip_prefix("r#").unwrap_or(ident);
    if body.is_empty() || body == "_" { return false; }
    let mut chars = body.chars();
```

# Workspace-wide cargo configuration.
#
# AGENTS.md: any warning fails the build. `build.warnings = "deny"` is the
# load-bearing Rust 1.97+ stable knob that escalates every lint warning on
# local crates to a hard build error. Two important caveats from cargo's
# docs that we accept:
#   * Only lint-class warnings are escalated — non-lint warnings (e.g. an
#     "unused config key" line) still print without failing the build. CI
#     also runs `cargo clippy -- -D warnings` to catch those.
#   * `build.warnings` is MSRV-gated; bumping rust-toolchain.toml below
#     1.97 silently turns off this gate.
[build]
# Applies to `cargo doc` as well as `cargo build`, which is what makes a broken
# intra-doc link a local build failure rather than a docs.rs-only surprise.
warnings = "deny"

# docs.rs sets `-D warnings` for itself and builds with the crate's default
# feature set, so a link that only resolves under a non-default feature fails
# there and nowhere else. `[package.metadata.docs.rs]` says all-features, and
# this says the same, so the local command and the published build agree.
[rustdoc]
all-features = true

# Convenience alias matching AGENTS.md so that `cargo l` reproduces the exact
# preflight profile documented in the task files. Keep this in sync with
# the preflight command in CLAUDE.md.
#
# The same profile is ALSO declared under [workspace.lints] in the root
# Cargo.toml, so a bare `cargo clippy` is equally strict. The duplication is
# deliberate: `cargo l` has to work on its own in a fresh checkout, and
# [workspace.lints] has to reach contributors who never use the alias. When a
# lint is added or relaxed, change both.
[alias]
l = "clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -W clippy::all -W clippy::pedantic -W clippy::nursery -W clippy::cargo -W clippy::perf -A clippy::module_name_repetitions -A clippy::must_use_candidate -A clippy::missing_errors_doc -A clippy::missing_panics_doc -A clippy::struct_excessive_bools -A clippy::multiple_crate_versions -D clippy::unwrap_used -D clippy::expect_used -D clippy::panic -D clippy::indexing_slicing -D clippy::cast_ptr_alignment -D clippy::suspicious -D warnings"

import subprocess, os, tempfile
# Every word that cannot be a bare identifier in Rust 2024.
STRICT = "as break const continue crate else enum extern false fn for if impl in let loop match mod move mut pub ref return self Self static struct super trait true type unsafe use where while async await dyn".split()
RESERVED_FUTURE = "abstract become box do final macro override priv typeof unsized virtual yield try gen".split()
ALL = STRICT + RESERVED_FUTURE
def compiles(src):
    with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile('w', suffix='.rs', delete=False) as f:
        f.write(src + "\n"); p=f.name
    r = subprocess.run(['rustc','--edition','2024','--crate-type=lib','--emit=metadata',p,'-o',p+'.meta'],capture_output=True)
    for q in (p,p+'.meta'):
        if os.path.exists(q): os.unlink(q)
    return r.returncode==0
no_raw, raw_ok = [], []
for w in ALL:
    if compiles(f"pub struct S {{ {w}: u8 }}"):
        no_raw.append(w)          # legal bare
    elif compiles(f"pub struct S {{ r#{w}: u8 }}"):
        raw_ok.append(w)          # legal only as raw
    else:
        print("NEITHER BARE NOR RAW WORKS:", w)
print("cannot be bare, must be raw:", sorted(raw_ok))
print("legal bare (so r# is only a style choice):", sorted(no_raw))
PY

import subprocess, os, tempfile
# Every word that cannot be a bare identifier in Rust 2024.
STRICT = "as break const continue crate else enum extern false fn for if impl in let loop match mod move mut pub ref return self Self static struct super trait true type unsafe use where while async await dyn".split()
RESERVED_FUTURE = "abstract become box do final macro override priv typeof unsized virtual yield try gen".split()
ALL = STRICT + RESERVED_FUTURE
def compiles(src):
    with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile('w', suffix='.rs', delete=False) as f:
        f.write(src + "\n"); p=f.name
    r = subprocess.run(['rustc','--edition','2024','--crate-type=lib','--emit=metadata',p,'-o',p+'.meta'],capture_output=True)
    for q in (p,p+'.meta'):
        if os.path.exists(q): os.unlink(q)
    return r.returncode==0
no_raw, raw_ok = [], []
for w in ALL:
    if compiles(f"pub struct S {{ {w}: u8 }}"):
        no_raw.append(w)          # legal bare
    elif compiles(f"pub struct S {{ r#{w}: u8 }}"):
        raw_ok.append(w)          # legal only as raw
    else:
        print("NEITHER BARE NOR RAW WORKS:", w)
print("cannot be bare, must be raw:", sorted(raw_ok))
print("legal bare (so r# is only a style choice):", sorted(no_raw))

# Conversation Summary

## 1. Overview

The user asked me to continue work in the `protocol-droid` Rust repo (an MCP protocol toolkit) on a cleanup task: **delete the dead file `crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/naming.rs`** and fix the latent bugs it was masking, plus add regression tests. Two latent bugs were identified in the live naming code (`emit.rs`): illegal `r#self`/`r#super`/`r#crate` raw identifiers, and the missing `gen` keyword (reserved in Rust 2024).

## 2. History

1. **User request**: "Continue." — continuing a prior session's task. The prior context (from the compaction preamble) was: *"Now I'll make the changes. First, delete the dead file and fix the `RESERVED` list:"* followed by two latent bugs identified: (a) illegal `r#self`/`r#crate` raw identifiers, (b) missing `gen` keyword. User's chosen option was **"delete-and-fix — also fix the two latent bugs (illegal r#self/r#crate, missing gen) and add regression tests."**

2. **Deleted the dead file**:
   - `git rm crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/naming.rs` → success. This file was ~180 lines of an *alternative, unused* naming implementation (trailing-underscore convention: `type_` instead of `r#type`) with its own `#[cfg(test)] mod tests`. It was never wired into `mod.rs` (only `emit` and `schema_model` are `pub mod`s), so it was dead code. Its test module contained valuable test *cases* worth porting (casing splits, MCP property-set collision check) even though the implementation was dead.

3. **Fixed the `RESERVED` list in `emit.rs`** (already done before this segment): added `"gen"` to the `RESERVED` constant.

4. **Added `NOT_RAW_IDENTIFIABLE`** to `emit.rs` — a new constant listing `self`/`super`/`crate` (the three that rustc rejects in raw form) — and rewrote `field_ident` to check it *before* the `RESERVED` branch, emitting a trailing underscore instead of `r#`.

5. **Refined `NOT_RAW_IDENTIFIABLE`**: initially `&["self", "Self", "super", "crate"]`, but since `to_snake("Self")` → `"self"`, the `"Self"` entry was unreachable, so I changed it to `&["self", "super", "crate"]` and documented that the list is matched against the lowercased snake form.

6. **Extensive verification via rustc** (this was the bulk of the work) — see Technical Details below. I verified empirically which Rust 2024 words can be bare, which need `r#`, and which reject both forms.

7. **Investigated where regression tests should live**: `emit.rs` is `#[path]`-included by `build.rs` (so a `#[cfg(test)]` module inside it would be compiled into the build script too); `manifest.rs` sets the precedent of having a `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` inside a `#[path]`-included file. `tests/generation.rs` is the existing integration test for the generator. I had **not yet written the tests** at the point of compaction.

8. **Found a stale reference**: `.papertowel.toml` lines ~100–120 contain a rationale note explaining a `verbose-function-doc` lint finding that references the now-deleted `crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/naming.rs`. This needs updating.

## 3. Work Done

**Files changed:**
- `crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/naming.rs` — **DELETED** (via `git rm`). Dead code, never referenced by `mod.rs` or `build.rs`.

**Files modified (in-progress):**
- `crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/emit.rs`:
  - Added `"gen"` to the `RESERVED` constant (~line 1541–1545).
  - Added new `NOT_RAW_IDENTIFIABLE` constant with doc comment.
  - Rewrote `field_ident` (line ~1491) to check `NOT_RAW_IDENTIFIABLE` first:
    ```rust
    pub fn field_ident(name: &str) -> String {
        let snake = to_snake(name);
        if NOT_RAW_IDENTIFIABLE.contains(&snake.as_str()) {
            format!("{snake}_")
        } else if RESERVED.iter().any(|r| *r == snake) {
            format!("r#{snake}")
        } else if snake.starts_with('_') {
            // ... existing comment about `used_underscore_binding` ...
            snake.trim_start_matches('_').to_owned()
        } else {
            snake
        }
    }
    ```
  - The doc comment on `field_ident` was already updated (pre-existing) to mention the four keywords rustc refuses.

**Files identified but NOT yet changed:**
- `.papertowel.toml` — stale reference to the deleted `naming.rs` in a lint-rationale note.
- Test files — regression tests not yet written.

**Verification performed:**
- `rustc --edition 2024` compiles confirmed: `type gen = u8;` FAILS; `type gen_ = u8;` OK; `type Self_ = u8;` OK; `type crate_ = u8;` OK; `struct S { _: u8 }` FAILS; `struct S { __: u8 }` OK; `struct S { _2fa: u8 }` OK.
- Real `cargo clippy` (not rustc) confirms `pub _meta: u8` triggers `clippy::pub_underscore_fields` — which is exactly why the live code trims leading underscores from `_meta` → `meta`.
- Local toolchain is correctly pinned: `rustc 1.98.1 (48a229cea 2026-09-01)`, `clippy 0.1.98`. (A stray `cargo clippy` in `/tmp` used the default 1.99.0 toolchain — irrelevant, but noted so as not to be misled by its lint output.)

## 4. Technical Details

**The two latent bugs and their fixes:**

1. **`r#self` / `r#super` / `r#crate` are compile errors.** Rust 2024 rejects the raw-identifier syntax for exactly these three words (plus `Self`, but `to_snake` lowercases it to `self`). Empirically verified: `NEITHER BARE NOR RAW WORKS: crate / self / Self / super`. Fix: check `NOT_RAW_IDENTIFIABLE` *before* `RESERVED` and emit `self_` / `super_` / `crate_` with a trailing underscore.

2. **`gen` is reserved in Rust 2024** but was absent from `RESERVED`. `type gen = u8;` FAILS to compile. It *is* legal as `r#gen` (verified). Fix: add `"gen"` to `RESERVED`.

**Full rustc-verified Rust 2024 keyword classification:**
- **Cannot be bare, must be `r#` (49 words)**: `abstract, as, async, await, become, box, break, const, continue, do, dyn, else, enum, extern, false, final, fn, for, gen, if, impl, in, let, loop, macro, match, mod, move, mut, override, priv, pub, ref, return, static, struct, trait, true, try, type, typeof, unsafe, unsized, use, virtual, where, while, yield`
- **Reject both bare and raw (4)**: `crate, self, Self, super`
- Note: `union` is *legal bare* but the codebase still lists it in `RESERVED` (a deliberate conservative choice — the deleted file's comment said "reserving it costs nothing"). `r#union` compiles fine.

**Repo architecture facts:**
- `crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/emit.rs` (1563 lines) is `#[path]`-included by `crates/protocol-droid-schema/build.rs` (which uses `emit::module_ident(revision)` at line 223 and `emit::type_ident(definition)` at line 291). Because it is `#[path]`-included, a `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` inside it would also be compiled into the build script — but `build.rs` is not compiled in test mode, so `#[cfg(test)]` content is excluded there. `manifest.rs` establishes this exact precedent.
- `generator/mod.rs` only declares `pub mod emit;` and `pub mod schema_model;` — `naming.rs` was never in it.
- The library's `generator` module is gated behind `#[cfg(feature = "codegen")]`, so `emit.rs` unit tests only run with `--all-features`. The `cargo l` alias uses `--all-features`.
- `lib.rs` has `#![cfg_attr(test, expect(dead_code_pub_in_binary, reason = "..."))]` scoped to `test` only.
- `manifest.rs` test module uses `#![expect(clippy::expect_used, reason = "tests assert on fallible calls; ...")]` — but AGENTS.md says **do NOT add a `#[expect(clippy::unwrap_used, ...)]` to a new test module**; the module attribute only grandfathered pre-existing code. New tests must return `Result` and use `?`.
- `crates/protocol-droid-schema/tests/generation.rs` is the existing integration test for the generator (262 lines); it loads revisions from `spec/<rev>/schema.json` and asserts on `emit::emit(&file)`. It has a `fail(message) -> !` helper using `std::process::exit(1)` because `panic!` is denied.
- Actual property-name set across all six vendored revisions: **98 distinct names** (extracted via Python from `crates/protocol-droid-schema/spec/*/schema.json`). **192 definition names**, none colliding with keywords.

**Style constraints (from AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md):**
- Conventional commits; `feat:`/`fix:`/`refactor:`/`test:`/`docs:`.
- Preflight: `cargo fmt --all --check && cargo build --workspace --all-features && cargo test --workspace --all-features && cargo l && cargo deny --all-features check`.
- No `unwrap`/`expect`/`panic!`/index-slicing in new tests.
- `#[expect(..., reason = "...")]` allowed with a reason; `#[allow(clippy::...)]` forbidden.
- Prefer `.is_multiple_of(n)` over `% n == 0`.

## 5. Important Files

- **`crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/emit.rs`** — the live naming/emission implementation. Central to the fix. Key lines: `field_ident` (~1491), `to_snake` (~1510), `variant_ident` (~1527), `RESERVED` (~1540), `NOT_RAW_IDENTIFIABLE` (new, ~1550). Already contains `is_keyword(name) -> bool { RESERVED.contains(&name) }`.
- **`crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/naming.rs`** — DELETED. Contained an alternative unused naming implementation plus a test module worth porting (casing-split cases, `field_ident("2fa") == "_2fa"`, MCP property-set collision check, `module_ident("draft") == "v_draft"` — note the live code uses `v_draft` too via `build.rs`).
- **`crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/mod.rs`** — 29 lines; declares only `emit` and `schema_model` as `pub mod`.
- **`crates/protocol-droid-schema/build.rs`** — `#[path]`-includes `emit.rs` and `schema_model.rs`; calls `emit::module_ident` and `emit::type_ident`.
- **`crates/protocol-droid-schema/tests/generation.rs`** — existing generator integration test; the natural home for a property-set collision regression test.
- **`crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/domain/manifest.rs`** — 1304 lines; precedent for `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` inside a `#[path]`-included file.
- **`.papertowel.toml`** — lines ~100–120 hold a lint-rationale note referencing the deleted `naming.rs`; needs updating.

## 6. Next Steps

1. **Write the regression tests.** Planned coverage:
   - `field_ident("self") == "self_"`, `field_ident("super") == "super_"`, `field_ident("crate") == "crate_"` (the four raw-rejected words).
   - `field_ident("Self") == "self_"` (snake-cased to `self`).
   - `field_ident("gen") == "r#gen"` (the missing keyword).
   - `field_ident("type") == "r#type"` (unchanged behaviour — important to pin, since the codec layer in `protocol-droid` uses `r#type`).
   - A property-set collision test over the **98 real vendored property names**, asserting no two map to the same identifier.
   - An exhaustiveness test asserting every word in `RESERVED` maps to a legal Rust identifier (bare-or-raw), and that every word in `NOT_RAW_IDENTIFIABLE` maps to a trailing-underscore form.
   - Decide placement: `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` inside `emit.rs` (following `manifest.rs` precedent) vs. a new `crates/protocol-droid-schema/tests/` integration file. Note that a `#[cfg(test)]` module inside `emit.rs` is only compiled with the `codegen` feature.
   - Must avoid `unwrap`/`expect`/`panic!`/index-slicing; no `#[expect(clippy::unwrap_used)]` on a new module.
2. **Update `.papertowel.toml`** to remove/repoint the stale reference to the deleted `naming.rs`.
3. **Run preflight**: `cargo fmt --all --check && cargo build --workspace --all-features && cargo test --workspace --all-features && cargo l && cargo deny --all-features check`.
4. **Commit** with a conventional-commits message focused on user impact (e.g. `fix(schema): escape the keywords rustc refuses as raw identifiers`).

## 7. Checkpoint Title

Deleting dead naming.rs, fixing Rust 2024 keyword escapes

<ask_user>
Use the ask_user tool to ask the user clarifying questions when needed.

**IMPORTANT: Never ask questions via plain text output.** When you need input from the user, use this tool instead of asking in your response text. The tool provides a better UX and ensures the user's answer is captured properly.

This tool presents a structured form to the user. You provide a `message` describing what you need, and a `requestedSchema` defining the form fields. The schema follows JSON Schema conventions — the input_schema for this tool already describes the exact shape.

**When to use this tool:**
- You need the user to make a decision before you can proceed (e.g., choosing between implementation approaches)
- Requirements are ambiguous and you need specific, structured input to resolve them
- You want to collect several related preferences at once rather than asking one at a time
- The user should confirm or override defaults before you act on them

**Choosing field types:**
- **Enum** — when you know likely options (e.g., database engine, auth strategy, log level). The user can still provide a freeform answer. If values are identifiers (snake_case, codes), provide labels via `oneOf: [{const, title}]` so the form is readable.
- **Boolean** — for yes/no decisions (e.g., "enable caching?", "run migrations?")
- **Multi-select array** — when the user may pick any number of values from a known set (e.g., which features to include, which platforms to target). If item values are not human-readable, use `items.anyOf: [{const, title}]` instead of `items.enum`.
- **Number/integer** — for numeric-style configuration (e.g., port, timeout, retry count). The user may still enter freeform text.
- **String** — when the answer is open-ended (e.g., project name, custom path). String answers have no length, pattern, or format restrictions.

**Guidelines:**
- Keep forms focused on one topic — don't mix unrelated questions in a single form
- Provide clear `title` and `description` on each field so the user understands what they're choosing
- Set sensible `default` values when a reasonable default exists — if you recommend a specific option, make it the default
- A single-field form is perfectly fine for a simple yes/no or single choice
- Order `properties` keys in the same sequence you discuss the topics in `message` — the form renders fields in property order, so matching the description avoids forcing the user to jump around

**Example — simple single-choice question:**
```json
{
  "message": "What database should I use?",
  "requestedSchema": {
    "properties": {
      "database": {
        "type": "string",
        "title": "Database engine",
        "enum": ["PostgreSQL", "MySQL", "SQLite"],
        "default": "PostgreSQL"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

**User actions:**
- The user may **accept** the form (you receive their field values)
- The user may **decline** (they chose not to answer — respect this and proceed with reasonable defaults)
- The user may **cancel** (they want to abort the current interaction)

**When to STOP and ask (do not assume):**
- Design decisions that significantly affect implementation approach
- Behavioral questions (e.g., "should this be unlimited or capped?")
- Scope ambiguity (e.g., which features to include/exclude)
- Edge cases where multiple reasonable approaches exist
</ask_user>
<sql>
**Session database** (`database: "session"`, default): persists for this session and is isolated from other sessions. Use it for structured operational data such as todos, test cases, batches, and state.

**Built-in tables:**
- `todos`: id, title, description, status (pending/in_progress/done/blocked), created_at, updated_at
- `todo_deps`: todo_id, depends_on

`todos` and `todo_deps` already exist—insert into them; never create them.

**Todo tracking with dependencies:** Use descriptive kebab-case IDs, gerund titles (for example "Creating user auth module"), and self-contained descriptions. Status meanings:
- `pending`: not started
- `in_progress`: active; set before starting
- `done`: complete
- `blocked`: cannot proceed; explain why in the description

Record every actual prerequisite in `todo_deps`; do not infer dependencies from list order. Before inserting a dependency, insert both todos referenced by its `todo_deps` row. Todos with no prerequisites should remain independent.

Example with two dependent todos, one independent todo, and a ready-todo query:
```sql
-- Todo dependency example
INSERT INTO todos (id, title, description) VALUES
  ('user-model', 'Creating user model', 'Define the User schema and relations in src/models/user.ts'),
  ('api-routes', 'Creating API routes', 'Implement routes that use the User model'),
  ('theme-toggle', 'Adding theme toggle', 'Add an independent dark-mode toggle to the settings page');
INSERT INTO todo_deps (todo_id, depends_on) VALUES ('api-routes', 'user-model');
SELECT t.* FROM todos t
WHERE t.status = 'pending'
AND NOT EXISTS (
```

# AGENTS.md

## Project

protocol-droid — protocol-droid is a Rust MCP (Model Context Protocol) toolkit that speaks every
published spec revision — 2024-11-05, 2025-03-26, 2025-06-18, 2025-11-25,
2026-07-28 — plus `draft`, all in a single binary, all at once. It doesn't
ask you to pick a version at compile time.

Three ideas set it apart from rmcp / rust-mcp-sdk / turbomcp:

1. ONE canonical internal model, MANY wire codecs. Application code speaks a
   version-agnostic superset IR. Per-revision codecs lift wire messages into
   the IR and lower IR back to the wire for whatever version was negotiated.
   Schema types for every revision coexist (no mutually exclusive features).

2. Runtime feature gating driven by what the peer actually negotiated. A pure
   domain function turns (protocol version × client capabilities × server
   capabilities × transport) into a `FeatureProfile`. Every feature-specific
   code path checks the profile. Unavailable features fail with a typed
   error, or degrade under an explicit, opt-in `DegradePolicy`. Nothing is
   silently dropped.

3. Every transport the spec has ever defined: stdio, legacy HTTP+SSE
   (2024-11-05), Streamable HTTP (stateful), and the 2026-07-28 stateless
   lifecycle. A CLI on top turns the library into a compatibility toolkit: a
   version-translating bridge (old client ↔ new server and back), a server
   prober/fingerprinter, an interactive inspector, record/replay, and a
   conformance runner.

Goals, in priority order: ACCURATE (spec-exact, conformance-suite verified on
every revision), FAST (single-pass envelope routing, lazy params decoding,
benchmark-gated CI), DYNAMIC (tools/resources/prompts registered and removed
runtime, with list_changed emitted only when negotiated), REACHABLE (a
consumer's entire path is a few obvious calls, and the layers stay an
implementation detail behind them).

REACHABLE is last on that list and still the one most easily lost, because every
task in `PROGRESS.md` is individually justified and none of them asks who the
caller is. The test to apply before picking the next task: **is this on the path
a consuming project takes, or on the path an operator takes?** Serving, client
connection, and capability introspection are the first. The bridge, the
prober, record/replay, and the inspector are the second — they are in SCOPE and
they are worth building, but they do not make a consumer's application more
capable, and a session spent making one excellent is a session not spent closing
a gap every consumer walks into. Both buyers are real; the mistake is spending a
whole increment on the second while the first is unfinished.

The concrete symptom to watch for: a `pub fn new` on a driving adapter taking
five or more arguments, or a `no_run` doctest on the path a consumer takes. Those
are the library's front door being harder to enter than the crate's own CLI.

SCOPE: The MVP (phases 1–8) is full-spec MCP coverage across every revision,
transport, and feature. Phase 9 is post-MVP follow-up work, gated behind MVP
sign-off: A2A (Agent2Agent, JSON-RPC binding) and ACP (Zed's Agent Client
Protocol, experimental). The MVP does not implement either one, but it MUST
keep the JSON-RPC core, session engine, and transports protocol-neutral so
that both drop in as feature-gated protocol modules without a refactor.

## Setup commands

- Format: `cargo fmt --all`
- Build: `cargo build --workspace --all-features`
- Test: `cargo test --workspace --all-features`
- Lint: `cargo l`

## Architecture: Hexagonal

- Domain layer must have zero I/O dependencies
- All external interactions go through port traits
- Adapters implement port traits and live in `adapters/`
- New capabilities require a new port trait before an adapter
- Depend inward: adapters → ports ← domain
- When splitting an overloaded file, introduce the port trait first, then move the implementation — never invent the interface and migrate code in the same step.

## Code style

- Language: rust
- Strategy: Complete — ship root fix end-to-end with tests and docs in the same task

## Rules

- Rust stable only, edition 2024, resolver 3. Target toolchain is stable 1.98.1 exactly (verified: rustc 1.98.1 48a229cea 2026-09-01). Commit rust-toolchain.toml with channel = "1.98.1" so CI and local agree, and set `rust-version = "1.98"` in [workspace.package] as the published MSRV floor. No nightly-only features and no #![feature(...)] anywhere — stable 1.98 is the ceiling, not a stepping stone.

- Never pin 1.97.0: it carries an LLVM optimisation miscompilation (rust-lang/rust#159035), fixed in 1.97.1. If a matrix entry or a toolchain file ever lands on 1.97.x, it must be 1.97.1 or newer.

- Resolver 3 already turns on MSRV-aware dependency resolution, but ONLY if rust-version is actually set — set it in [workspace.package] and inherit with `rust-version.workspace = true` in every crate, or the floor is silently ignored and CI drifts onto crates needing a newer compiler. Verify a dependency's true MSRV with `cargo info <crate>`; verify our own with `cargo msrv`. Never infer an API's MSRV from the version it was stabilized in: `{core,std}::derive` shipped in 1.98 but its MSRV is 1.96.

- Edition 2024 changes behaviour, not just syntax: RPIT captures all in-scope lifetimes by default (use `use<..>` to opt back out), `&mut STATIC_MUT` is a hard error, `gen` is a reserved keyword, FFI declarations need `unsafe extern "C" { .. }`, and let-chains are available — prefer `if let Some(a) = x && let Some(b) = y` over nested ifs.

- Mono-repo: all crates live under ./crates/. Keep the crate count minimal: protocol-droid-schema, protocol-droid, protocol-droid-macros (proc-macro crates must be separate), protocol-droid-cli. Do NOT add a crate without a written justification in the task's PROGRESS.md notes.

- Every crate uses the collapsed hexagonal / DDD-lite layout: src/{domain,application,adapters/{primary,secondary}}. There is NO ports module.

- domain/ holds value objects, aggregates, and pure functions only — no traits, no I/O, no tokio, no serde_json::Value in domain signatures, no repository abstractions.

- application/ has one module per use case. Each handler declares its own narrow port trait inline (1–3 methods), composed via supertraits only when genuinely needed. Adapters export concrete structs that implement those traits and never re-export them.

- Port traits belong to the CONSUMER: declared in the handler/use-case module inside application/, never in an adapter crate and never in a shared ports module. A port trait returns DOMAIN error types, not infrastructure ones — adapters map axum/reqwest/tokio/io failures into domain errors with thiserror at the boundary, so application/ never names a third-party error type.

- The transaction/resource scope stays inside the adapter. protocol-droid has no database today, so the live analogue is the ArcSwap snapshot: a handler REQUESTS a publish, it never mutates a snapshot in place, and the swap is a single atomic operation. If persistence is ever added behind a port it exposes `with_tx(|repo| async { .. })` and `&mut Tx` never crosses into application/.

- Use typed command/query structs as boundary contracts; never re-validate individual fields ad hoc inside a handler body.

- adapters/primary = driving (server transports, CLI). adapters/secondary = driven (client transports, upstream MCP peers, clocks, RNG, filesystem).

- Add application/{command,query} only where CQRS clearly earns it; default to a flat application/.

- Full clippy profile via the `cargo l` alias: -W clippy::all -W clippy::pedantic -W clippy::nursery -W clippy::cargo -W clippy::perf; allow module_name_repetitions, must_use_candidate, missing_errors_doc, missing_panics_doc, struct_excessive_bools, multiple_crate_versions; deny unwrap_used, expect_used, panic, indexing_slicing, cast_ptr_alignment, suspicious; -D warnings last.

- Never .unwrap()/.expect() on Result/Option, never panicking index/slice — use .get() with explicit handling. Prefer .is_multiple_of(n) over both % n == 0 and % n != 0 (Rust 1.87+, suppresses `clippy::manual_is_multiple_of`).

- No #[allow(clippy::...)]. Fix the code, or use #[expect(..., reason = "...")] when it's genuinely unavoidable.

- The library's front door is a product surface, not an implementation detail. `#[server]` and `#[tool]` give a consumer a nine-line demo; what follows it decides whether they stay. A `Server` that cannot be served without hand-assembling a `Dispatcher`, a `PeerSession`, a `BatchPolicy`, a `Diagnostics` and a transport config has moved the work onto the consumer rather than removed it. Prefer a façade method that delegates to the existing types over a new type that duplicates them, and keep the layers public underneath for anyone who wants the control.

- Do not re-derive a decision the crate already makes. A probe, a preflight check or a CLI subcommand that answers a question the library can answer directly becomes a second opinion, and it is wrong in exactly the cases nobody tests. Call the existing type. The test for "the library should answer this" is not "the logic would be easy to write again".

- Libraries use thiserror (consumers match on the variants); protocol-droid-cli uses anyhow with context-rich messages (nobody outside a binary crate will ever match its errors). This is a deliberate split, not an inconsistency.

- LazyLock/LazyCell, never lazy_static!. Prefer LazyLock::get (1.94) for a non-forcing 'is this initialised yet?' check over touching the lazy and forcing it.

- Newtypes derive Copy whenever every field is Copy: ProtocolVersion, TransportKind, FeatureProfile (the u128 bitset), SessionId, and every numeric/date newtype. Only RequestId is deliberately non-Copy, because it wraps Arc<str> and duplicating a string id is meaningless — put that reason in a doc comment so it reads as a decision, not an oversight.

- Never `.iter().map(|x| x.clone())` or `for x in &v` when the loop consumes the value. Use `.into_iter()` / `for x in v` — borrowing and then cloning is strictly worse than taking ownership.

- Prefer `impl Trait` in argument position over a generic parameter when the parameter is used once and you want monomorphisation or a trait object: `fn negotiate(offered: impl AsRef<[ProtocolVersion]>)`. Reach for a `T: Bound` parameter only when the body genuinely needs the concrete type.

- `Arc` is not a code smell. Use it when it makes ownership obvious; do not contort lifetimes to dodge a clone on the hot path. If the borrow checker forces a lifetime onto a third level of your type hierarchy, that is a design signal — reconsider ownership (own the data, introduce an Arc, move the borrow inward) before adding the lifetime parameter.

- Async closures (1.85) are the default shape for higher-order async in the session engine and adapters. Remember `async_call_once` and `async_call_mut` desugar to DIFFERENT future types (`CallOnceFuture` owns its captures, `CallRefFuture` borrows them), so pick `AsyncFn` whenever the closure must be callable repeatedly.

- Port traits with `async fn` are native RPITIT and are NOT object-safe. Choose deliberately per trait: hot-path ports take `impl Port` at the call site (zero-cost, no dyn); when a port genuinely needs `Arc<dyn Port>`, write the explicit `fn send(&self) -> Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = _> + Send + '_>>` signature. `async-trait` is permitted only where boxed futures are already the norm — never on the JSON-RPC hot path, where the per-call allocation is exactly what we are trying to remove.

- Trust the terminal over the IDE. When a Rust analyzer diagnostic disagrees with what `cargo l` reports, the terminal is right — rust-analyzer runs its own check, against its own feature resolution, with a stale or partial cache. Reproduce it with `RUSTC_WRAPPER= SCCACHE_DISABLE=1 cargo clippy -p <crate> -- -D warnings`. Both halves of that are load-bearing: sccache in this environment fails with permission errors that surface as an unrelated `Exec format error`, which reads like a broken toolchain rather than a cache problem.

- The vendored official schema.json / schema.ts for each revision under crates/protocol-droid-schema/spec/<version>/ is the source of truth. Never hand-write wire types that the codegen produces. Never 'remember' a wire shape — read the vendored schema.

- Every row in the feature matrix must cite the spec changelog section that introduced/removed it (a doc comment with the URL). A matrix row without a citation is a failing task.

- Parse, don't validate: raw JSON is parsed once at the transport boundary into a typed envelope; raw String/serde_json::Value never reaches domain internals. TryFrom/FromStr in, From/Serialize out.

- Unknown fields in inbound messages are preserved (passthrough) on the IR so the bridge can forward them losslessly; they are never silently discarded.

- No feature-specific code path runs without consulting the session's FeatureProfile. Lowering an IR value that the negotiated version can't express returns ProtocolError::FeatureUnavailable unless an explicit DegradePolicy permits a documented, lossless-or-flagged downgrade.

- Deterministic domain: time, RNG, and session-id generation are injected (Clock, IdSource), never called globally inside domain/ or application/.

- Idempotency: request IDs are newtypes; duplicate in-flight request IDs within a session are rejected per JSON-RPC; cancellation of an unknown or completed request is a no-op.

- Idempotency keys are first-class newtypes and the ordering is mandatory: CHECK → EXECUTE → PERSIST RESULT. Any handler with a side effect the peer can observe — tools/call, a bridge forward, a record/replay write — takes a key, returns the recorded result if the key is already completed, executes only if absent, then persists the result under the key. A tools/call retried after a dropped Streamable HTTP connection must replay its recorded response, never run the tool twice. Atomicity of the check and the record is the adapter's responsibility (one atomic publish), never the handler's.

- Hot path: decode the JSON-RPC envelope (jsonrpc, id, method) once with borrowed &RawValue params; decode params lazily into the concrete type only after routing. No double-parse, no intermediate serde_json::Value on the hot path.

- Every perf-sensitive task adds or updates a divan benchmark. CI fails on a >10% regression against the committed baseline.

- Protocol-neutral core: JSON-RPC envelope/routing, session tracking, and all transports live in protocol-agnostic modules (e.g. domain/jsonrpc, application/session, adapters/_/transport) with no MCP types in their signatures. MCP-specific code lives in mcp/ submodules within each layer (domain/mcp, application/mcp, adapters/_/mcp). Post-MVP protocols (a2a/, acp/) slot in the same way. No new crates per protocol.

- MVP scope is MCP only. Do not implement A2A or ACP before the post-MVP gate. Do not add speculative abstraction for them beyond the protocol-neutral seams above.

- Feature-gate heavy or optional integrations (each transport, oauth, legacy-sse, cli extras) so `default-features = false` builds a lean core. All schema revisions are ALWAYS compiled; they are data, not optional features.

- Cross-platform first: stdio and process spawning must work on Windows, macOS, and Linux; guard Unix-only code with #[cfg(unix)].

- Fail-secure, default deny. AuthContext is a required parameter on every stateful port method. Authorization predicates are pure domain functions.

- Never log tokens, Authorization headers, session IDs in full, or elicitation responses. Redaction happens at the tracing-layer boundary and is tested.

- Public APIs and every handler-owned port trait are rustdoc-complete, with an example for implementors.

- `cargo deny` reads a CACHED advisory database locally, so a green local pass can be missing an advisory that CI — which always fetches fresh — will fail on. Before removing or narrowing an `ignore` entry in deny.toml, re-run `cargo deny --all-features check` WITH network access and confirm the advisory is genuinely gone from the dependency graph, not merely absent from the stale cache. Never suppress an advisory because the local run was green.

- Add `[build.warnings]` to .cargo/config.toml so plain `cargo build` (not just `cargo clippy`) denies warnings — CI runs both. Cargo has warned about linker output by default since 1.97; silence it with `RUSTFLAGS=-A linker-message` only on targets where that output is a known-good signal.

- 1.94-1.98 changed what `cargo l` sees, and two of the changes are silent-behaviour traps. Since 1.94 `dead_code` is inherited by impls from the trait they implement, so a `#![deny(missing_docs)]` on a port trait now propagates to every adapter impl — document every impl item, not just the trait. `ambiguous_glob_imported_traits` (1.95, future-incompat) fires on glob re-exports that mix a module and a same-named trait: never `use module::*` where `module` also defines a trait. `uninhabited_static` (1.96) is deny-by-default. On 1.98 `invalid_runtime_symbol_definitions` is deny-by-default and `suspicious_runtime_symbol_definitions` is warn-by-default; both catch accidental redefinitions of memcmp/memset/strlen and friends in `unsafe extern` blocks.

- 1.98 also has two real traps. `derive(PartialOrd)` now has a fast path that ASSUMES a hand-written `PartialOrd` agrees with a derived `Ord`: for every ordered type (ProtocolVersion, TransportKind, any ordered enum) derive BOTH from the same ordering and add a test proving they agree — an inconsistent pair silently changes comparison results. And `repr(transparent)` no longer treats repr(C) fields, private fields, or `#[non_exhaustive]` types as trivial, so re-check every FFI newtype.

- Before hand-rolling a helper, check whether it was stabilized between 1.86 and 1.98. Use `HashMap::get_disjoint_mut` for several mutable borrows at once (the in-flight request map); `assert_matches!` / `debug_assert_matches!` in tests (they print Debug on failure, which `assert!(matches!(..))` does not); `if let` guards in match arms; `RwLockWriteGuard::downgrade`; `Atomic<T>::from_mut` / `from_mut_slice` / `get_mut_slice`; `Vec::extract_if`; `array_windows`; `strip_circumfix` for prefix+suffix stripping in one call; `str::substr_range` / `<[T]>::subslice_range` / `element_offset` instead of manual index arithmetic; and `core::range::{Range, RangeFrom, RangeInclusive}` (1.95-1.96), which are Copy and IntoIterator and replace the legacy `ops::Range` types in new code.

- On the integer-formatting hot path (JSON-RPC ids, error codes, byte counts) use `core::fmt::NumBuffer` with `<{integer}>::format_into` (1.98) to format into a stack buffer with no allocation. Replace `% n == 0` with `.is_multiple_of(n)`, and hand-written bit-twiddling loops with the 1.97 integer bit ops (`bit_width`, `isolate_highest_one`).

- clap validates arguments, but the typed struct it produces is the contract. Parse once at the adapter boundary into typed value objects (TransportSpec: FromStr), map clap parse errors into domain error types, and never pass a raw String or a raw clap type into domain logic or shared code. Custom validation and secondary parsing return Result — no panic and no exit() inside a handler. anyhow::Context is for user-facing messages only. Test invalid inputs explicitly (malformed, missing, out-of-range) instead of relying on clap's exit codes.

- Every CLI subcommand owes the same two things: a non-interactive form that does one thing and exits, and machine-readable JSON on stdout with the human summary on stderr. A REPL or an interactive prompt is an addition to that, never a replacement — a subcommand that can only be driven by a human at a terminal is unusable by the agent this toolkit exists to serve, which is the larger half of its audience. One serialiser, two sinks: `--json` is the presence or absence of the stderr writer, never a second code path that can drift from the first. When a one-shot call hits a callback it cannot service (elicitation, sampling), return the typed error naming the callback — never block and never answer on the user's behalf. An agent loop that hangs is worse than one that fails.
- A directive the IR does not model is forwarded byte-for-byte, not dropped, and not "helpfully" interpreted. The bridge cannot know whether the peer honoured a directive it does not understand, so it has no loss to record: a DegradeRule here would report a loss the bridge did not observe, which is worse than reporting nothing. Test the forwarding on the wire, not on the parsed IR — an IR-only assertion passes even when the wire form is mangled.
- Conventional commits. Don't force-add files ignored by .gitignore. Never perform in-place shell rewrites like printf '%s' "$(cat f)" > f; use direct edit tools and verify with git diff --stat.

- Use Coraline (coraline\_\* MCP tools) for code navigation when exploring the codebase.

## Testing instructions

- Run `cargo test --workspace --all-features` before committing
- Every new public function needs at least one test
- Fix all test failures before marking a task complete

- Write tests without `.unwrap()`, `.expect()`, `.expect_err()`, or `panic!()`.
  These are the same tools the production rules forbid, and a test that uses
  them cannot tell a failed assertion from a failed fixture. Instead:
  - Return `Result<(), E>` from the test and use `?` where the call is
    fallible. Asserting `text.parse::<ProtocolVersion>() == Ok(expected)` is
    better than parsing then unwrapping, because the failure prints the
    engine's own account of what it refused.
  - When a test module's fallible calls answer unrelated error types, collect
    them in a small `enum Failure` with a `From` impl each, and return
    `Result<(), Failure>`. See `engine.rs` and `registry.rs`.
  - For a hand-rolled poll loop, return `Option<Output>` and assert on that,
    rather than panicking on `Poll::Pending`.
  - Never `assert!(false, ..)` as a stand-in for a panic; `clippy::
assertions_on_constants` rejects it, and it was a panic in disguise.
  - Compare whole `Result`/`Option` values where the type is `PartialEq` and
    its payload is a public field, instead of matching then unwrapping.
- Write tests without panic-prone index slicing either — `&vec[i]`, `&s[0..n]`,
  `arr[0]`, `s[..n]`. A test that indexes to reach the value it is checking
  has built the same trap the production rule forbids, and the fix is the
  same: `.get(i)` / `.get(..n)` with explicit handling, or a pattern that
  cannot be out of range.
  - For a fixed table of cases, iterate rather than index: `for case in cases`
    over a `[(..); N]` array, or `cases.iter().enumerate()` when the position
    is part of the message.
  - For the first element, `slice.first()` and assert on the `Option`, or
    match with `let [first, ..] = slice else { .. }` when the shape is itself
    the claim.
  - `clippy::indexing_slicing` is denied across `--all-targets` the same as
    `unwrap_used`, so a new test index on a runtime value fails the lint with
    no suppression needed. It does **not** fire on a constant index into a
    fixed-size array — `cases[0]` on a `[(..); N]` passes clean — and that is
    exactly the case a test reaches for, so the lint will not catch it for
    you. Iterate instead.
- Do NOT add a `#[expect(clippy::unwrap_used, ...)]` to a test module to make
  the above pass. The `cargo l` alias already runs `-D clippy::unwrap_used
-D clippy::expect_used -D clippy::panic -D clippy::indexing_slicing` across
  `--all-targets`, so a new `.unwrap()` in a test fails the lint with no
  suppression needed — the module attribute only exists to grandfather code
  that predates the rule, and adding one to a new test is how the rule gets
  skipped wholesale rather than obeyed.

## Claude hooks

A `.claude/settings.json` is generated alongside these files. It registers a
`PreCompact` hook that blocks context compression while any task is in the `[~]`
(in-progress) state, preventing the loss of mid-task context.

- Do **not** delete or edit `.claude/settings.json` manually
- The hook exit-code controls: `0` = safe to compact, `1` = blocked

- For object-safe async port traits (`Arc<dyn Trait>` ports used for DI), use `async-trait` (boxed `Pin<Box<dyn Future + Send>>`) instead of native `async fn` in traits. One heap allocation per call is acceptable for HTTP handlers / DB ops; reserve concrete `impl Trait` for hot paths.
- Parse invalid CLI input at adapter boundaries: map clap parse errors to domain error types via `From`/`FromStr`; never let raw `String` from clap cross into domain code. Bin crates use `anyhow::Context` / `with_context` for user-facing messages.
- Prefer `LazyCell` (stable since 1.80) over `LazyLock` in single-threaded contexts. `LazyLock` is for multi-threaded initialisation only — using it thread-locally is overkill and signals a confused ownership model.
- Prefer `#[expect(lint)]` over `#[allow(lint)]` for temporary suppressions: the compiler warns when the suppression becomes unnecessary, so dead attributes don't accumulate. `#[allow]` is reserved for permanent, intentional deviations with a documented reason.
- Web-facing projects default to OWASP Top 10 baseline: fail-secure deny, least-privilege CI/runtime identities, automated SAST (CodeQL) + dependency audit in CI, never use `pull_request_target` for untrusted PRs, never log secrets.
- Rust 1.95+ syntax: prefer match arm `if let` guards for cleaner pattern control flow; use let chains (`if let X = opt && let Ok(y) = x.parse() && y > 0 { ... }`) on 2024 edition codebases.
- Rust 1.87+: use `std::io::pipe()` for in-process piped IO in helper scripts and tests instead of spawning `sh -c`. Use `Vec::extract_if` instead of the nightly `drain_filter`.
- Rust 1.97 soundness: the `pin!` macro deref coercion fix changes how `Pin<Box<T>>` coerces through projections — audit `Pin` usage in async code that previously relied on implicit deref through a pinned projection. Treat as a soundness fix.
- Tight binary crates: add `#[deny(dead_code_pub_in_binary)]` at the bin crate root to catch unused `pub` items that the new warn-by-default lint would otherwise let through.
- Cross-platform first: avoid Unix-only assumptions in tests/tools unless `#[cfg(unix)]`-guarded. Note Windows-specific fixes from 1.97 — `WSAESHUTDOWN` now maps to `BrokenPipe` (was `ConnectionReset`), and `Send`/`Sync` for `std::env::Vars` / `VarsOs` were adjusted.

## Writing style (non-negotiable)

Avoid patterns that reveal AI authorship.

- Avoid slop vocabulary: never use 'robust', 'comprehensive', 'streamlined', 'leverage', 'utilize', 'facilitate', 'innovative', 'cutting-edge', 'pivotal', 'seamless', 'synergistic', 'transformative', 'harness', 'delve', 'embark'.
- Avoid filler phrases: never write 'it's worth noting that', 'at its core', 'let's break this down', 'in order to', 'from a broader perspective', 'a key takeaway is', 'this underscores the importance of'.
- Avoid AI prompt leakage: never include phrases like 'as an AI', 'I cannot help with', 'here's the updated', 'let me explain', 'analysis:'.
- Write naturally: prefer short, direct sentences. Vary sentence length. Use contractions where appropriate. Don't over-explain obvious things.
- Code should speak for itself: prefer meaningful names over comments. Only comment non-obvious decisions, safety invariants, and 'why' explanations.

### Commenting guidelines

- Only comment to explain WHY, not WHAT — the code shows what happens; comments explain non-obvious reasoning.
- Preserve safety/security comments: keep comments containing 'Safety:', 'SAFETY:', 'security', 'invariant', 'caveat', 'trade-off'.

## File structure (non-negotiable)

- Do not create or expand "God" files. Keep each file focused on one primary responsibility.
- If a change introduces a new concern, create a focused module/file instead of extending an unrelated one.
- Avoid catch-all files (`utils`, `helpers`, `common`) containing unrelated logic.
- Keep domain logic, adapters, and orchestration in separate files that mirror the selected architecture.
- If an existing file is already overloaded, prefer extracting cohesive pieces into new files before adding more behavior.

## Workflow

1. Read `IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md` and `PROGRESS.md` to understand current state.
2. Find the next task marked `[ ]` (or `[!]` retry) whose dependencies are all `[x]`.
3. Before committing to it, apply the caller test: **is this on the path a consuming project takes, or on the path an operator takes?** Serving, client connection and capability introspection are the consumer path; the bridge, prober, record/replay and inspector are the operator path. Both are in SCOPE and both are worth doing — but the list is not a ranking, and a session spent making one excellent while the consumer path has a known gap is a session spent on the wrong thing. If the next task is operator-side, check first whether a consumer-side gap is cheaper and more valuable; say so out loud either way.
4. Mark it `[~]` (in-progress) before any code changes.
5. Read the task file `tasks/T{NN}-{slug}.md` for goal, hints, test hints, must-haves, and exit criteria.
6. Implement the task end-to-end. Touch only files within the task's scope.
7. Run preflight. Fix every error and warning until preflight passes.
8. Update `PROGRESS.md`: change `[~]` to `[x]`; append any learnings to "Accumulated Learnings"; update "Codebase State" with what now exists.
9. Commit with a conventional-commits message focused on user impact.
10. Repeat from step 1.

**Complete** — ship root fix end-to-end with tests and docs in the same task. No workarounds; no "follow-up" stubs.

- Conventional commits: `feat:`, `fix:`, `refactor:`, `test:`, `docs:`

## 1. Overview

The user asked me to continue work in the `protocol-droid` Rust repo (an MCP protocol toolkit) on a cleanup task: **delete the dead file `crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/naming.rs`** and fix the latent bugs it was masking, plus add regression tests. Two latent bugs were identified in the live naming code (`emit.rs`): illegal `r#self`/`r#super`/`r#crate` raw identifiers, and the missing `gen` keyword (reserved in Rust 2024).

## 2. History

1. **User request**: "Continue." — continuing a prior session's task. The prior context (from the compaction preamble) was: *"Now I'll make the changes. First, delete the dead file and fix the `RESERVED` list:"* followed by two latent bugs identified: (a) illegal `r#self`/`r#crate` raw identifiers, (b) missing `gen` keyword. User's chosen option was **"delete-and-fix — also fix the two latent bugs (illegal r#self/r#crate, missing gen) and add regression tests."**

2. **Deleted the dead file**:
   - `git rm crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/naming.rs` → success. This file was ~180 lines of an *alternative, unused* naming implementation (trailing-underscore convention: `type_` instead of `r#type`) with its own `#[cfg(test)] mod tests`. It was never wired into `mod.rs` (only `emit` and `schema_model` are `pub mod`s), so it was dead code. Its test module contained valuable test *cases* worth porting (casing splits, MCP property-set collision check) even though the implementation was dead.

3. **Fixed the `RESERVED` list in `emit.rs`** (already done before this segment): added `"gen"` to the `RESERVED` constant.

4. **Added `NOT_RAW_IDENTIFIABLE`** to `emit.rs` — a new constant listing `self`/`super`/`crate` (the three that rustc rejects in raw form) — and rewrote `field_ident` to check it *before* the `RESERVED` branch, emitting a trailing underscore instead of `r#`.
