result.content:
`CrossBridgePeer::new` lost its `downstream_side` parameter. The codec is
  built from a downstream adapter and an upstream adapter, so it knows which
  side it is; a caller that passed the side separately could disagree with
  the codec, and the disagreement would have shown up as a method the bridge
  refused for no visible reason.

### Fixed

- **The A2A leg of the bridge sent the agent arguments it could not read.**
  (`2289b30c`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/a2a_adapter.rs`) An MCP
  `tools/call` carried `arguments` as an object, and the bridge put it on the
  A2A wire inside a data part as `{"data": {"data": {…}}}`. The agent read
  the call's arguments out of the nested object rather than the object
  itself, so a tool that expected `{"query": "weather"}` was handed
  `{"data": {"query": "weather"}}`.

- **The A2A leg of the bridge wrote a `kind` key the spec does not name.**
  (`2289b30c`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/a2a_adapter.rs`) A part was
  written as `{"kind": "data", "data": {…}}`. The spec's part shape is the
  proto's `oneof content`: the object has exactly one of `text`, `file` or
  `data` as a top-level field, with no discriminator. That is what the
  crate's own A2A server sends, what the A2A conformance fixtures expect,
  and what the vendored `a2a.proto` describes — so the bridge was speaking
  a dialect of A2A that the rest of the crate does not speak.

- **A generated union picked its arm by member order.** (`c22bfd84`,
  `crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/emit.rs`) A `tools/call`
  request decoded as an `InitializeRequest`, and a `2026-07-28` result landed
  in the generic `Result` arm. Nothing showed it: every generated type
  carries a flattened catch-all, so a value in the wrong arm re-serialises to
  byte-identical JSON. A union now reads the member the specification
  requires of every alternative — `type`, `method` — and an absent or
  unknown value is a decode error. Where no such member exists the arm is
  chosen by the value's shape, and the specification's order breaks a tie.

- **A schema member named `self`, `super` or `crate` generated a field that
  did not compile.** (`09732f65`,
  `crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/emit.rs`) `field_ident` tried
  the raw-identifier branch first and the trailing-underscore branch second,
  on the same predicate, so the second could never run and `self` came out as
  `r#self`, which rustc rejects. The three now take a trailing underscore,
  `gen` is reserved for edition 2024, and a member that starts with a digit
  gains a leading underscore. No vendored schema has such a member today; the
  next upstream one would have broken the build. An unreferenced 305-line
  `naming.rs` carrying a second, drifted copy of these rules is gone.

- **A bridge session's inbound queue grew without limit, and its errors went
  nowhere.** (`2da5507d`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/adapters/primary/transport/http/bridge.rs`) A
  client could `POST` faster than the upstream answered and the queue took
  all of it. It now holds 256 messages and answers `429` with `Retry-After`
  past that. A session whose loop ended in an error — an upstream that could
  not be reached, a client channel that failed — was dropped by `let _ =`;
  `with_session_report` hands it to the operator, and the `bridge` command
  prints it to stderr.

- **Eight rustdoc links named private or ambiguous items.** (`b7d73634`)
  `cargo doc` failed on the branch, and the lean `--no-default-features`
  build failed because the CLI read a library constant that only exists with
  `http`.

### Tests

- **Every definition of every revision round-trips.** (`fc097e9f`,
  `1828c10f`) The property suite covered 62 of 708 `(revision, definition)`
  pairs; `build.rs` now writes the table from the schemas themselves, so a
  revision that gains a definition gains a case. Field identifiers are
  pinned across all six revisions — no two members of an object collapse to
  one field, and every identifier is legal.

result.content:
## Security model

The library is **default deny**:

- An `AuthContext` is a required parameter on every stateful
  port method. There is no path through the library that does
  not carry one.
- Authorization predicates are pure domain functions. The
  predicate that says "this user can see this resource" lives
  in `domain/`, not in an adapter; the adapter hands it the
  data and applies the answer.
- TLS verification is on by default. A `reqwest` client with
  certificate verification disabled is not constructed; the
  library has no path to do so.
- Path canonicalisation refuses a `..` traversal that escapes
  the allowed root with a typed error, not a panic.
- Tokens, Authorization headers, session ids in full, and
  elicitation responses are redacted at the tracing-layer
  boundary. The test that proves the redaction list is
  complete is `tests/secret_logging.rs`.

The full design, including what the library does *not* do
(token storage, rate limiting, CORS) and what the consumer is
responsible for, is in the
[Security model guide](https://greysquirr3l.github.io/protocol-droid/guides/security/)
on the docs site. The audit that backs the no-finding summary
in this policy is in
[`SECURITY-REVIEW.md`](https://github.com/greysquirr3l/protocol-droid/blob/main/SECURITY-REVIEW.md).

## Coordinated disclosure

A 90-day window is the default. A reporter who needs more time
(an embargoed CVE, a downstream rollout that takes longer than
the patch) names the date in the first message; the maintainer
confirms or counters. An embargo that runs past 180 days is
reviewed at 180 days; a longer embargo is honoured only if the
reporter and the maintainer agree in writing.

A patch lands **before** the advisory is public, and the
advisory text is shared with the reporter for review at least
48 hours before publication. The patch is credited in the
advisory, in the release notes, and in the git history; the
reporter's preferred attribution (name, handle, or anonymous)
is honoured.

## Past advisories

None. The repository's first release was tagged after the

result.content:
`crates/protocol-droid/src/adapters/primary/transport/http/reaper.rs`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/adapters/secondary/clock.rs`) The first sweeps
  idle sessions out of a `SessionStore`, the second is the production
  `Clock` the port never had, and the third tells an operator why a bridge
  session ended. `bridge --idle-timeout <SECONDS>` sets the window.

### Changed

- **An HTTP server evicts a session that has been idle for 30 minutes.**
  (`2da5507d`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/adapters/primary/transport/http/serve/builder.rs`)
  A session used to live until the client sent `DELETE`. A client that opened
  sessions and left cost the server a map entry each time, and a bridge a
  task and an upstream connection each time, with no limit. `HttpBuilder`
  now sweeps by default; `with_idle_reaper` changes the window and
  `without_idle_reaper` restores the old behaviour. A client whose session
  was evicted gets `404` on its next request, which the specification tells
  it to answer by starting a new session — including one that held only a
  standing `GET` stream and sent nothing.

  `HttpBridge::with_idle_reaper` is opt-in, because the bridge is handed its
  store and cannot know what else shares it. It refuses a store built without
  `SessionStore::with_idle_reaper` rather than reaping nothing. The `bridge`
  command turns it on with a 30 minute default and `--idle-timeout 0` turns
  it off. `tokio/time` is now part of the `http` feature.

- **Every feature-matrix row cites the URL that documents it.** (`22cd58bf`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/domain/feature.rs`) 32 rows named a revision,
  12 an SEP number and one a URL, so a reader could follow almost none of
  them. Each row now carries a `citation`, and the same URL is in the doc
  comment on its `Feature` variant, with a test reading the file back to
  hold the two together.

### Changed

- **The cross-protocol bridge is two protocol adapters and one composition,
  not a hand-written translator for every pair of protocols.** (`2289b30c`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/protocol_adapter.rs`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/mcp_adapter.rs`,

  protocol would have needed two more, and the pair nobody wrote about would
  have been the pair nobody tested.

  The translation now lives in per-protocol adapters behind a
  `ProtocolAdapter` seam, and `ComposedCodec` puts two of them together:
  lift on the way out, lower on the way back, with the IR in between. An
  adapter knows one protocol and does not mention the other, so a bridge
  between two protocols nobody wrote a translator for works the same way as
  the one that was.

  The IR gained the types the adapters meet at — `IrCall`, `IrMethod` and
  `IrOutcome` at `crates/protocol-droid/src/domain/ir/call.rs` — and a loss
  that has no counterpart on the other side is now recorded in the
  translation report rather than dropped in silence: an A2A part with no MCP
  counterpart, a task's artifacts, and structured content with no A2A
  counterpart are all reported.

  `CrossBridgePeer::new` lost its `downstream_side` parameter. The codec is
  built from a downstream adapter and an upstream adapter, so it knows which
  side it is; a caller that passed the side separately could disagree with
  the codec, and the disagreement would have shown up as a method the bridge
  refused for no visible reason.

## What the library does not do

- **Token storage.** The `AuthorizationSecrets` port trait
  is the consumer-side seam. `OsSecrets` is one
  implementation (reads from the OS keyring); a consumer
  that wants a different source implements the trait.
- **Choosing the rate limit.** Both HTTP transports enforce one; the
  allowance is the consumer's to set.
- **CORS.** The Streamable HTTP server's CORS configuration
  is a transport-level concern; the library does not
  second-guess it.

## What the consumer is responsible for

- Choosing the `TokenSource` and `TokenEndpoint` adapters
  that match their deployment.
- Setting `Content-Security-Policy`, `Strict-Transport-Security`,
  and `X-Frame-Options` on the HTTP server they wrap around
  the library.
- Wiring the rate limit and request size limit at the
  transport level.

## Threat model

The library is designed against a peer that:

- may send malformed JSON-RPC frames,
- may send a method name the server does not register,
- may send a capability the server did not negotiate,

=== 0.5.1 Security section ===
### Security

- **`webpki-roots` 1.0.9 → 1.0.10** (`24bf997`) — RUSTSEC-2026-0381. The
  bundled root store contained a distrusted emSign intermediate; 1.0.10 removes
  it. [`rustsec`](https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2026-0381)
- **`rustls-webpki` 0.103.15 → 0.103.16** (`24bf997`) — RUSTSEC-2026-0382.
  Certificate verification may have accepted distrusted intermediates.
  [`rustsec`](https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2026-0382)

Both are transitive, reached through `reqwest` on the server and client halves
and `ureq` in `xtask`, so this is a lockfile change with no manifest edit. Both
resolve within the 1.98 MSRV floor.

## [0.5.0] — 2026-10-20

A token's `aud` can now be bound independently of the RFC 9728 resource
identifier, and `aud` is no longer modelled as one. Closes
[#46](https://github.com/greysquirr3l/protocol-droid/issues/46).

### Fixed

- **Every token from Microsoft Entra was refused.** (`deb220d`) `verify`
  compared a token's `aud` only against `policy.resource`, with no way to
  configure anything else. Entra's v2.0 tokens carry the web API's *client ID* —
  a bare GUID — in `aud`, while RFC 9728 §3.1 requires the resource to be the
  HTTPS URL because the metadata path is derived from it. A server fronted by
  Entra therefore refused every valid token with `AudienceMismatch`, silently,
  until its first real request.
- **An `aud` that is not a URI was dropped before it could be compared.**
  (`deb220d`) `aud` was modelled as `ResourceUri`, which requires an http(s)
  scheme, so it could hold neither Entra form — not the bare GUID, and not
  `api://<guid>` either. `with_audience_string` then discarded any entry that
  did not parse, so such a token reached `verify` with an *empty* audience and
  was refused however the policy was configured, reporting a mismatch that
  blamed the token for a decode which had thrown the answer away. RFC 7519 §4.1.3
  defines `aud` as a `StringOrURI` and puts no URI requirement on it.

### Added

- **`TokenPolicy::with_expected_audience` / `with_expected_audiences`,** and the
  matching `OAuthAuthenticator` builders, naming audiences to accept *in
  addition to* the resource. Comparison stays exact equality per identifier — no
  host, prefix or case folding — so a sibling path and a second web API's GUID
  both still fail, and the resource stays accepted so configuring an audience
  never withdraws the RFC 8707 binding. Defaults to `None`, leaving existing
  deployments unchanged.
- **`Audience`** (`deb220d`) — one `aud` entry, held verbatim and never
  canonicalised. Exported from `application::oauth`.

### Changed

- **`TokenClaims::audience` returns `&[Audience]`,** not `&[ResourceUri]`, and
  `with_audience` accepts `impl Into<Audience>`. **This is a breaking change**
  and the reason for the minor bump: RFC 7519 §4.1.3 places no URI requirement
  on `aud`, so `ResourceUri` was the wrong type for it — it could not represent
  the identifiers authorization servers actually mint. `impl Into<Audience>`

---
title: Security model
description: What protocol-droid does to keep a peer on the safe side of the trust boundary, what it does not, and where the consumer's responsibility begins.
---

The library's security model is *default deny*. The auth context
is a required parameter on every stateful port method, and the
authorization predicates are pure domain functions.

## What the library does

- **Token redaction at the tracing boundary.** Tokens,
  Authorization headers, session ids in full, and elicitation
  responses are redacted by the tracing layer. The redaction
  is tested in `tests/secret_logging.rs`.
- **TLS verification on by default.** A `reqwest` client that
  disables certificate verification is not constructed; the
  library has no path to do so.
- **Path canonicalisation for filesystem-backed resources.** A
  resource whose path traverses outside the allowed root is
  refused with a typed error.
- **Fail-secure on auth.** A `?` operator on a failed auth
  check is the default; an `?`-skipped check is not in the
  library.

## Protecting a server, and signing in to one

Both HTTP transports a server offers (Streamable HTTP and the legacy
HTTP+SSE routes) check the `Origin` header and the `Host` header
(the second catches a rebound DNS name, since `Origin` is absent from
every non-browser client), count requests against a per-subject rate
limit before authenticating, and put the same security headers on every
response, including the ones no handler wrote. A request with no
`Host` is refused.

### Requiring a credential on a server

Requiring OAuth is two builders, and the second one is the part that
is easy to leave off. An authenticator answers "is this token valid?";
a policy answers "does this endpoint need one?". The library treats an
authenticator without a policy as the silent fail-open it is, and
`into_router` refuses to build the route table rather than serve the
endpoint unprotected:

> ## [0.8.0] — 2026-11-04

>   the only thing the caller supplies, so everything else comes out of the
>   document that URL served — and the document is not trusted to widen its own

>   registration, defaults to the manual's own protocol type and nothing else,

>   (`964c6a28`, `6b6801f1`, `7ade7487`,
>   `crates/protocol-droid/src/adapters/secondary/acp/`,
>   `crates/protocol-droid/src/domain/acp/`) `serve_acp_agent` reads the
>   editor's requests, routes them to a handler, and writes the replies, with a
>   handler error becoming a JSON-RPC error of the matching code.
>   `send_request` and `send_typed_request` carry the other direction —

accepted but the response is slower. A report of an active exploit
should also carry a phone number in the first message; an
"actively exploited" report that is only on a tracker is read in
working-hours order, not in incident order.

## What is in scope

Anything in the four crates' source that affects a consumer's trust
boundary, the wire surface, or a peer of the library:

- **JSON-RPC envelope routing** — wrong id routing, wrong method
  dispatch, frame framing errors that let a peer smuggle extra
  bytes through a `&RawValue` parse.
- **Wire codec behaviour** — a `tools/call` argument that the
  application refused but the codec accepted, or a result the
  application trusted but the codec lost a field on. The codec
  never silently drops a field; if it appears to, that is a bug.
- **Capability gating** — a `FeatureProfile::is_enabled` answer
  that lets a path run when the negotiated capabilities do not
  cover it. A `list_changed` notification sent to a peer that
  did not advertise `list_changed` is always a bug.
- **Token handling** — redaction failures at the tracing layer
  (the test is `tests/secret_logging.rs`), bearer-token leaks
  in error paths, PKCE verifier leakage, OAuth state
  non-entropy.
- **HTTP transport hardening** — `Origin` allowlist bypass,
  DNS-rebinding via `Host`-header mismatch, request-deadline
  or concurrency-ceiling bypass, missing or wrong rate-limit
  knob.
- **Filesystem-backed resources** — path canonicalisation
  failures, a `..` traversal that escapes the allowed root,
  symlink handling that lets a resource read outside its
  declared scope.
- **Fuzz harness regressions** — the harness in
  `crates/protocol-droid/fuzz/` runs nightly; a found input
  is itself a reproducer and is in scope.
- **Build / supply chain** — a `cargo deny` finding that
  bypasses the CI gate, a vendored schema that drifted from
  the manifest, a transitive dependency that drops a security
  patch.

## How a vulnerability gets found

=== site guide threat model ===

## Threat model

The library is designed against a peer that:

- may send malformed JSON-RPC frames,
- may send a method name the server does not register,
- may send a capability the server did not negotiate,
- may retry an in-flight request id,
- may cancel an unknown or completed request.

The library is *not* designed against a peer that has
compromised the consumer's process. The library's input
parsers are tested against malicious inputs (the fuzz
harness in `crates/protocol-droid/fuzz/` runs nightly), but
a compromised process is the consumer's problem.

:::tip
Read the [architecture overview](/protocol-droid/architecture/overview/) for how the
`AuthContext` requirement and the port-trait returns-DOMAIN-error rule fit
together. The split between "library does" and "consumer does" is the line
that makes the `AuthorizationSecrets` trait a seam, not a check.
:::

## [0.8.0] — 2026-11-04

### Added

- **A UTCP v1.1 client.** (`6cecc9ec`, `f2bf39b6`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/adapters/secondary/utcp/`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/utcp/`) Point it at a provider's URL,
  read the manual it publishes, and call one of the tools in it. The URL is
  the only thing the caller supplies, so everything else comes out of the
  document that URL served — and the document is not trusted to widen its own
  permissions: `allowed_communication_protocols` is taken from the caller's
  registration, defaults to the manual's own protocol type and nothing else,
  and is applied at registration and again before every call. Behind the
  `utcp` feature.

- **An ACP agent can be served over stdio, and can call the editor back.**
  (`964c6a28`, `6b6801f1`, `7ade7487`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/adapters/secondary/acp/`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/domain/acp/`) `serve_acp_agent` reads the
  editor's requests, routes them to a handler, and writes the replies, with a
  handler error becoming a JSON-RPC error of the matching code.
  `send_request` and `send_typed_request` carry the other direction —
  `session/request_permission`, `fs/read_text_file`, `terminal/create` — and
  `authenticate`, `session/set_mode` and `session/set_config_option` are now
  typed, which leaves all twelve agent request methods typed. Behind
  `acp-experimental`, because the ACP specification is pre-1.0.

- **`IdleReaper`, `MonotonicClock` and `SessionReport`.** (`2da5507d`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/adapters/primary/transport/http/reaper.rs`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/adapters/secondary/clock.rs`) The first sweeps
  idle sessions out of a `SessionStore`, the second is the production
  `Clock` the port never had, and the third tells an operator why a bridge
  session ended. `bridge --idle-timeout <SECONDS>` sets the window.

### Changed

- **An HTTP server evicts a session that has been idle for 30 minutes.**
  (`2da5507d`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/adapters/primary/transport/http/serve/builder.rs`)

=== 0.5.3: does Fixed overlap with Security? ===
### Fixed

- **The `#[server]` macro no longer needs the consumer to depend on
  `schemars`.** (`dbea59a3`, #63) A consumer of `protocol-droid` that used
  `#[server]` / `#[tool]` had to add `schemars` to its own `Cargo.toml` to
  make the generated code compile, and the error pointed at the `#[server]`
  attribute rather than at the macro.

  The generated argument struct derives `JsonSchema` through this crate's
  re-export, but the derive expands to unqualified `schemars::…` paths that
  resolve against the *consuming* crate's root. `schemars` 1.x honours the
  derive's `crate` attribute — it emits `use <path> as schemars;` inside the
  `const _` block it wraps the expansion in, shadowing the unresolved name
  for every path it expands to, including the `where`-clause bounds — so one
  attribute per generated struct fixes it.

  The regression test lives in `crates/protocol-droid-cli/tests/` because
  that crate is the workspace's one consumer of `protocol-droid` that does
  *not* depend on `schemars`. Every test inside `protocol-droid` is blind to
  this: that crate depends on `schemars` itself, so it is in the extern
  prelude of its own tests whatever the expansion does. The test also reads
  the generated `inputSchema` back out of the registry, so a redirect
  pointing at the wrong crate fails there rather than passing a compile
  check.

### Documentation

- **`docs/benchmarks.md` described a CI bench job that does not exist.**
  (`c69b77ac`, `docs/benchmarks.md`) The document described a job that runs the divan
  benches and compares their medians against `baselines.json` with a 10 %
  threshold in either direction. There is no such job, and `baselines.json`
  is read by nothing but the documentation. The document now says what is
  actually there: the `bench_gate` smoke test is the automated performance
  gate, and the committed baselines are reference data for a human reading a
  bench run.

Author: Nick Campbell <ncampbell@smartofficesinc.com>

    fix: a session now reports the revision it negotiated, not the transport's ceiling (#76)
    
    `PeerSession::negotiated` is documented as "the revision this session
    actually settled on", and it answered with the ceiling — the newest
    revision the build could speak — whatever the peer asked for. The
    handshake narrowed the session's *profile* and left its *revision* alone,
    so the version `negotiate` had already resolved was used to build the
    reply and then dropped.
    
    Every consumer of `negotiated()` was written expecting the negotiated
    revision. The router's docs say the `MCP-Protocol-Version` header is
    compared "against the revision the session negotiated", and the domain
    module says a header that disagrees with the negotiated version is a
    protocol error. The code was right and the value was wrong.
    
    ## What a peer could hit
    
    A handler could not learn what it was speaking, so a consumer that wanted
    to report its own version had to report a range of revisions rather than
    the one in use. The crate's own `stdio_server` example has a tool that
    reports the negotiated revision, and it reported the ceiling to every
    peer.

    its own codec, so a `2024-11-05` peer was sent `2025-11-25` shapes: a

  Authorization headers, session ids in full, and elicitation

=== 'Two gaps' and the actual gap paragraphs in v0.8.0 ===

Two gaps are worth stating plainly rather than leaving to be discovered:

**Every committed lockfile now gets a CI-side advisory watch.** Until the
`supply chain` job was extended, it scanned the root lockfile only.
`crates/protocol-droid/fuzz/`, `crates/protocol-droid/tests/interop_rmcp/`
and `crates/protocol-droid/tests/interop_ts_sdk/` are excluded from the
workspace, so `cargo deny` never saw their dependency graphs; the pre-push
hook covered them locally, which is a mitigation, not equivalent coverage.

The job now scans all four, one step per lockfile, and each of those
steps passes `--locked`. Without `--locked`, `cargo metadata` re-resolves
the graph and rewrites the lockfile on disk, so the scan would report on
a dependency set nobody committed — a different check, not a stricter
one. With `--locked`, the scan reports on the lockfile as committed, and
fails loudly when that lockfile is stale.

That gap was not theoretical. When `ctutils` was bumped to 0.4.5 for
RUSTSEC-2026-0385, the root `Cargo.lock` was updated and the interop
fixture's was not, so the fixture kept `ctutils 0.4.3` until the pre-push
hook blocked the push. The hook was the only thing that saw it, and the
lockfile it caught was stale on more than the advisory: it still pinned
`protocol-droid 0.1.0` against a workspace at 0.5.2.

The `interop_ts_sdk` fixture is the one case where a manifest *is* watched:
Dependabot's security updates reach it, and it is declared in
`dependabot.yml` so a transitive advisory gets a bump proposal rather than
sitting unnoticed. Note that `npm install` honours the committed lockfile,
so it will not self-heal — the lockfile has to be updated on purpose. The
other two are Rust, and are now covered by CI as well as by the hook.

**The site is built in CI, but the peer-range gap is still worth knowing.**
The `site` job installs with `--frozen-lockfile`, runs `astro check` and
`astro build`, and asserts the output has the expected shape, so a change
under `site/` that does not build fails the PR rather than passing every
check. It was not always so: Dependabot's astro 5 → 7 PR passed fourteen green
Rust checks without building, because starlight 0.30 pins `astro: ^5.0.0` and
`pnpm install` does not enforce peer ranges — the failure appears only at
build time. `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` does not change that; it
enforces the *lockfile*, not the peer ranges.

`deny.toml` is the single list of accepted advisories, and it is the same
list the `pre-push` hook reads. A waiver belongs there with a reason saying
why the advisory is unreachable from this code; there is no second place to
record one.

- **The consumer's deployment.** A consumer that disables TLS

=== what 65c3f9a7 added to CHANGELOG.md ===
+++ b/CHANGELOG.md
+### Fixed
+
+- **A session reported the transport's ceiling instead of the revision it
+  negotiated.** (`crates/protocol-droid/src/application/server/dispatch/mod.rs`,
+  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/server/context.rs`) `PeerSession::negotiated`
+  is documented as "the revision this session actually settled on", and it
+  answered with the ceiling — the newest revision the build could speak —
+  whatever the peer asked for. The handshake narrowed the session's *profile*
+  and left its *revision* alone, so the version that `negotiate` had already
+  resolved was used to build the reply and then dropped.
+
+  A handler could not learn which revision it was speaking, so a consumer
+  that wanted to report its own version had to report a range of revisions
+  rather than the one in use. The gate's refusal named the ceiling too, and
+  the refusal exists precisely to say what was negotiated: "elicitation is
+  unavailable" is an answer nobody can act on without knowing what *was*
+  agreed.
+
+  The fix narrows the revision with the profile, in the same place the
+  profile was already narrowed. The two move together because the profile is
+  resolved *for* the revision: the profile says which features exist, and the
+  revision says how to spell them, so a session that knew one but not the
+  other refused the features the older revision does not have and still
+  answered in the newer revision's shape for everything else.
+
+  The shape is not a detail. A tool result is lowered for the session's
+  revision, and each revision has its own codec, so a `2024-11-05` peer was
+  sent results spelled for `2025-11-25` — a `structuredContent` its schema
+  has no field for, and content blocks such as `audio` that its schema has

=== origin/main CHANGELOG lines 73-106 (the second Changed block) ===
### Changed

- **The cross-protocol bridge is two protocol adapters and one composition,
  not a hand-written translator for every pair of protocols.** (`2289b30c`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/protocol_adapter.rs`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/mcp_adapter.rs`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/a2a_adapter.rs`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/composed.rs`) The MCP ↔ A2A
  translation was a pair of functions that knew both vocabularies — one that
  turned `SendMessage` into `tools/call`, one that turned it back. A third
  protocol would have needed two more, and the pair nobody wrote about would
  have been the pair nobody tested.

  The translation now lives in per-protocol adapters behind a
  `ProtocolAdapter` seam, and `ComposedCodec` puts two of them together:
  lift on the way out, lower on the way back, with the IR in between. An
  adapter knows one protocol and does not mention the other, so a bridge
  between two protocols nobody wrote a translator for works the same way as
  the one that was.

  The IR gained the types the adapters meet at — `IrCall`, `IrMethod` and
  `IrOutcome` at `crates/protocol-droid/src/domain/ir/call.rs` — and a loss
  that has no counterpart on the other side is now recorded in the
  translation report rather than dropped in silence: an A2A part with no MCP
  counterpart, a task's artifacts, and structured content with no A2A
  counterpart are all reported.

  `CrossBridgePeer::new` lost its `downstream_side` parameter. The codec is
  built from a downstream adapter and an upstream adapter, so it knows which
  side it is; a caller that passed the side separately could disagree with
  the codec, and the disagreement would have shown up as a method the bridge
  refused for no visible reason.

### Fixed

## What is in scope

Anything in the four crates' source that affects a consumer's trust
boundary, the wire surface, or a peer of the library:

- **JSON-RPC envelope routing** — wrong id routing, wrong method
  dispatch, frame framing errors that let a peer smuggle extra
  bytes through a `&RawValue` parse.
- **Wire codec behaviour** — a `tools/call` argument that the
  application refused but the codec accepted, or a result the
  application trusted but the codec lost a field on. The codec
  never silently drops a field; if it appears to, that is a bug.
- **Capability gating** — a `FeatureProfile::is_enabled` answer
  that lets a path run when the negotiated capabilities do not
  cover it. A `list_changed` notification sent to a peer that
  did not advertise `list_changed` is always a bug.
- **Token handling** — redaction failures at the tracing layer
  (the test is `tests/secret_logging.rs`), bearer-token leaks
  in error paths, PKCE verifier leakage, OAuth state
  non-entropy.
- **HTTP transport hardening** — `Origin` allowlist bypass,
  DNS-rebinding via `Host`-header mismatch, request-deadline
  or concurrency-ceiling bypass, missing or wrong rate-limit
  knob.
- **Filesystem-backed resources** — path canonicalisation
  failures, a `..` traversal that escapes the allowed root,
  symlink handling that lets a resource read outside its
  declared scope.
- **Fuzz harness regressions** — the harness in
  `crates/protocol-droid/fuzz/` runs nightly; a found input
  is itself a reproducer and is in scope.
- **Build / supply chain** — a `cargo deny` finding that
  bypasses the CI gate, a vendored schema that drifted from
  the manifest, a transitive dependency that drops a security
  patch.

Session: `00ecf7f2-acba-4582-a148-8d4c26efc71b`
Repo: `/Users/ncampbell/Projects/rust/protocol-droid` (branch unknown — check `git status`)

---

## 1. Where the work came from

An earlier review of the schema generator raised three gaps:

1. **Union discrimination is hard-coded.** The generator dispatches union arms on a
   fixed `type` property. The reviewer's point: the discriminator should be
   *discovered* — look for a property common to every member whose value is a
   distinct `const`. Where no member pins a const (2026-07-28's `resultType` is
   free-form), the untagged fallback is unsafe unless the generic `Result` member
   sorts most-specific-first, or the build fails rather than emitting a union
   that silently mis-assigns.
2. **Feature-matrix citations.** 39 variants: 32 cite a revision, 12 an SEP number,
   **1 a URL**. `AGENTS.md` requires "a doc comment with the URL".
   `every_row_is_cited_and_ordered` (`domain/mcp/feature.rs:1184`) only checks the
   revision is known and ordered — the name over-promises.
3. **Verification coverage was 9%.** The property suite covered 62 of 708
   (revision, definition) pairs; the arm-level test covered 5 of 65 tagged unions.

**Gaps 2 and 3 are DONE** (see the commit list in §2). Gap 1 was partially addressed
by `c22bfd84` (tag dispatch), and the *residual* bug class it documents turned out
to be the naming layer, which is what this segment is about.

## 2. Commits already landed (relevant, recent)

```
fc097e9f test(schema): round-trip every definition of every revision   <- closes gap 3
22cd58bf feat(feature): cite every matrix row with the URL that documents it  <- closes gap 2
c22bfd84 fix(schema): dispatch union arms on the member that tells them apart  <- gap 1, partial
9b437d9b style: apply rustfmt to the ACP modules
```

So the *naming* work below is a cleanup that fell out of gap 1's aftermath, not a
gap-1 deliverable.

## 3. What this segment actually did

### 3.1 Deleted dead code

`crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/naming.rs` (305 lines) — **deleted, staged**.

It was a *parallel* naming implementation: its own `RUST_KEYWORDS` list, its own
`words()` / `push_camel_words()` / `field_ident()`, and its own `#[cfg(test)] mod tests`.
It had **zero callers** — `generator/mod.rs` declares only `pub mod emit;` and
`pub mod schema_model;`. It survived in the tree because `build.rs` `#[path]`-includes
`emit.rs` and `schema_model.rs`, so the file compiled without ever being wired to
anything.

Its naming rules had *drifted* from the live ones in `emit.rs` (it used the
trailing-underscore convention universally; the live code uses `r#` for keywords).
Two live bugs were hiding behind the dead file:

### 3.2 Bug #1 — `r#self` / `r#super` / `r#crate` are compile errors

**The dead branch.** The original `field_ident` was:

```rust
if RESERVED.iter().any(|r| *r == snake) {
    format!("r#{snake}")          // <-- fires for "self"/"super"/"crate"
} else if is_keyword(&snake) {
    format!("{snake}_")           // <-- UNREACHABLE
}
```

`is_keyword(name)` is `RESERVED.contains(&name)` — the *same predicate* as the first
branch. The `else if` could never run, so the trailing-underscore fallback existed in
source but never executed. Every keyword therefore became `r#word`, and four of those
are not legal Rust:

> rustc rejects raw-identifier syntax for exactly four words: `self`, `Self`, `super`,
> `crate`. `r#self` is not an identifier. Neither is bare `self` as a field name.

**The fix** (`emit.rs`, `field_ident`): check a new `NOT_RAW_IDENTIFIABLE` list
*first* → `{snake}_`; then `RESERVED` → `r#{snake}`; then the pre-existing
leading-underscore trim; else bare `snake`.

```rust
const NOT_RAW_IDENTIFIABLE: &[&str] = &["self", "super", "crate"];
```

The list is matched against the *lowercased snake* form, so a member named `Self`
arrives as `self` and is covered by that one entry — no separate `"Self"` needed.

### 3.2b Bug #3 (found late, during primer verification) — digit-leading member names

**Not yet fixed.** Found while verifying the primer's claims; recording it here because
it is the same bug class and it is *not* covered by the two fixes above.

`field_ident` output is used directly as the Rust field name (`emit.rs:1184-1199`
writes `pub {field}: {ty}`), and `to_snake` does **not** guard a leading digit:

```
to_snake("2fa")    -> "2fa"
field_ident("2fa") -> "2fa"      // ILLEGAL — `pub 2fa: u8` does not compile
```

Verified with rustc, edition 2024:

```
error: expected identifier, found `2fa`
help: identifiers cannot start with a number
```

`pub _2fa: u8` compiles fine. Note the asymmetry: `type_ident` *does* guard this
(`if i == 0 && ch.is_ascii_digit() { out.push('_') }`, `emit.rs:1467-1470`) — only the
*field* path is unguarded.

**Why the dead file mattered here.** `naming.rs`'s `field_ident` produced `_2fa`
(trailing-underscore convention with a leading-underscore guard). The live
implementation regressed to bare `2fa`. So deleting the dead file did not cause this,
but the dead file was the only place the case was handled — and it had a test for it
(`field_ident("2fa") == "_2fa"`).

// A member name may start with a digit — upstream's `"2fa"` does. Rust
    // identifiers may not, so the field gains a leading underscore and keeps
    // the serde rename back to the wire name.
    format!("_{snake}")
}
```

Order matters: this check must come **before** the leading-underscore-trim branch
(which would otherwise strip the very underscore that makes it legal), and after the
`RESERVED` / `NOT_RAW_IDENTIFIABLE` branches.

### 3.3 Bug #2 — `gen` was missing from `RESERVED`

Rust 2024 (this crate's edition) reserves `gen`. It is *not* a strict keyword, but it
cannot be used as an identifier at all: `type gen = u8;` and `struct gen;` both fail to
compile in edition 2024, while `type gen_ = u8;` compiles. The old `RESERVED` list had
no `gen`, so a schema member named `gen` would have emitted a bare `gen` field.

**The fix:** added `"gen"` to `RESERVED`. It now maps to `r#gen` (which *is* legal —
verified).

Note: `union` was already in `RESERVED` and is not actually reserved in 2024. It was
left in place deliberately — a plausible MCP member name, and reserving it costs
nothing. The doc comment on `RESERVED` now says so explicitly.

### 3.4 Verification sweep (all rustc/clippy-verified, not eyeballed)

- rustc keyword matrix: exactly 4 words (`crate`, `self`, `Self`, `super`) are neither
  bare-legal nor raw-legal; every other reserved word works as `r#word`.
- `r#union`, `r#typeof`, `r#become`, `r#gen`, `r#try`, `r#box` all compile.
- Real clippy run on candidate identifiers: `pub _meta: u8` trips
  `clippy::pub_underscore_fields` — this confirms the existing leading-underscore

=== 0.8.0 Changed section #1 (absolute lines 46-72) ===
### Changed

- **An HTTP server evicts a session that has been idle for 30 minutes.**
  (`2da5507d`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/adapters/primary/transport/http/serve/builder.rs`)
  A session used to live until the client sent `DELETE`. A client that opened
  sessions and left cost the server a map entry each time, and a bridge a
  task and an upstream connection each time, with no limit. `HttpBuilder`
  now sweeps by default; `with_idle_reaper` changes the window and
  `without_idle_reaper` restores the old behaviour. A client whose session
  was evicted gets `404` on its next request, which the specification tells
  it to answer by starting a new session — including one that held only a
  standing `GET` stream and sent nothing.

  `HttpBridge::with_idle_reaper` is opt-in, because the bridge is handed its
  store and cannot know what else shares it. It refuses a store built without
  `SessionStore::with_idle_reaper` rather than reaping nothing. The `bridge`
  command turns it on with a 30 minute default and `--idle-timeout 0` turns
  it off. `tokio/time` is now part of the `http` feature.

- **Every feature-matrix row cites the URL that documents it.** (`22cd58bf`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/domain/feature.rs`) 32 rows named a revision,
  12 an SEP number and one a URL, so a reader could follow almost none of
  them. Each row now carries a `citation`, and the same URL is in the doc
  comment on its `Feature` variant, with a test reading the file back to
  hold the two together.

=== site guide: What the library does ===

`with_resource_metadata` mounts the document on the MCP router and
points the `401` challenge at that same URL, both read from one value, so
the challenge cannot name a document that is not being served. The
document route deliberately skips the authenticator — the escape route
cannot require the credential it explains how to obtain — but it still
passes the same `Host` and rate-limit checks as every other route.

A single-issuer deployment should also name the issuer, which is off by
default because RFC 9728 publishes a *list* of trusted authorization
servers:

```rust
let authenticator = authenticator.with_expected_issuer("https://login.example.com");
```

On the client side, the OAuth flow:

- refuses a server whose metadata describes a different resource,
- refuses an authorization server that does not advertise PKCE `S256`,
- sends `resource` as the metadata published it and checks `iss` on the
  response,
- never takes a client id from one authorization server to another,
- only opens web URLs in the browser, and receives the redirect on
  `127.0.0.1`,
- gives up after three refusals instead of asking a person forever.

A client registered ahead of time is named through
`PROTOCOL_DROID_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` and `PROTOCOL_DROID_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET`
in the CLI, never a flag, so a secret does not reach shell history or a
process listing.

## What the library does not do

- **Token storage.** The `AuthorizationSecrets` port trait
  is the consumer-side seam. `OsSecrets` is one
  implementation (reads from the OS keyring); a consumer
  that wants a different source implements the trait.
- **Choosing the rate limit.** Both HTTP transports enforce one; the
  allowance is the consumer's to set.
- **CORS.** The Streamable HTTP server's CORS configuration
  is a transport-level concern; the library does not
  second-guess it.

10:## What the library does
11-
12-- **Token redaction at the tracing boundary.** Tokens,
13-  Authorization headers, session ids in full, and elicitation
14-  responses are redacted by the tracing layer. The redaction
15-  is tested in `tests/secret_logging.rs`.
16-- **TLS verification on by default.** A `reqwest` client that
17-  disables certificate verification is not constructed; the
18-  library has no path to do so.
19-- **Path canonicalisation for filesystem-backed resources.** A
20-  resource whose path traverses outside the allowed root is
21-  refused with a typed error.
22-- **Fail-secure on auth.** A `?` operator on a failed auth
23-  check is the default; an `?`-skipped check is not in the
24-  library.
25-
26-## Protecting a server, and signing in to one
27-
28-Both HTTP transports a server offers (Streamable HTTP and the legacy
29-HTTP+SSE routes) check the `Origin` header and the `Host` header
30-(the second catches a rebound DNS name, since `Origin` is absent from
31-every non-browser client), count requests against a per-subject rate
32-limit before authenticating, and put the same security headers on every
33-response, including the ones no handler wrote. A request with no
34-`Host` is refused.
35-
36-### Requiring a credential on a server
37-
38-Requiring OAuth is two builders, and the second one is the part that
39-is easy to leave off. An authenticator answers "is this token valid?";
40-a policy answers "does this endpoint need one?". The library treats an
41-authenticator without a policy as the silent fail-open it is, and
42-`into_router` refuses to build the route table rather than serve the
43-endpoint unprotected:

# Security Policy

## Supported versions

`protocol-droid` is published as four crates (`protocol-droid-schema`,
`protocol-droid`, `protocol-droid-macros`, `protocol-droid-cli`) on
crates.io. Security advisories are issued against the latest released
minor version; the previous minor receives advisories for **30 days**
after a new minor ships. The `main` branch is built and tested on
every push; advisories against `main` only are evaluated case by case
because the work to backport a fix is small but a backport is not
guaranteed to be free of merge conflicts on the older minor.

| Crate                    | Latest stable | Previous minor |
| ------------------------ | ------------- | -------------- |
| `protocol-droid-schema`  | `0.7`         | `0.6`          |
| `protocol-droid`         | `0.7`         | `0.6`          |
| `protocol-droid-macros`  | `0.7`         | `0.6`          |
| `protocol-droid-cli`     | `0.7`         | `0.6`          |

=== SECURITY.md 'Security model' section ===
## Security model

The library is **default deny**:

- An `AuthContext` is a required parameter on every stateful
  port method. There is no path through the library that does
  not carry one.
- Authorization predicates are pure domain functions. The
  predicate that says "this user can see this resource" lives
  in `domain/`, not in an adapter; the adapter hands it the
  data and applies the answer.
- TLS verification is on by default. A `reqwest` client with
  certificate verification disabled is not constructed; the
  library has no path to do so.
- Path canonicalisation refuses a `..` traversal that escapes
  the allowed root with a typed error, not a panic.
- Tokens, Authorization headers, session ids in full, and
  elicitation responses are redacted at the tracing-layer
  boundary. The test that proves the redaction list is
  complete is `tests/secret_logging.rs`.

The full design, including what the library does *not* do
(token storage, rate limiting, CORS) and what the consumer is
responsible for, is in the
[Security model guide](https://greysquirr3l.github.io/protocol-droid/guides/security/)
on the docs site. The audit that backs the no-finding summary
in this policy is in
[`SECURITY-REVIEW.md`](https://github.com/greysquirr3l/protocol-droid/blob/main/SECURITY-REVIEW.md).

## Coordinated disclosure

A 90-day window is the default. A reporter who needs more time
(an embargoed CVE, a downstream rollout that takes longer than
the patch) names the date in the first message; the maintainer
confirms or counters. An embargo that runs past 180 days is
reviewed at 180 days; a longer embargo is honoured only if the
reporter and the maintainer agree in writing.

A patch lands **before** the advisory is public, and the
advisory text is shared with the reporter for review at least
48 hours before publication. The patch is credited in the
advisory, in the release notes, and in the git history; the
reporter's preferred attribution (name, handle, or anonymous)
is honoured.

None. The repository's first release was tagged after the

=== codeql.yml ===
name: CodeQL

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
  schedule:
    # Weekly, off the hour, so the run does not pile onto the top-of-hour rush
    # that every other scheduled workflow shares.
    - cron: "17 4 * * 1"
  workflow_dispatch:

# The CodeQL analysis needs to write its results; nothing else in this workflow
# needs any write access.
permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  analyze:
    name: analyze (rust)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      security-events: write
      packages: read
      actions: read
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - name: Initialize CodeQL
        uses: github/codeql-action/init@v4
        with:
          languages: rust
          queries: security-and-quality
      # For Rust, CodeQL builds the project to capture the source. The pinned
      # toolchain in rust-toolchain.toml is what gets used.
      - name: Autobuild
        uses: github/codeql-action/autobuild@v4
      - name: Analyze
        uses: github/codeql-action/analyze@v4
        with:
          category: "/language:rust"

## What is in scope

Anything in the four crates' source that affects a consumer's trust
boundary, the wire surface, or a peer of the library:

- **JSON-RPC envelope routing** — wrong id routing, wrong method
  dispatch, frame framing errors that let a peer smuggle extra
  bytes through a `&RawValue` parse.
- **Wire codec behaviour** — a `tools/call` argument that the
  application refused but the codec accepted, or a result the
  application trusted but the codec lost a field on. The codec
  never silently drops a field; if it appears to, that is a bug.
- **Capability gating** — a `FeatureProfile::is_enabled` answer
  that lets a path run when the negotiated capabilities do not
  cover it. A `list_changed` notification sent to a peer that
  did not advertise `list_changed` is always a bug.
- **Token handling** — redaction failures at the tracing layer
  (the test is `tests/secret_logging.rs`), bearer-token leaks
  in error paths, PKCE verifier leakage, OAuth state
  non-entropy.
- **HTTP transport hardening** — `Origin` allowlist bypass,
  DNS-rebinding via `Host`-header mismatch, request-deadline
  or concurrency-ceiling bypass, missing or wrong rate-limit
  knob.
- **Filesystem-backed resources** — path canonicalisation
  failures, a `..` traversal that escapes the allowed root,
  symlink handling that lets a resource read outside its
  declared scope.
- **Fuzz harness regressions** — the harness in
  `crates/protocol-droid/fuzz/` runs nightly; a found input
  is itself a reproducer and is in scope.
- **Build / supply chain** — a `cargo deny` finding that
  bypasses the CI gate, a vendored schema that drifted from
  the manifest, a transitive dependency that drops a security
  patch.

## How a vulnerability gets found

A report is the best route and not the only one. Three things run without
anyone looking:

| Where | What it checks | Coverage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `supply chain` CI job | `cargo deny` against a freshly fetched advisory database | all four committed lockfiles |
| Dependabot alerts | advisory database against every manifest | root, `site/`, and the interop fixture |
| Secret scanning | credential patterns across the history and every push | whole repository |
| `pre-push` hook | `cargo audit` over every committed lockfile | all four, including the three outside the workspace |

Two gaps are worth stating plainly rather than leaving to be discovered:

**Every committed lockfile now gets a CI-side advisory watch.** Until the
`supply chain` job was extended, it scanned the root lockfile only.
`crates/protocol-droid/fuzz/`, `crates/protocol-droid/tests/interop_rmcp/`
and `crates/protocol-droid/tests/interop_ts_sdk/` are excluded from the
workspace, so `cargo deny` never saw their dependency graphs; the pre-push
hook covered them locally, which is a mitigation, not equivalent coverage.

The job now scans all four, one step per lockfile, and each of those
steps passes `--locked`. Without `--locked`, `cargo metadata` re-resolves
the graph and rewrites the lockfile on disk, so the scan would report on
a dependency set nobody committed — a different check, not a stricter
one. With `--locked`, the scan reports on the lockfile as committed, and
fails loudly when that lockfile is stale.

That gap was not theoretical. When `ctutils` was bumped to 0.4.5 for
RUSTSEC-2026-0385, the root `Cargo.lock` was updated and the interop
fixture's was not, so the fixture kept `ctutils 0.4.3` until the pre-push
hook blocked the push. The hook was the only thing that saw it, and the
lockfile it caught was stale on more than the advisory: it still pinned
`protocol-droid 0.1.0` against a workspace at 0.5.2.

The `interop_ts_sdk` fixture is the one case where a manifest *is* watched:
Dependabot's security updates reach it, and it is declared in
`dependabot.yml` so a transitive advisory gets a bump proposal rather than
sitting unnoticed. Note that `npm install` honours the committed lockfile,
so it will not self-heal — the lockfile has to be updated on purpose. The
other two are Rust, and are now covered by CI as well as by the hook.

**The site is built in CI, but the peer-range gap is still worth knowing.**
The `site` job installs with `--frozen-lockfile`, runs `astro check` and
`astro build`, and asserts the output has the expected shape, so a change
under `site/` that does not build fails the PR rather than passing every
check. It was not always so: Dependabot's astro 5 → 7 PR passed fourteen green
Rust checks without building, because starlight 0.30 pins `astro: ^5.0.0` and
`pnpm install` does not enforce peer ranges — the failure appears only at
build time. `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` does not change that; it
enforces the *lockfile*, not the peer ranges.

`deny.toml` is the single list of accepted advisories, and it is the same
list the `pre-push` hook reads. A waiver belongs there with a reason saying
why the advisory is unreachable from this code; there is no second place to
record one.

## What is out of scope

- **The consumer's deployment.** A consumer that disables TLS

=== 5f8849e7 content (OSSF Scorecard posture) ===
+++ b/docs/dev/repo-operations.md
+    - [The OSSF Scorecard posture](#the-ossf-scorecard-posture)
+    - [The two-account review pattern](#the-two-account-review-pattern)
+| Status checks           | 10, strict  | See below                                 |
+### The OSSF Scorecard posture
+
+The [OpenSSF Scorecard](https://scorecard.dev/viewer/?uri=github.com/greysquirr3l/protocol-droid)
+is the closest thing to an outside audit this repository has, and the score it
+reports is mostly a consequence of the settings above rather than of anything
+in the tree. There is no `scorecard.yml` workflow in `.github/workflows/`, so
+nothing here is currently *reported* by the service — the scores below are
+what the service would compute if the workflow were added, checked by hand
+against the API on 2026-10-30.
+
+| Check | State | Notes |
+| ----- | ----- | ----- |
+| Branch-Protection | pass | 10 required contexts, strict, `enforce_admins` on, 1 approving review, conversation resolution required, no force-push |
+| CI-Tests | pass | `ci.yml` runs the full matrix on every PR, plus conformance, interop and CodeQL |
+| Code-Review | **partial** | Every merged PR carries an approving review, but none carries an **inline** review comment — and the Scorecard's `Code-Review` check looks for the latter. See below |
+| Signed-Releases | **partial** | Every tag is annotated, but none is GPG- or Sigstore-signed. See below |
+| Token-Permissions | pass | Every workflow declares a narrow `permissions:` block |
+| Dependency-Update-Tool | pass | Dependabot is on and opened five update PRs; their content was landed on `release/0.6.1` and the PRs were closed rather than merged, to avoid duplicating the commits |
+| Security-Policy | pass | `SECURITY.md` exists and names the supported versions |
+| Pinned-Dependencies | **partial** | Rust dependencies are pinned by `Cargo.lock`, but the Actions are pinned to a **tag**, not a SHA. See below |
+| SAST | pass | CodeQL runs on every push |
+| Fuzzing | pass | `cargo-fuzz` targets are in the tree and fuzz is a CI job |
+| Packaging | pass | Published to crates.io with `cargo publish` |
+| Maintained | **partial** | One maintainer, though the commit history is active: 420 commits in the last 90 days |
+| Contributors | partial | One human contributor, under three email identities, plus `dependabot[bot]` |
+
+Four of those are worth being honest about rather than leaving to a badge.
+
+**The reviews are approvals, not review comments.** Every merged pull request
+carries an approving review from the other account, and the branch protection
+requires one — but none of them carries an **inline** comment on the diff.
+The Scorecard's `Code-Review` check looks for review comments specifically,
+because an approval with no comment says that somebody looked, not what they
+thought. The `Pull-Request-Review` check passes on the same evidence. This
+is a property of the workflow rather than a policy: the reviews are written
+to be substantive in the body, and the Scorecard reads the other place.
+
+**The tags are not signed.** `auto-tag.yml` creates an annotated tag and
+`release.yml` creates the GitHub Release, but neither signs them — the tag
+object carries a `tagger` and a message and no signature block. The
+`Signed-Releases` check looks for a signature, so it scores partial or worse
+depending on how many releases it samples. Fixing it means giving the
+release workflow a signing key, which is a credential in a GitHub secret and
+therefore a decision with its own risk: a key that can sign releases is a key
+that can be used to impersonate one. It is not a change to make casually.
+

  `crates/protocol-droid/src/adapters/primary/transport/http/reaper.rs`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/adapters/secondary/clock.rs`) The first sweeps
  idle sessions out of a `SessionStore`, the second is the production

  session ended. `bridge --idle-timeout <SECONDS>` sets the window.

### Changed

- **An HTTP server evicts a session that has been idle for 30 minutes.**
  (`2da5507d`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/adapters/primary/transport/http/serve/builder.rs`)
  A session used to live until the client sent `DELETE`. A client that opened
  sessions and left cost the server a map entry each time, and a bridge a
  task and an upstream connection each time, with no limit. `HttpBuilder`
  now sweeps by default; `with_idle_reaper` changes the window and
  `without_idle_reaper` restores the old behaviour. A client whose session
  was evicted gets `404` on its next request, which the specification tells
  it to answer by starting a new session — including one that held only a
  standing `GET` stream and sent nothing.

  `HttpBridge::with_idle_reaper` is opt-in, because the bridge is handed its
  store and cannot know what else shares it. It refuses a store built without
  `SessionStore::with_idle_reaper` rather than reaping nothing. The `bridge`
  command turns it on with a 30 minute default and `--idle-timeout 0` turns
  it off. `tokio/time` is now part of the `http` feature.

- **Every feature-matrix row cites the URL that documents it.** (`22cd58bf`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/domain/feature.rs`) 32 rows named a revision,
  12 an SEP number and one a URL, so a reader could follow almost none of
  them. Each row now carries a `citation`, and the same URL is in the doc
  comment on its `Feature` variant, with a test reading the file back to
  hold the two together.

### Changed

- **The cross-protocol bridge is two protocol adapters and one composition,
  not a hand-written translator for every pair of protocols.** (`2289b30c`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/protocol_adapter.rs`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/mcp_adapter.rs`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/a2a_adapter.rs`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/composed.rs`) The MCP ↔ A2A
  translation was a pair of functions that knew both vocabularies — one that
  turned `SendMessage` into `tools/call`, one that turned it back. A third
  protocol would have needed two more, and the pair nobody wrote about would
  have been the pair nobody tested.

  The translation now lives in per-protocol adapters behind a
  `ProtocolAdapter` seam, and `ComposedCodec` puts two of them together:
  lift on the way out, lower on the way back, with the IR in between. An
  adapter knows one protocol and does not mention the other, so a bridge

=== site guide security.md headings ===
10:## What the library does
26:## Protecting a server, and signing in to one
36:### Requiring a credential on a server
162:## What the library does not do
174:## What the consumer is responsible for
184:## Threat model

=== 'What the library does' section ===
## What the library does

- **Token redaction at the tracing boundary.** Tokens,
  Authorization headers, session ids in full, and elicitation
  responses are redacted by the tracing layer. The redaction
  is tested in `tests/secret_logging.rs`.
- **TLS verification on by default.** A `reqwest` client that
  disables certificate verification is not constructed; the
  library has no path to do so.
- **Path canonicalisation for filesystem-backed resources.** A
  resource whose path traverses outside the allowed root is
  refused with a typed error.
- **Fail-secure on auth.** A `?` operator on a failed auth
  check is the default; an `?`-skipped check is not in the
  library.

## Protecting a server, and signing in to one
## What the library does not do

- **Token storage.** The `AuthorizationSecrets` port trait
  is the consumer-side seam. `OsSecrets` is one
  implementation (reads from the OS keyring); a consumer
  that wants a different source implements the trait.
- **Choosing the rate limit.** Both HTTP transports enforce one; the
  allowance is the consumer's to set.
- **CORS.** The Streamable HTTP server's CORS configuration
  is a transport-level concern; the library does not
  second-guess it.

## What the consumer is responsible for

# Conversation Summary

## Overview

The user resumed a paused session on the `protocol-droid` Rust MCP toolkit with the message "oh, we forgot to update the CHANGELOG and probably SECURITY" (preceded by "Continue"). The working hypothesis was that a recent release's changelog and the `SECURITY.md` policy had been left un-updated. Through extensive repository archaeology against `origin/main`, `v0.8.0`, and `v0.7.0` tags, the investigation established that the premise was **partly wrong** — the 0.8.0 release notes and the `SECURITY.md` version table were in fact already updated on `origin/main` — but that several **real, concrete defects** did exist. No file edits have been made yet; the session was in the final scoping/reporting phase.

## History

1. **User request:** "Continue." then "oh, we forgot to update the CHANGELOG and probably SECURITY"
   - Investigation began by reading the session primer at `/Users/ncampbell/.copilot/session-state/00ecf7f2-acba-4582-a148-8d4c26efc71b/files/primer.md`, which described schema-generator naming work (deleting `naming.rs`, folding it into `emit.rs`), a digit-leading-identifier bug (Bug #3), regression tests, a stale `.papertowel.toml` reference, and an unrun preflight.
   - Established the git topology: current branch is `fix/reaper-test-timing`, HEAD = `9c68414a` ("test: give the reaper tests room against a stalled runner"), which **is an ancestor of `origin/main`**. `origin/main` = `4c5e8c0a` (merge of PR #83), which is exactly what `v0.8.0` points to. There are **zero commits after `v0.8.0`** in `origin/main`.

2. **Verified the CHANGELOG was NOT forgotten (for 0.8.0):**
   - `CHANGELOG.md` on `origin/main` has a full `## [0.8.0] — 2026-11-04` section with `### Added` (3 entries), `### Changed` (2 entries), `### Fixed` (6 entries), `### Tests`. Every entry cites its commit hash, matching the file's stated policy: *"Every entry cites the commit that made the change, so a claim here can be checked against the code rather than taken on the changelog's word."*
   - The release commit `81ac5567` ("release: 0.8.0 — UTCP, ACP, and sessions that expire") created this section.
   - `crates.io` confirms 0.8.0 is published (updated_at `2026-11-04T17:36:29Z`).
   - **Local branch state was stale**: the working-tree `CHANGELOG.md` still has `## [Unreleased]` with the bridge entry; `origin/main` has folded it into 0.8.0.

3. **Verified `SECURITY.md` was already bumped:** the version table on `origin/main` reads `0.8` / `0.7`; the local copy still read `0.7` / `0.6`. This is purely a "branch is behind" artifact, not a missed edit.

4. **Found the real CHANGELOG defects:**
   - **Duplicate `### Changed` heading** inside the 0.8.0 block — `### Changed` appears at both relative line 35 and relative line 62 (absolute lines 46 and 73). Cause: the release commit `81ac5567` added `+### Changed` while the earlier `e7970419` docs commit had already added its own `### Changed` block under `[Unreleased]`, which the release folded in without merging the two headings.
   - **Two uncited shipped commits:**
     - `c4fc1826` "fix: give the A2A interop server a startup budget that survives a busy runner" — in `v0.8.0` and in `81ac5567`, but not mentioned anywhere in the changelog (no "budget" hit in the 0.8.0 block). Precedent exists: 0.7.0 cites the analogous `a2a_js_interop` flakiness fix under `### Fixed`.
     - `9c68414a` "test: give the reaper tests room against a stalled runner" — in `v0.8.0` but **not** in `81ac5567` (landed after the release notes were written), and uncited.
   - **Non-issues confirmed via precedent analysis:** `style:` commits (`52bbeb48`, `9b437d9b`) are never cited in this changelog; `chore(deps):` commits *are* cited when they carry an advisory (`24bf997`, `b85bcb31`, `e8d878bd`); `docs:` commits are cited when they change user-facing docs (`67e076a`, `7d8902d`, `ad7ce31`). `a057bfe7` (chore(deps): bump qs) touches only the interop fixture's `package-lock.json`; `ca801eb6` ("Enable Entire") is tooling config; `e7970419`, `5f8849e7`, `b4fea4b8` are docs commits (the latter two are not changelog material — `5f8849e7` only touched `docs/dev/repo-operations.md`).

5. **Found the real SECURITY.md defects:**
   - **"Three things run without anyone looking" but the table lists FOUR rows** — `supply chain` CI job, Dependabot alerts, Secret scanning, `pre-push` hook. The count is off by one. Note: at `v0.5.1` there was no such table; it was introduced at `f290a261` (0.5.2) with three rows and the prose already said "Three" — the fourth row (pre-push hook) was added later without updating the prose.
   - **CodeQL is not mentioned anywhere in `SECURITY.md` or the site guide** — yet `.github/workflows/codeql.yml` runs `security-and-quality` queries on every push to `main`, every PR to `main`, and weekly (cron `17 4 * * 1`), and the OSSF Scorecard posture doc records SAST as a `pass` because "CodeQL runs on every push". `52bbeb48` exists precisely because CodeQL could not see two generator variables.
   - **The "What is in scope" list omits the resource-exhaustion / unbounded-growth class** — no hit for exhaust|denial|dos|unbounded|memory — even though 0.8.0 shipped exactly that hardening (bounded bridge inbox → `429` + `Retry-After`; idle-session eviction).

6. **Investigated the site guide** `site/src/content/docs/guides/security.md`: headings are `What the library does`, `Protecting a server, and signing in to one`, `What the library does not do`, `What the consumer is responsible for`, `Threat model`. Its "What the library does" list has 4 bullets (token redaction, TLS verification, path canonicalisation, fail-secure auth) — **none** mention the 0.8.0 hardening (idle session eviction, bounded inbox). It also never mentions CodeQL, the bridge, idle reaping, or the Scorecard. Also confirmed the bridge inherits rate limiting: `HttpBridge::into_router` → `McpRouter::into_router`, and `McpRouter::new` sets `rate_limiter: RateLimiter::new(*config.rate_limit())` plus `origin: OriginPolicy::strict(None)`.

7. **Confirmed the digit bug (primer "Bug #3") is already fixed upstream** — commit `09732f65` "fix(schema): escape the keywords rustc refuses as raw identifiers" added the `snake.starts_with(|c: char| c.is_ascii_digit())` branch to `field_ident`. `naming.rs` is already deleted (only `emit.rs`, `mod.rs`, `schema_model.rs` remain in `crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/`).

## Work Done

**No files modified yet.** All work so far has been read-only investigation.

Findings compiled (pending edits):
- `CHANGELOG.md`: duplicate `### Changed` in the 0.8.0 block; uncited `c4fc1826` and `9c68414a`.
- `SECURITY.md`: "Three things" vs. four table rows; CodeQL absent from the finding-channel table; in-scope list missing resource exhaustion.
- `site/src/content/docs/guides/security.md`: "What the library does" missing the 0.8.0 hardening.

33	  session ended. `bridge --idle-timeout <SECONDS>` sets the window.
    34	
    35	### Changed
    36	
    37	- **An HTTP server evicts a session that has been idle for 30 minutes.**
    38	  (`2da5507d`,
    39	  `crates/protocol-droid/src/adapters/primary/transport/http/serve/builder.rs`)
    40	  A session used to live until the client sent `DELETE`. A client that opened
    41	  sessions and left cost the server a map entry each time, and a bridge a
    42	  task and an upstream connection each time, with no limit. `HttpBuilder`
    43	  now sweeps by default; `with_idle_reaper` changes the window and
    44	  `without_idle_reaper` restores the old behaviour. A client whose session
    45	  was evicted gets `404` on its next request, which the specification tells
    46	  it to answer by starting a new session — including one that held only a
    47	  standing `GET` stream and sent nothing.
    48	
    49	  `HttpBridge::with_idle_reaper` is opt-in, because the bridge is handed its
    50	  store and cannot know what else shares it. It refuses a store built without
    51	  `SessionStore::with_idle_reaper` rather than reaping nothing. The `bridge`
    52	  command turns it on with a 30 minute default and `--idle-timeout 0` turns
    53	  it off. `tokio/time` is now part of the `http` feature.
    54	
    55	- **Every feature-matrix row cites the URL that documents it.** (`22cd58bf`,
    56	  `crates/protocol-droid/src/domain/feature.rs`) 32 rows named a revision,
    57	  12 an SEP number and one a URL, so a reader could follow almost none of
    58	  them. Each row now carries a `citation`, and the same URL is in the doc
    59	  comment on its `Feature` variant, with a test reading the file back to
    60	  hold the two together.
    61	
    62	### Changed
    63	
    64	- **The cross-protocol bridge is two protocol adapters and one composition,
    65	  not a hand-written translator for every pair of protocols.** (`2289b30c`,
    66	  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/protocol_adapter.rs`,
    67	  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/mcp_adapter.rs`,
    68	  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/a2a_adapter.rs`,
    69	  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/composed.rs`) The MCP ↔ A2A
    70	  translation was a pair of functions that knew both vocabularies — one that
    71	  turned `SendMessage` into `tools/call`, one that turned it back. A third
    72	  protocol would have needed two more, and the pair nobody wrote about would
    73	  have been the pair nobody tested.
    74	
    75	  The translation now lives in per-protocol adapters behind a
    76	  `ProtocolAdapter` seam, and `ComposedCodec` puts two of them together:
    77	  lift on the way out, lower on the way back, with the IR in between. An
    78	  adapter knows one protocol and does not mention the other, so a bridge
    79	  between two protocols nobody wrote a translator for works the same way as
    80	  the one that was.
    81	
    82	  The IR gained the types the adapters meet at — `IrCall`, `IrMethod` and
    83	  `IrOutcome` at `crates/protocol-droid/src/domain/ir/call.rs` — and a loss
    84	  that has no counterpart on the other side is now recorded in the
    85	  translation report rather than dropped in silence: an A2A part with no MCP
    86	  counterpart, a task's artifacts, and structured content with no A2A
    87	  counterpart are all reported.
    88	
    89	  `CrossBridgePeer::new` lost its `downstream_side` parameter. The codec is

=== 0.7.0 Documentation section ===
### Documentation

- **`docs/benchmarks.md` described a CI bench job that does not exist.**
  (`c69b77ac`, `docs/benchmarks.md`) The document described a job that runs the divan
  benches and compares their medians against `baselines.json` with a 10 %
  threshold in either direction. There is no such job, and `baselines.json`
  is read by nothing but the documentation. The document now says what is
  actually there: the `bench_gate` smoke test is the automated performance
  gate, and the committed baselines are reference data for a human reading a
  bench run.

  The reason the divan benches are not in CI is the same reason the smoke
  test now reads the fastest of ten samples: a wall-clock measurement on a
  shared runner measures the runner. A 10 % threshold there is not a
  stricter gate, it is a noisier one. Wiring those benches into CI needs a
  runner that is not shared, and is its own piece of work.

- **The release guide did not say what a stalled release leaves behind.**
  (`site/src/content/docs/guides/release.md`) The guide described the
  `release` environment and the approval it needs, and stopped there. It did
  not say what happens when the approval never comes — which is what happened
  to `v0.4.2` and `v0.6.1`, so crates.io skips those two numbers and a reader
  who sees `0.5.3 → 0.7.0` has no explanation for the gap.

  The guide now says that a stalled run is not a failure to diagnose: the
  crates were never uploaded, so there is nothing to un-publish, and what the
  run needs is either an approval or a decision to abandon it and move to the
  next version. It also says that a superseding release folds the abandoned
  one's contents forward rather than backfilling the number.

## 0.6.1 — never published

`v0.6.1` was tagged and its release run built every binary and verified
packaging, but it stopped at the `release` environment gate and was
abandoned rather than forced. No 0.6.1 was ever uploaded, so crates.io
goes 0.6.0 → 0.7.0 with nothing at 0.6.1. The tag is still on the commit
it marked, because that commit is real history; only the publish never
happened.

Its contents are folded into 0.7.0 above. Nothing that was written for
0.6.1 was lost — it was superseded, not abandoned mid-flight.

1	# Security Policy

     3	## Supported versions
     4	
     5	`protocol-droid` is published as four crates (`protocol-droid-schema`,
     6	`protocol-droid`, `protocol-droid-macros`, `protocol-droid-cli`) on
     7	crates.io. Security advisories are issued against the latest released
     8	minor version; the previous minor receives advisories for **30 days**
     9	after a new minor ships. The `main` branch is built and tested on
    10	every push; advisories against `main` only are evaluated case by case
    11	because the work to backport a fix is small but a backport is not
    12	guaranteed to be free of merge conflicts on the older minor.

    14	| Crate                    | Latest stable | Previous minor |
    15	| ------------------------ | ------------- | -------------- |
    16	| `protocol-droid-schema`  | `0.8`         | `0.7`          |
    17	| `protocol-droid`         | `0.8`         | `0.7`          |
    18	| `protocol-droid-macros`  | `0.8`         | `0.7`          |
    19	| `protocol-droid-cli`     | `0.8`         | `0.7`          |

    66	
    67	Anything in the four crates' source that affects a consumer's trust
    68	boundary, the wire surface, or a peer of the library:

    72	  bytes through a `&RawValue` parse.
    73	- **Wire codec behaviour** — a `tools/call` argument that the
    74	  application refused but the codec accepted, or a result the
    75	  application trusted but the codec lost a field on. The codec
    76	  never silently drops a field; if it appears to, that is a bug.
    77	- **Capability gating** — a `FeatureProfile::is_enabled` answer
    78	  that lets a path run when the negotiated capabilities do not
    79	  cover it. A `list_changed` notification sent to a peer that
    80	  did not advertise `list_changed` is always a bug.
    81	- **Token handling** — redaction failures at the tracing layer
    82	  (the test is `tests/secret_logging.rs`), bearer-token leaks
    83	  in error paths, PKCE verifier leakage, OAuth state
    84	  non-entropy.

    86	  DNS-rebinding via `Host`-header mismatch, request-deadline
    87	  or concurrency-ceiling bypass, missing or wrong rate-limit
    88	  knob.
    89	- **Filesystem-backed resources** — path canonicalisation
    90	  failures, a `..` traversal that escapes the allowed root,

   110	| Secret scanning | credential patterns across the history and every push | whole repository |

name: CodeQL

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
  schedule:
    # Weekly, off the hour, so the run does not pile onto the top-of-hour rush
    # that every other scheduled workflow shares.
    - cron: "17 4 * * 1"
  workflow_dispatch:

# The CodeQL analysis needs to write its results; nothing else in this workflow
# needs any write access.
permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  analyze:
    name: analyze (rust)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      security-events: write
      packages: read
      actions: read
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - name: Initialize CodeQL
        uses: github/codeql-action/init@v4
        with:
          languages: rust
          queries: security-and-quality
      # For Rust, CodeQL builds the project to capture the source. The pinned
      # toolchain in rust-toolchain.toml is what gets used.
      - name: Autobuild
        uses: github/codeql-action/autobuild@v4
      - name: Analyze

    11

    13	  Authorization headers, session ids in full, and elicitation

    15	  is tested in `tests/secret_logging.rs`.
    16	- **TLS verification on by default.** A `reqwest` client that

    18	  library has no path to do so.
    19	- **Path canonicalisation for filesystem-backed resources.** A
    20	  resource whose path traverses outside the allowed root is
    21	  refused with a typed error.
    22	- **Fail-secure on auth.** A `?` operator on a failed auth
    23	  check is the default; an `?`-skipped check is not in the
    24	  library.
    25	
    26	## Protecting a server, and signing in to one
    27	
    28	Both HTTP transports a server offers (Streamable HTTP and the legacy
    29	HTTP+SSE routes) check the `Origin` header and the `Host` header
    30	(the second catches a rebound DNS name, since `Origin` is absent from
    31	every non-browser client), count requests against a per-subject rate

Author: Nick Campbell <s0ma@protonmail.com>

    The `a2a_js_interop` test gave the Node reference server five seconds to
    print its `listening on <port>` line. On an idle machine that takes about
    150 ms, so five seconds looked like a hundred-and-thirty-fold margin.

    reference server did not start within 5 seconds" — four of the five cases,
    every one of them a *startup* failure with no assertion run at all.

    was how many other jobs were sharing the runner: a merge to `main` starts
    the CI matrix, the conformance suite, the interop suite and CodeQL at
    once, and `ubuntu-latest` runners are not free.
