+  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/protocol_adapter.rs`,
+  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/mcp_adapter.rs`,
+  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/a2a_adapter.rs`,
+  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/composed.rs`) The MCP ↔ A2A
+  translation was a pair of functions that knew both vocabularies — one that
+  turned `SendMessage` into `tools/call`, one that turned it back. A third
+  protocol would have needed two more, and the pair nobody wrote about would
+  have been the pair nobody tested.
+
+  The translation now lives in per-protocol adapters behind a
+  `ProtocolAdapter` seam, and `ComposedCodec` puts two of them together:
+  lift on the way out, lower on the way back, with the IR in between. An
+  adapter knows one protocol and does not mention the other, so a bridge
+  between two protocols nobody wrote a translator for works the same way as
+  the one that was.
+
+  The IR gained the types the adapters meet at — `IrCall`, `IrMethod` and
+  `IrOutcome` at `crates/protocol-droid/src/domain/ir/call.rs` — and a loss
+  that has no counterpart on the other side is now recorded in the
+  translation report rather than dropped in silence: an A2A part with no MCP
+  counterpart, a task's artifacts, and structured content with no A2A
+  counterpart are all reported.
+
+  `CrossBridgePeer::new` lost its `downstream_side` parameter. The codec is
+  built from a downstream adapter and an upstream adapter, so it knows which
+  side it is; a caller that passed the side separately could disagree with
+  the codec, and the disagreement would have shown up as a method the bridge
+  refused for no visible reason.
+
+### Fixed
+
+- **The A2A leg of the bridge sent the agent arguments it could not read.**
+  (`2289b30c`,
+  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/a2a_adapter.rs`) An MCP
+  `tools/call` carried `arguments` as an object, and the bridge put it on the
+  A2A wire inside a data part as `{"data": {"data": {…}}}`. The agent read
+  the call's arguments out of the nested object rather than the object
+  itself, so a tool that expected `{"query": "weather"}` was handed
+  `{"data": {"query": "weather"}}`.
+
+- **The A2A leg of the bridge wrote a `kind` key the spec does not name.**
+  (`2289b30c`,
+  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/a2a_adapter.rs`) A part was
+  written as `{"kind": "data", "data": {…}}`. The spec's part shape is the
+  proto's `oneof content`: the object has exactly one of `text`, `file` or
+  `data` as a top-level field, with no discriminator. That is what the

### Security

- **`ctutils` is fixed rather than waived.** (`RUSTSEC-2026-0385`, medium)
  `ctutils 0.4.3`'s `Choice` mask generation could compile to a branch on
  secret values, and `ctutils`' `u128` comparisons were not constant-time on
  32-bit targets. `ctutils 0.4.4` fixes it; this workspace takes `0.4.5`.

  This one is reachable, and it is worth being precise about where. The path
  is `protocol-droid` → `hmac 0.13` → `digest 0.11.3` → `ctutils`, and
  `ctutils` is pulled in by `digest`'s `mac` feature rather than by
  `hmac`'s own use of it — `digest/src/mac.rs` does `use ctutils::CtEq;` and
  calls `ct_eq(tag)` to compare a MAC tag. Our own HMAC comparison in
  `application/mcp/input_required.rs` is exactly that path:
  `StateKey::open` verifies a `requestState` MAC with `verify_slice`. A
  constant-time regression there is a real defect and not a theoretical one.

  0.5.2 shipped the vulnerable version in all four crates' `Cargo.lock`, and
  `protocol-droid-cli` publishes its lockfile, so the published binary
  carried it. A consumer who resolves fresh gets `0.4.5` from the caret
  requirement on `ctutils 0.4`; a consumer whose own lockfile still pins
  `0.4.3` needs `cargo update -p ctutils`.

- **All four committed lockfiles now carry the patched `ctutils` and the
  current `protocol-droid` version.** The three excluded from the workspace
  (`fuzz`, `interop_rmcp`, `interop_ts_sdk`) had drifted: the root lockfile
  moved to `ctutils 0.4.5` and the interop fixture's did not, so it kept the
  vulnerable `0.4.3` until the pre-push hook blocked the push. The other two
  were staler still, pinning `protocol-droid 0.1.0` against a workspace at
  0.5.2.

  All four are current now, and each records `ctutils 0.4.5`. The hook scans
  every committed lockfile, so this is the state it was already asking for;
  the drift was that nobody had run it since the advisory landed. The CI gap
  this exposes is recorded in `SECURITY.md` rather than closed here.

- **`RUSTSEC-2026-0387` on `crypto-bigint 0.5.5` is waived, with the
  argument written down.** (`deny.toml`) It is reached through
  `jsonwebtoken`'s `rust_crypto` backend → `p256`/`p384` → `ecdsa` →
  `elliptic-curve`, and there is no upgrade path: the fix sits behind
  `p256`/`p384 0.14`, which `jsonwebtoken 11.1.0`'s caret requirements
  (`^0.13.2` / `^0.13.0`) do not admit, and 11.1.0 is the latest release
  whose `master` carries the same pins.

# protocol-droid — Implementation Progress

> Orchestrator reads this file at the start of each loop iteration.

**T15 stage 1 — the `event:` name.** The legacy transport names _every_ frame, and the name is the only thing that tells an `endpoint` frame (where to POST) from a `message` frame (a JSON-RPC payload). `SseEvent` had no name field, on a comment asserting "`event`, `retry` and anything a future revision adds are ignored, per the standard. MCP does not use them." That was true of Streamable HTTP and false of `2024-11-05`, and it is now `event` alone: read, written, round-tripped, and the stale claim corrected in place with the reason. 12 new tests, **7 mutation checks, 0 survivors**, and one of those checks exposed an unreachable test.

`EventName` is a newtype in `domain/stream/event_name.rs` because a name is a wire token: a name containing a newline does not render oddly, it becomes a **second field**, so `event: message\ndata: {...}` is a payload the peer never sent. `const_new` is `pub(crate)`, not `pub` — a `const fn` cannot scan for a terminator, so making it public would hand every caller the exact injection the type closes, in the shape of the safe constructor. It is a `Cow<'static, str>` rather than an `Arc<str>` for one reason that decided the design: `Arc::from` is not `const`, so an `Arc`-backed name cannot be a constant, and the two names the transport is _defined_ by should not have to be built at first use.

**T15 stage 2 — `MessageEndpoint`, the `endpoint` event's payload.** The 2024-11-05 spec says one sentence about this: "the server MUST send an `endpoint` event containing a URI for the client to use for sending messages." **The `sessionId` query parameter and the `202 Accepted` are absent** — they are SDK conventions, and this crate cites the spec, so `domain/transport/endpoint.rs` says which is which rather than encoding a convention and attributing it to the standard.

The type is a newtype over the **whole** target, not a decomposed `(path, query, session)`, and a client uses it **verbatim**: the server chose the URI and the client is not entitled to know how it encoded the session. Decomposing makes the next move "rebuild the URL", and rebuilding is where the server's encoding choice becomes this client's bug.

It refuses two shapes that escape the origin the client dialled. The `endpoint` value arrives **from the peer**, so accepting an absolute URI makes the event an SSRF primitive — point it at `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/` and the client sends its session there. `ProtocolRelative` is a separate variant because `//evil.example/steal` has no scheme and walks straight past a `://` check. The scheme test is RFC 3986 §3.1 hand-written rather than a URI parser, because the interesting failure is the false negative: a `://`-only check passes `data:text/plain,hello`. 18 tests, **5 mutants, 0 survivors**.

**The surviving mutant.** The ALPHA rule — a scheme cannot start with a digit — was **unpinned**: deleting it left all sixteen then-existing tests green, because a digit-led colon is refused either way and only the _reason_ changes. It is an equivalent mutant for acceptance, so it would not have shown up in any accept/reject count. Two tests now pin the specific refusal, because the reason is what a client reading a log actually looks at. Count accept/reject mutations and a mutant that only relabels a diagnostic reads as a survivor.

**T15 stage 3a — the `Origin` gate.** The 2024-11-05 spec's only **MUST** in the security block: "Servers **MUST** validate the `Origin` header on all incoming connections to prevent DNS rebinding attacks." `Refusal::ForeignOrigin` joins the existing enum (403, code `-32008`, slug `foreign_origin`) rather than a parallel type — it is a refusal like any other, and two refusal types is how a client ends up matching on one and treating the other as an internal error.

The check is **deliberately asymmetric** and the asymmetry is the design: a _present_ `Origin` that is not ours is refused (the browser case, and the only one carrying a forged cross-site request), an _absent_ one is allowed (every CLI, SDK and curl omits it — failing closed on absent would be secure against browsers and unusable for everyone else). The default is fail-secure: no listed origins, and a server that was never told its own origin refuses every `Origin` present rather than answering all of them.

Comparison is **exact**, lowercased in scheme and host per RFC 6454 §6.2.2 — no wildcard, no suffix, no parent domain, because an allowlist of `localhost` that also answers `localhost.evil.example` is a rebinding defence that rebinds. `ProtocolRelative`-shaped holes are closed the same way as in `MessageEndpoint`. 15 tests, **6 mutants, 0 survivors** after one was killed by a new test.

**The second surviving mutant, and a worse one than the first.** Replacing the allowlist's `any()` with `first()` passed all fourteen then-existing tests, because **every test allowed exactly one origin** — with one permitted entry, "the first matches" and "any matches" are the same predicate. A user listing a dev server on `:3000` and a second client on `:3001` would have been silently refused, which reads as "the allowlist is broken" and gets diagnosed by deleting the allowlist. A one-element collection cannot distinguish `first` from `any`; a test that never builds a two-element one is not testing the collection. Three origins are listed now, deliberately.

**T15 stage 3b — the two routes.** `legacy_sse/router.rs` mounts `/sse` (GET only)
and `/messages` (POST only) over T14's session store, tail, and security headers.
The two are genuinely different shapes: there is no `Mcp-Session-Id` header on
this revision, so the session lives in the `?sessionId=` of the **query string**,
which is why axum's `query` feature is on. A `GET` opens a session, pushes an
`endpoint` frame naming where to POST, and streams; a `POST` parses the frame,
hands it to `LegacyDispatcher`, and answers `202` with an empty body because on
this transport the answer goes to the stream and never to the `POST`. Neither
route grows the other's method, and the tests pin that as a `405` rather than
leaving it to axum's default.

`legacy_sse/frame.rs` is `LegacyFrame`, and it exists for one reason: **the
`endpoint` event's data is a bare URI, not a JSON string.** A `Value::String`
holding `/messages?sessionId=1` serialises to `"/messages?sessionId=1"` — quotes
and all — and a client that reads `data` gets those quotes as part of the URL.
The first test in `frame/tests.rs` is a byte comparison against the exact frame
the spec describes, not a round trip, because a round trip passes with the quotes
in place: the decoder is the same code that wrote them.

consequence of the first: validating the path at assembly makes the per-request

     1	## What is out of scope
     2	
     3	- **The consumer's deployment.** A consumer that disables TLS
     4	  verification on its own `reqwest` client, that does not set
     5	  `Content-Security-Policy` on its own HTTP server, that picks
     6	  a token-storage adapter that is not `OsSecrets` and stores
     7	  the token in a world-readable file — that is the consumer's
     8	  deployment, not this library.
     9	- **A2A peers that are not under the consumer's control.** A
    10	  push-notification webhook URL that resolves to a private
    11	  network is refused by the SSRF denylist at config time, and
    12	  re-validated at delivery time. A URL that resolves to a
    13	  public network the consumer did not intend to send to is a
    14	  consumer-configuration problem.
    15	- **A peer that has compromised the consumer's process.** The
    16	  library's parsers are fuzzed against malicious input; a peer
    17	  that already has code execution on the consumer's host is
    18	  not in the threat model.
    19	- **MCP revisions older than the lowest vendored one.** The
    20	  library does not claim to speak revisions it does not have
    21	  wire types for. A consumer who needs revision `X` and
    22	  `X` is not in `crates/protocol-droid-schema/spec/` is not
    23	  in scope.
    24	- **The CLI's own configuration file format.** The CLI is a
    25	  thin adapter; the configuration it parses is the consumer's
    26	  to validate, and a bad config is the consumer's error, not
    27	  a security issue.
    28	
    29	## Response timeline
    30	
    31	| Step                                        | Window          |
    32	| ------------------------------------------- | --------------- |
    33	| Initial acknowledgement                     | 7 days          |
    34	| Triage and impact assessment                | 30 days         |
    35	| Patch landed (or status update)             | 60 days         |
    36	| Public advisory and CVE request (if needed) | 90 days         |
    37	| Embargoed release at the consumer's request | by request      |
    38	
    39	A "status update" in the 60-day row is a maintainer message in
    40	the original advisory thread explaining what is blocking and
    41	what the next step is — a patch that needs a contract change,
    42	a reproducer that does not reproduce, a CVE that is still in
    43	the CNA queue. The status update is what prevents a silent
    44	60-day pause.
    45	
    46	## Security model
    47	
    48	The library is **default deny**:
    49	
    50	- An `AuthContext` is a required parameter on every stateful
    51	  port method. There is no path through the library that does
    52	  not carry one.
    53	- Authorization predicates are pure domain functions. The
    54	  predicate that says "this user can see this resource" lives
    55	  in `domain/`, not in an adapter; the adapter hands it the
    56	  data and applies the answer.
    57	- TLS verification is on by default. A `reqwest` client with
    58	  certificate verification disabled is not constructed; the
    59	  library has no path to do so.
    60	- Path canonicalisation refuses a `..` traversal that escapes
    61	  the allowed root with a typed error, not a panic.
    62	- Tokens, Authorization headers, session ids in full, and
    63	  elicitation responses are redacted at the tracing-layer
    64	  boundary. The test that proves the redaction list is
    65	  complete is `tests/secret_logging.rs`.
    66	
    67	The full design, including what the library does *not* do
    68	(token storage, rate limiting, CORS) and what the consumer is
    69	responsible for, is in the
    70	[Security model guide](https://greysquirr3l.github.io/protocol-droid/guides/security/)
    71	on the docs site. The audit that backs the no-finding summary
    72	in this policy is in
    73	[`SECURITY-REVIEW.md`](https://github.com/greysquirr3l/protocol-droid/blob/main/SECURITY-REVIEW.md).
    74	
    75	## Coordinated disclosure
    76	
    77	A 90-day window is the default. A reporter who needs more time
    78	(an embargoed CVE, a downstream rollout that takes longer than
    79	the patch) names the date in the first message; the maintainer
    80	confirms or counters. An embargo that runs past 180 days is
    81	reviewed at 180 days; a longer embargo is honoured only if the
    82	reporter and the maintainer agree in writing.

    88	reporter's preferred attribution (name, handle, or anonymous)

`crates/protocol-droid/src/adapters/primary/transport/http/reaper.rs`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/adapters/secondary/clock.rs`) The first sweeps
  idle sessions out of a `SessionStore`, the second is the production
  `Clock` the port never had, and the third tells an operator why a bridge
  session ended. `bridge --idle-timeout <SECONDS>` sets the window.

### Changed

- **An HTTP server evicts a session that has been idle for 30 minutes.**
  (`2da5507d`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/adapters/primary/transport/http/serve/builder.rs`)
  A session used to live until the client sent `DELETE`. A client that opened
  sessions and left cost the server a map entry each time, and a bridge a
  task and an upstream connection each time, with no limit. `HttpBuilder`
  now sweeps by default; `with_idle_reaper` changes the window and
  `without_idle_reaper` restores the old behaviour. A client whose session
  was evicted gets `404` on its next request, which the specification tells
  it to answer by starting a new session — including one that held only a
  standing `GET` stream and sent nothing.

  `HttpBridge::with_idle_reaper` is opt-in, because the bridge is handed its
  store and cannot know what else shares it. It refuses a store built without
  `SessionStore::with_idle_reaper` rather than reaping nothing. The `bridge`
  command turns it on with a 30 minute default and `--idle-timeout 0` turns
  it off. `tokio/time` is now part of the `http` feature.

- **Every feature-matrix row cites the URL that documents it.** (`22cd58bf`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/domain/feature.rs`) 32 rows named a revision,
  12 an SEP number and one a URL, so a reader could follow almost none of
  them. Each row now carries a `citation`, and the same URL is in the doc
  comment on its `Feature` variant, with a test reading the file back to
  hold the two together.

### Changed

- **The cross-protocol bridge is two protocol adapters and one composition,
  not a hand-written translator for every pair of protocols.** (`2289b30c`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/protocol_adapter.rs`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/mcp_adapter.rs`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/a2a_adapter.rs`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/composed.rs`) The MCP ↔ A2A
  translation was a pair of functions that knew both vocabularies — one that
  turned `SendMessage` into `tools/call`, one that turned it back. A third
  protocol would have needed two more, and the pair nobody wrote about would
  have been the pair nobody tested.

  The translation now lives in per-protocol adapters behind a
  `ProtocolAdapter` seam, and `ComposedCodec` puts two of them together:
  lift on the way out, lower on the way back, with the IR in between. An
  adapter knows one protocol and does not mention the other, so a bridge
  between two protocols nobody wrote a translator for works the same way as
  the one that was.

  The IR gained the types the adapters meet at — `IrCall`, `IrMethod` and
  `IrOutcome` at `crates/protocol-droid/src/domain/ir/call.rs` — and a loss
  that has no counterpart on the other side is now recorded in the
  translation report rather than dropped in silence: an A2A part with no MCP
  counterpart, a task's artifacts, and structured content with no A2A
  counterpart are all reported.

  `CrossBridgePeer::new` lost its `downstream_side` parameter. The codec is
  built from a downstream adapter and an upstream adapter, so it knows which
  side it is; a caller that passed the side separately could disagree with
  the codec, and the disagreement would have shown up as a method the bridge
  refused for no visible reason.

### Fixed

- **The A2A leg of the bridge sent the agent arguments it could not read.**
  (`2289b30c`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/a2a_adapter.rs`) An MCP

=== CodeQL workflow on origin/main ===
name: CodeQL

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
  schedule:
    # Weekly, off the hour, so the run does not pile onto the top-of-hour rush
    # that every other scheduled workflow shares.
    - cron: "17 4 * * 1"
  workflow_dispatch:

# The CodeQL analysis needs to write its results; nothing else in this workflow
# needs any write access.
permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  analyze:
    name: analyze (rust)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      security-events: write
      packages: read
      actions: read
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - name: Initialize CodeQL
        uses: github/codeql-action/init@v4
        with:
          languages: rust
          queries: security-and-quality
      # For Rust, CodeQL builds the project to capture the source. The pinned
      # toolchain in rust-toolchain.toml is what gets used.
      - name: Autobuild
        uses: github/codeql-action/autobuild@v4
      - name: Analyze
        uses: github/codeql-action/analyze@v4

# Security Policy

## Supported versions

`protocol-droid` is published as four crates (`protocol-droid-schema`,
`protocol-droid`, `protocol-droid-macros`, `protocol-droid-cli`) on
crates.io. Security advisories are issued against the latest released
minor version; the previous minor receives advisories for **30 days**
after a new minor ships. The `main` branch is built and tested on
every push; advisories against `main` only are evaluated case by case
because the work to backport a fix is small but a backport is not
guaranteed to be free of merge conflicts on the older minor.

| Crate                    | Latest stable | Previous minor |
| ------------------------ | ------------- | -------------- |

## How a vulnerability gets found

A report is the best route and not the only one. Three things run without
anyone looking:

| Where | What it checks | Coverage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `supply chain` CI job | `cargo deny` against a freshly fetched advisory database | all four committed lockfiles |
| Dependabot alerts | advisory database against every manifest | root, `site/`, and the interop fixture |
| Secret scanning | credential patterns across the history and every push | whole repository |
| `pre-push` hook | `cargo audit` over every committed lockfile | all four, including the three outside the workspace |

Two gaps are worth stating plainly rather than leaving to be discovered:

**Every committed lockfile now gets a CI-side advisory watch.** Until the
`supply chain` job was extended, it scanned the root lockfile only.
`crates/protocol-droid/fuzz/`, `crates/protocol-droid/tests/interop_rmcp/`
and `crates/protocol-droid/tests/interop_ts_sdk/` are excluded from the
workspace, so `cargo deny` never saw their dependency graphs; the pre-push
hook covered them locally, which is a mitigation, not equivalent coverage.

The job now scans all four, one step per lockfile, and each of those
steps passes `--locked`. Without `--locked`, `cargo metadata` re-resolves
the graph and rewrites the lockfile on disk, so the scan would report on
a dependency set nobody committed — a different check, not a stricter
one. With `--locked`, the scan reports on the lockfile as committed, and
fails loudly when that lockfile is stale.

That gap was not theoretical. When `ctutils` was bumped to 0.4.5 for
RUSTSEC-2026-0385, the root `Cargo.lock` was updated and the interop
fixture's was not, so the fixture kept `ctutils 0.4.3` until the pre-push
hook blocked the push. The hook was the only thing that saw it, and the
lockfile it caught was stale on more than the advisory: it still pinned
`protocol-droid 0.1.0` against a workspace at 0.5.2.

The `interop_ts_sdk` fixture is the one case where a manifest *is* watched:
Dependabot's security updates reach it, and it is declared in
`dependabot.yml` so a transitive advisory gets a bump proposal rather than
sitting unnoticed. Note that `npm install` honours the committed lockfile,
so it will not self-heal — the lockfile has to be updated on purpose. The
other two are Rust, and are now covered by CI as well as by the hook.

**The site is built in CI, but the peer-range gap is still worth knowing.**
The `site` job installs with `--frozen-lockfile`, runs `astro check` and
`astro build`, and asserts the output has the expected shape, so a change
under `site/` that does not build fails the PR rather than passing every
check. It was not always so: Dependabot's astro 5 → 7 PR passed fourteen green
Rust checks without building, because starlight 0.30 pins `astro: ^5.0.0` and
`pnpm install` does not enforce peer ranges — the failure appears only at
build time. `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` does not change that; it
enforces the *lockfile*, not the peer ranges.

`deny.toml` is the single list of accepted advisories, and it is the same
list the `pre-push` hook reads. A waiver belongs there with a reason saying
why the advisory is unreachable from this code; there is no second place to
record one.

---
title: Security model
description: What protocol-droid does to keep a peer on the safe side of the trust boundary, what it does not, and where the consumer's responsibility begins.
---

The library's security model is *default deny*. The auth context
is a required parameter on every stateful port method, and the
authorization predicates are pure domain functions.

## What the library does

- **Token redaction at the tracing boundary.** Tokens,
  Authorization headers, session ids in full, and elicitation
  responses are redacted by the tracing layer. The redaction
  is tested in `tests/secret_logging.rs`.
- **TLS verification on by default.** A `reqwest` client that
  disables certificate verification is not constructed; the
  library has no path to do so.
- **Path canonicalisation for filesystem-backed resources.** A
  resource whose path traverses outside the allowed root is
  refused with a typed error.
- **Fail-secure on auth.** A `?` operator on a failed auth
  check is the default; an `?`-skipped check is not in the
  library.

## Protecting a server, and signing in to one

Both HTTP transports a server offers (Streamable HTTP and the legacy
HTTP+SSE routes) check the `Origin` header and the `Host` header
(the second catches a rebound DNS name, since `Origin` is absent from
every non-browser client), count requests against a per-subject rate
limit before authenticating, and put the same security headers on every
response, including the ones no handler wrote. A request with no
`Host` is refused.

### Requiring a credential on a server

Requiring OAuth is two builders, and the second one is the part that
is easy to leave off. An authenticator answers "is this token valid?";
a policy answers "does this endpoint need one?". The library treats an
..... 160-205 .....
process listing.

## What the library does not do

- **Token storage.** The `AuthorizationSecrets` port trait
  is the consumer-side seam. `OsSecrets` is one
  implementation (reads from the OS keyring); a consumer
  that wants a different source implements the trait.
- **Choosing the rate limit.** Both HTTP transports enforce one; the
  allowance is the consumer's to set.
- **CORS.** The Streamable HTTP server's CORS configuration
  is a transport-level concern; the library does not
  second-guess it.

## What the consumer is responsible for

- Choosing the `TokenSource` and `TokenEndpoint` adapters
  that match their deployment.
- Setting `Content-Security-Policy`, `Strict-Transport-Security`,
  and `X-Frame-Options` on the HTTP server they wrap around
  the library.
- Wiring the rate limit and request size limit at the
  transport level.

## Threat model

The library is designed against a peer that:

- may send malformed JSON-RPC frames,
- may send a method name the server does not register,
- may send a capability the server did not negotiate,
- may retry an in-flight request id,
- may cancel an unknown or completed request.

The library is *not* designed against a peer that has
compromised the consumer's process. The library's input
parsers are tested against malicious inputs (the fuzz
harness in `crates/protocol-droid/fuzz/` runs nightly), but
a compromised process is the consumer's problem.

:::tip
Read the [architecture overview](/protocol-droid/architecture/overview/) for how the
`AuthContext` requirement and the port-trait returns-DOMAIN-error rule fit
together. The split between "library does" and "consumer does" is the line
that makes the `AuthorizationSecrets` trait a seam, not a check.
:::

10:## [Unreleased]
12:## [0.8.0] — 2026-11-04
14:### Added
46:### Changed

361:## [0.6.0] — 2026-10-26
374:### Added
=== 0.8.0 Fixed block, abs lines ===
  that has no counterpart on the other side is now recorded in the
  translation report rather than dropped in silence: an A2A part with no MCP
  counterpart, a task's artifacts, and structured content with no A2A
  counterpart are all reported.

  `CrossBridgePeer::new` lost its `downstream_side` parameter. The codec is
  built from a downstream adapter and an upstream adapter, so it knows which
  side it is; a caller that passed the side separately could disagree with
  the codec, and the disagreement would have shown up as a method the bridge
  refused for no visible reason.

### Fixed

- **The A2A leg of the bridge sent the agent arguments it could not read.**
  (`2289b30c`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/a2a_adapter.rs`) An MCP
  `tools/call` carried `arguments` as an object, and the bridge put it on the
  A2A wire inside a data part as `{"data": {"data": {…}}}`. The agent read
  the call's arguments out of the nested object rather than the object
  itself, so a tool that expected `{"query": "weather"}` was handed
  `{"data": {"query": "weather"}}`.

- **The A2A leg of the bridge wrote a `kind` key the spec does not name.**
  (`2289b30c`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/a2a_adapter.rs`) A part was
  written as `{"kind": "data", "data": {…}}`. The spec's part shape is the
  proto's `oneof content`: the object has exactly one of `text`, `file` or
  `data` as a top-level field, with no discriminator. That is what the
  crate's own A2A server sends, what the A2A conformance fixtures expect,
  and what the vendored `a2a.proto` describes — so the bridge was speaking
  a dialect of A2A that the rest of the crate does not speak.

- **A generated union picked its arm by member order.** (`c22bfd84`,
  `crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/emit.rs`) A `tools/call`
  request decoded as an `InitializeRequest`, and a `2026-07-28` result landed
  in the generic `Result` arm. Nothing showed it: every generated type
  carries a flattened catch-all, so a value in the wrong arm re-serialises to
  byte-identical JSON. A union now reads the member the specification
  requires of every alternative — `type`, `method` — and an absent or
  unknown value is a decode error. Where no such member exists the arm is
  chosen by the value's shape, and the specification's order breaks a tie.

- **A schema member named `self`, `super` or `crate` generated a field that
  did not compile.** (`09732f65`,
  `crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/emit.rs`) `field_ident` tried
  the raw-identifier branch first and the trailing-underscore branch second,
  on the same predicate, so the second could never run and `self` came out as
  `r#self`, which rustc rejects. The three now take a trailing underscore,
  `gen` is reserved for edition 2024, and a member that starts with a digit
  gains a leading underscore. No vendored schema has such a member today; the
  next upstream one would have broken the build. An unreferenced 305-line
  `naming.rs` carrying a second, drifted copy of these rules is gone.

- **A bridge session's inbound queue grew without limit, and its errors went
  nowhere.** (`2da5507d`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/adapters/primary/transport/http/bridge.rs`) A
  client could `POST` faster than the upstream answered and the queue took
  all of it. It now holds 256 messages and answers `429` with `Retry-After`
  past that. A session whose loop ended in an error — an upstream that could
  not be reached, a client channel that failed — was dropped by `let _ =`;
  `with_session_report` hands it to the operator, and the `bridge` command
  prints it to stderr.

- **Eight rustdoc links named private or ambiguous items.** (`b7d73634`)

result.content:
fix: give the A2A interop server a startup budget that survives a busy runner

The `a2a_js_interop` test gave the Node reference server five seconds to
print its `listening on <port>` line. On an idle machine that takes about
150 ms, so five seconds looked like a hundred-and-thirty-fold margin.

It was not a margin. It was a bet that the runner would be quiet.

The test passed on the pull request and then failed on `main` with "the
reference server did not start within 5 seconds" — four of the five cases,
every one of them a *startup* failure with no assertion run at all.
Nothing about the code had changed between the two runs. What had changed
was how many other jobs were sharing the runner: a merge to `main` starts
the CI matrix, the conformance suite, the interop suite and CodeQL at
once, and `ubuntu-latest` runners are not free.

Re-running the failed job passed, which is the point. A re-run that fixes
it proves the code was never the problem.

The budget is now 30 seconds, as a named constant with the reasoning
attached, because a bare number invites the next person to tighten it back
to five. The asymmetry sets it: a startup that is merely slow costs the
runner a few seconds, and a startup that times out costs the whole run its
green.

This is the second flake in this file from the same root cause. The first
was the port reservation, fixed in c69b77ac. A test whose failure mode is
"the machine was busy" rather than "the code is wrong" is not measuring
what it claims to measure.

build failed because the CLI read a library constant that only exists with
  `http`.

### Tests

- **Every definition of every revision round-trips.** (`fc097e9f`,
  `1828c10f`) The property suite covered 62 of 708 `(revision, definition)`
  pairs; `build.rs` now writes the table from the schemas themselves, so a
  revision that gains a definition gains a case. Field identifiers are
  pinned across all six revisions — no two members of an object collapse to
  one field, and every identifier is legal.

## [0.7.0] — 2026-10-27

A minor, and the reason is that the answer to "which revision is this
session speaking?" was wrong in a way a peer could not work around.
=== in-scope SECURITY.md ===
accepted but the response is slower. A report of an active exploit
should also carry a phone number in the first message; an
"actively exploited" report that is only on a tracker is read in
working-hours order, not in incident order.

## What is in scope

Anything in the four crates' source that affects a consumer's trust
boundary, the wire surface, or a peer of the library:

- **JSON-RPC envelope routing** — wrong id routing, wrong method
  dispatch, frame framing errors that let a peer smuggle extra
  bytes through a `&RawValue` parse.
- **Wire codec behaviour** — a `tools/call` argument that the
  application refused but the codec accepted, or a result the
  application trusted but the codec lost a field on. The codec
  never silently drops a field; if it appears to, that is a bug.
- **Capability gating** — a `FeatureProfile::is_enabled` answer
  that lets a path run when the negotiated capabilities do not
  cover it. A `list_changed` notification sent to a peer that
  did not advertise `list_changed` is always a bug.
- **Token handling** — redaction failures at the tracing layer
  (the test is `tests/secret_logging.rs`), bearer-token leaks
  in error paths, PKCE verifier leakage, OAuth state
  non-entropy.
- **HTTP transport hardening** — `Origin` allowlist bypass,
  DNS-rebinding via `Host`-header mismatch, request-deadline
  or concurrency-ceiling bypass, missing or wrong rate-limit
  knob.
- **Filesystem-backed resources** — path canonicalisation
  failures, a `..` traversal that escapes the allowed root,
  symlink handling that lets a resource read outside its
  declared scope.
- **Fuzz harness regressions** — the harness in
  `crates/protocol-droid/fuzz/` runs nightly; a found input
  is itself a reproducer and is in scope.
- **Build / supply chain** — a `cargo deny` finding that
  bypasses the CI gate, a vendored schema that drifted from
  the manifest, a transitive dependency that drops a security
  patch.

# Changelog

All notable changes to `protocol-droid` are recorded here. The format follows
[Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/), and the project
adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html).

Every entry cites the commit that made the change, so a claim here can be
checked against the code rather than taken on the changelog's word.

## [Unreleased]

## [0.8.0] — 2026-11-04

### Added

- **A UTCP v1.1 client.** (`6cecc9ec`, `f2bf39b6`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/adapters/secondary/utcp/`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/utcp/`) Point it at a provider's URL,
  read the manual it publishes, and call one of the tools in it. The URL is
  the only thing the caller supplies, so everything else comes out of the
  document that URL served — and the document is not trusted to widen its own
  permissions: `allowed_communication_protocols` is taken from the caller's
  registration, defaults to the manual's own protocol type and nothing else,
  and is applied at registration and again before every call. Behind the
  `utcp` feature.

- **An ACP agent can be served over stdio, and can call the editor back.**
  (`964c6a28`, `6b6801f1`, `7ade7487`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/adapters/secondary/acp/`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/domain/acp/`) `serve_acp_agent` reads the
  editor's requests, routes them to a handler, and writes the replies, with a
  handler error becoming a JSON-RPC error of the matching code.
  `send_request` and `send_typed_request` carry the other direction —
  `session/request_permission`, `fs/read_text_file`, `terminal/create` — and
  `authenticate`, `session/set_mode` and `session/set_config_option` are now
  typed, which leaves all twelve agent request methods typed. Behind
  `acp-experimental`, because the ACP specification is pre-1.0.

- **`IdleReaper`, `MonotonicClock` and `SessionReport`.** (`2da5507d`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/adapters/primary/transport/http/reaper.rs`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/adapters/secondary/clock.rs`) The first sweeps
  idle sessions out of a `SessionStore`, the second is the production
  `Clock` the port never had, and the third tells an operator why a bridge
  session ended. `bridge --idle-timeout <SECONDS>` sets the window.

### Changed

- **An HTTP server evicts a session that has been idle for 30 minutes.**
  (`2da5507d`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/adapters/primary/transport/http/serve/builder.rs`)
  A session used to live until the client sent `DELETE`. A client that opened
  sessions and left cost the server a map entry each time, and a bridge a
  task and an upstream connection each time, with no limit. `HttpBuilder`
  now sweeps by default; `with_idle_reaper` changes the window and
  `without_idle_reaper` restores the old behaviour. A client whose session
  was evicted gets `404` on its next request, which the specification tells
  it to answer by starting a new session — including one that held only a
  standing `GET` stream and sent nothing.

  `HttpBridge::with_idle_reaper` is opt-in, because the bridge is handed its
  store and cannot know what else shares it. It refuses a store built without
  `SessionStore::with_idle_reaper` rather than reaping nothing. The `bridge`
  command turns it on with a 30 minute default and `--idle-timeout 0` turns
  it off. `tokio/time` is now part of the `http` feature.

- **Every feature-matrix row cites the URL that documents it.** (`22cd58bf`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/domain/feature.rs`) 32 rows named a revision,
  12 an SEP number and one a URL, so a reader could follow almost none of
  them. Each row now carries a `citation`, and the same URL is in the doc
  comment on its `Feature` variant, with a test reading the file back to
  hold the two together.

- **The cross-protocol bridge is two protocol adapters and one composition,
  not a hand-written translator for every pair of protocols.** (`2289b30c`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/protocol_adapter.rs`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/mcp_adapter.rs`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/a2a_adapter.rs`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/composed.rs`) The MCP ↔ A2A
  translation was a pair of functions that knew both vocabularies — one that
  turned `SendMessage` into `tools/call`, one that turned it back. A third
  protocol would have needed two more, and the pair nobody wrote about would
  have been the pair nobody tested.

  The translation now lives in per-protocol adapters behind a
  `ProtocolAdapter` seam, and `ComposedCodec` puts two of them together:
  lift on the way out, lower on the way back, with the IR in between. An
  adapter knows one protocol and does not mention the other, so a bridge
  between two protocols nobody wrote a translator for works the same way as
  the one that was.

  The IR gained the types the adapters meet at — `IrCall`, `IrMethod` and
  `IrOutcome` at `crates/protocol-droid/src/domain/ir/call.rs` — and a loss
  that has no counterpart on the other side is now recorded in the
  translation report rather than dropped in silence: an A2A part with no MCP
  counterpart, a task's artifacts, and structured content with no A2A
  counterpart are all reported.

  `CrossBridgePeer::new` lost its `downstream_side` parameter. The codec is
  built from a downstream adapter and an upstream adapter, so it knows which
  side it is; a caller that passed the side separately could disagree with
  the codec, and the disagreement would have shown up as a method the bridge
  refused for no visible reason.

### Fixed

- **The A2A leg of the bridge sent the agent arguments it could not read.**
  (`2289b30c`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/a2a_adapter.rs`) An MCP
  `tools/call` carried `arguments` as an object, and the bridge put it on the
  A2A wire inside a data part as `{"data": {"data": {…}}}`. The agent read
  the call's arguments out of the nested object rather than the object
  itself, so a tool that expected `{"query": "weather"}` was handed
  `{"data": {"query": "weather"}}`.

- **The A2A leg of the bridge wrote a `kind` key the spec does not name.**
  (`2289b30c`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/bridge/a2a_adapter.rs`) A part was
  written as `{"kind": "data", "data": {…}}`. The spec's part shape is the
  proto's `oneof content`: the object has exactly one of `text`, `file` or
  `data` as a top-level field, with no discriminator. That is what the
  crate's own A2A server sends, what the A2A conformance fixtures expect,
  and what the vendored `a2a.proto` describes — so the bridge was speaking
  a dialect of A2A that the rest of the crate does not speak.

- **A generated union picked its arm by member order.** (`c22bfd84`,
  `crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/emit.rs`) A `tools/call`
  request decoded as an `InitializeRequest`, and a `2026-07-28` result landed
  in the generic `Result` arm. Nothing showed it: every generated type
  carries a flattened catch-all, so a value in the wrong arm re-serialises to
  byte-identical JSON. A union now reads the member the specification
  requires of every alternative — `type`, `method` — and an absent or
  unknown value is a decode error. Where no such member exists the arm is
  chosen by the value's shape, and the specification's order breaks a tie.

- **A schema member named `self`, `super` or `crate` generated a field that
  did not compile.** (`09732f65`,
  `crates/protocol-droid-schema/src/generator/emit.rs`) `field_ident` tried
  the raw-identifier branch first and the trailing-underscore branch second,
  on the same predicate, so the second could never run and `self` came out as
  `r#self`, which rustc rejects. The three now take a trailing underscore,
  `gen` is reserved for edition 2024, and a member that starts with a digit
  gains a leading underscore. No vendored schema has such a member today; the
  next upstream one would have broken the build. An unreferenced 305-line
  `naming.rs` carrying a second, drifted copy of these rules is gone.

- **A bridge session's inbound queue grew without limit, and its errors went
  nowhere.** (`2da5507d`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/adapters/primary/transport/http/bridge.rs`) A
  client could `POST` faster than the upstream answered and the queue took
  all of it. It now holds 256 messages and answers `429` with `Retry-After`
  past that. A session whose loop ended in an error — an upstream that could
  not be reached, a client channel that failed — was dropped by `let _ =`;
  `with_session_report` hands it to the operator, and the `bridge` command
  prints it to stderr.

- **Eight rustdoc links named private or ambiguous items.** (`b7d73634`)
  `cargo doc` failed on the branch, and the lean `--no-default-features`
  build failed because the CLI read a library constant that only exists with
  `http`.

### Tests

- **Every definition of every revision round-trips.** (`fc097e9f`,
  `1828c10f`) The property suite covered 62 of 708 `(revision, definition)`
  pairs; `build.rs` now writes the table from the schemas themselves, so a
  revision that gains a definition gains a case. Field identifiers are
  pinned across all six revisions — no two members of an object collapse to
  one field, and every identifier is legal.

## [0.7.0] — 2026-10-27

A minor, and the reason is that the answer to "which revision is this
session speaking?" was wrong in a way a peer could not work around.

A session now speaks the revision the peer negotiated. Before this it
spoke the newest revision the build could speak — the transport's ceiling —
whatever the peer asked for. Three things followed from that, and all three
were visible to a peer rather than to the library.

**A peer could be sent a shape it cannot parse.** A tool result is lowered
for the session's revision, and each revision has its own codec, so a
`2024-11-05` peer was sent `2025-11-25` shapes: a `structuredContent` its
schema has no field for, and content blocks such as `audio` that its schema
has no type for at all. A peer that asked for an older revision could be
sent something it could not parse.

**A client could be refused for being right.** `MCP-Protocol-Version` is an
assertion, not a fallback — a present header that disagrees with the
negotiated revision is a protocol error — but the comparison was against the
ceiling, so a client that sent the revision it had just negotiated was
answered `400`, while a client that sent the ceiling was accepted.

**A handler could not learn what it was speaking.** `PeerSession::negotiated`
is documented as "the revision this session actually settled on", and it
answered with the ceiling. A consumer that wanted to report its own version
had to report a *range* of revisions rather than the one in use.

This release carries everything since 0.6.0 in one entry. `v0.6.1` was
tagged and prepared but never published — its run stopped at the `release`
environment gate and was abandoned rather than forced — so there is no
0.6.1 on crates.io and there never will be. The version was skipped, not
backfilled.

### Fixed

- **A session reported the transport's ceiling instead of the revision it
  negotiated.** (`65c3f9a7`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/server/dispatch/mod.rs`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/application/server/context.rs`) `PeerSession::negotiated`
  is documented as "the revision this session actually settled on", and it
  answered with the ceiling — the newest revision the build could speak —
  whatever the peer asked for. The handshake narrowed the session's *profile*
  and left its *revision* alone, so the version that `negotiate` had already
  resolved was used to build the reply and then dropped.

  A handler could not learn which revision it was speaking, so a consumer
  that wanted to report its own version had to report a range of revisions
  rather than the one in use. The gate's refusal named the ceiling too, and
  the refusal exists precisely to say what was negotiated: "elicitation is
  unavailable" is an answer nobody can act on without knowing what *was*
  agreed.

  The fix narrows the revision with the profile, in the same place the
  profile was already narrowed. The two move together because the profile is
  resolved *for* the revision: the profile says which features exist, and the
  revision says how to spell them, so a session that knew one but not the
  other refused the features the older revision does not have and still
  answered in the newer revision's shape for everything else.

  The shape is not a detail. A tool result is lowered for the session's
  revision, and each revision has its own codec, so a `2024-11-05` peer was
  sent results spelled for `2025-11-25` — a `structuredContent` its schema
  has no field for, and content blocks such as `audio` that its schema has
  no type for at all. A peer that asked for an older revision could be sent
  something it cannot parse.

  Two paths were already right and are unchanged: the stateless lifecycle
  builds a peer per request from the revision the request names, and legacy
  HTTP+SSE negotiates the one revision its transport defines.

- **A client that sent the `MCP-Protocol-Version` header it had negotiated
  was refused.** (`65c3f9a7`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/src/adapters/primary/transport/http/serve/`)
  The header is an assertion, not a fallback: a present
  `MCP-Protocol-Version` that disagrees with the negotiated revision is a
  protocol error, and it is rejected rather than reconciled. But the
  comparison was against the session's ceiling rather than the revision it
  settled on, so a client that offered `2024-11-05` and sent
  `MCP-Protocol-Version: 2024-11-05` was answered `400`, while a client that
  sent the ceiling was accepted. Both follow from the same root cause.

- **The `a2a_js_interop` test could fail for a reason that had nothing to
  do with what it measures.** (`c69b77ac`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/tests/a2a_js_interop.rs`,
  `crates/protocol-droid/tests/fixtures/a2a_reference_server.mjs`) The test
  reserved a port by binding `127.0.0.1:0`, read the number, dropped the
  listener, and handed the number to the Node reference server. Between the
  drop and the child's bind, another process could take the port; the child
  died with `EADDRINUSE` and the test reported it as "the reference server
  closed stderr before listening", which says nothing about the A2A wire
  format. It failed twice on `macos-latest` in CI, both times with correct
  code.

  The kernel now assigns the port: the child asks for port 0, and the bind
  that claims the port and the bind that reports it are the same syscall, so
  there is no window for anything to slip into. The reference server reports
  the port it was actually given rather than the one it asked for, and its
  agent card is built from that same bound port. The test is also faster —
  3.48 s to 0.17 s — because it no longer waits on a port it has to race
  for.

- **The `bench_gate` smoke test measured the machine as much as the
  decoder.** (`c69b77ac`, `crates/protocol-droid/tests/bench_gate.rs`) It took one
  wall-clock sample and compared it to a threshold. A wall-clock sample
  measures the machine as much as the code: the same decoder measured
  4 300 ns per iteration on an idle machine and 59 563 ns on a busy one, a
  14× spread against a threshold of 15 100 ns. The failure said "the decoder
  got slower", which was false.

  The measurement is now the fastest of ten samples rather than a single
  one — the fastest sample is the one least disturbed by the OS preempting
  the test thread, and a real regression is present in every sample, so the
  minimum still catches it. Measured under a load average of 20, the fastest
  of ten samples was 4 640 ns while the median was 12 179 ns and the
  slowest was 22 079 ns: the minimum recovers the uncontended cost, the
  median does not.

  The threshold was wrong independently of the noise. It scaled the committed
  release-mode baseline by 15, a dev/release cost ratio guessed when the
  test was written and never revisited; the real ratio is about 21. A
  threshold computed from 15 is 15 100 ns, where the contract says 5× the
  baseline — which put the threshold *below* the cost of an uncontaminated
  decode on a loaded machine, and is why the test was tripping on noise.
  The 100 ns padding term is gone as well: a pad on top of "5× the
  baseline" means a decoder that is exactly 5× slower does not trip the
  gate, which is not what a 5× gate means.

  A second test now pins the contract, by asking the gate's own comparison
  whether a synthetic 5× slower decoder trips it and whether an
  uncontaminated one does not. Without it the constants could be loosened
  until the gate stopped catching anything, and nothing would say so — the
  failure mode of a gate that has quietly stopped gating is silence. The
  gate was checked against a real regression too: a slowdown injected into
  `decode` was caught at 25 615 ns against the 20 000 ns threshold, and
  reverted.

### Changed

- **Dependency bumps.** (`b85bcb31`, `e8d878bd`) `tokio` 1.53.3 → 1.54.1,
  `arc-swap` 1.9.2 → 1.9.3, `jsonschema` 0.58.6 → 0.60.2 and `ureq`
  3.4.2 → 3.5.0. The `jsonschema`
  bump crosses a minor version and the crate's API did move, but it is a
  dev-dependency — it validates generated values against the vendored
  `schema.json` and nothing else — so the change is confined to the test
  suite.

### Documentation

- **`docs/benchmarks.md` described a CI bench job that does not exist.**
  (`c69b77ac`, `docs/benchmarks.md`) The document described a job that runs the divan
  benches and compares their medians against `baselines.json` with a 10 %
  threshold in either direction. There is no such job, and `baselines.json`
  is read by nothing but the documentation. The document now says what is
  actually there: the `bench_gate` smoke test is the automated performance
  gate, and the committed baselines are reference data for a human reading a
  bench run.

  The reason the divan benches are not in CI is the same reason the smoke
  test now reads the fastest of ten samples: a wall-clock measurement on a
  shared runner measures the runner. A 10 % threshold there is not a
  stricter gate, it is a noisier one. Wiring those benches into CI needs a
  runner that is not shared, and is its own piece of work.

- **The release guide did not say what a stalled release leaves behind.**
  (`site/src/content/docs/guides/release.md`) The guide described the
  `release` environment and the approval it needs, and stopped there. It did
  not say what happens when the approval never comes — which is what happened
  to `v0.4.2` and `v0.6.1`, so crates.io skips those two numbers and a reader
  who sees `0.5.3 → 0.7.0` has no explanation for the gap.

  The guide now says that a stalled run is not a failure to diagnose: the
  crates were never uploaded, so there is nothing to un-publish, and what the
  run needs is either an approval or a decision to abandon it and move to the
  next version. It also says that a superseding release folds the abandoned
  one's contents forward rather than backfilling the number.

## 0.6.1 — never published

`v0.6.1` was tagged and its release run built every binary and verified
packaging, but it stopped at the `release` environment gate and was
abandoned rather than forced. No 0.6.1 was ever uploaded, so crates.io
goes 0.6.0 → 0.7.0 with nothing at 0.6.1. The tag is still on the commit
it marked, because that commit is real history; only the publish never
happened.

Its contents are folded into 0.7.0 above. Nothing that was written for
0.6.1 was lost — it was superseded, not abandoned mid-flight.

## [0.6.0] — 2026-10-26

A minor, and the reason is that the `#[server]` attribute grew a field.

`#[server]`'s `into_server()` built the server with `Server::builder(name)`
and no version, so `serverInfo.version` reported the version of the
`protocol-droid` crate the consumer happened to be linked against — not the
consumer's own version. The escape hatch (`ServerBuilder::version`) existed,
but reaching it meant hand-writing the builder chain, which means giving up
the macro's registration. A server that merely links `protocol-droid` is not
`protocol-droid`, and a peer asking which version a server is asks about the
server.

### Added

- **`version = ...` on the `#[server]` attribute.** The field takes an
  **expression** rather than a string literal:

  ```rust
  #[protocol_droid::server(name = "greeter", version = env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION"))]
  ```

  The `env!` is expanded in the *consuming* crate, because a proc-macro
  expansion is compiled in the crate that uses it. The version is therefore
  written once — there is no second copy to drift — and a consumer that
  bumps its own manifest has nothing else to update. A literal still works,
  for a server whose version is not in a manifest, and a non-string literal
  is refused with a message that names the fix rather than a trait-bound
  error about `Into<String>`.

  The cross-crate proof is a trybuild pass case
  (`crates/protocol-droid/tests/ui/pass/server_version.rs`). A test *inside*
  `protocol-droid` cannot make the claim, because there the consuming
  crate's version and the dependency's are the same string; a trybuild case
  is its own crate at version `0.0.0`, so the two are distinguishable. The
  case was checked against a mutation that hard-codes the dependency's
  version, and fails with the mismatch it is supposed to catch.

- **A test that fails if a committed lockfile stops being scanned.**
  (`crates/protocol-droid/tests/supply_chain_coverage.rs`) The failure mode
  is silent — a workflow edit that drops a step leaves a green CI run and a
  lockfile nobody scans. The test reads the workflow, works out which
  manifests are scanned, and fails if any committed lockfile is not among
  them.

### Changed

- **A server built by `#[server]` reports the version of the crate that
  wrote it.** With no `version` field, the default is now the consuming
  crate's own version rather than `protocol-droid`'s — the macro emits the
  same `env!` the explicit form would, so a server that names no version no
  longer claims to be the dependency.

  This is the one change here a consumer can notice without asking for it,
  so it is worth stating plainly: a peer that was told `0.5.3` is now told
  the consumer's own version. The old answer was wrong — it was a fact
  about the dependency rather than about the server — but a consumer
  matching on the old string will see a difference. That is why this is a
  minor and not a patch.

  A server built by hand through `Server::builder` is unaffected and still
  defaults to `protocol-droid`'s own version, which is right for a server
  that *is* this crate.

### Fixed

- **CI now scans every committed lockfile, not just the root one.** The
  `supply chain` job ran `cargo deny` against the root `Cargo.lock` only,
  while three lockfiles outside the workspace — `fuzz`, `interop_rmcp` and
  `interop_ts_sdk` — were excluded from the workspace and so from that
  scan. The gap was not theoretical: when `ctutils` was bumped to 0.4.5 for
  RUSTSEC-2026-0385, the root lockfile was updated and the interop
  fixture's was not, so the fixture kept the vulnerable version until the
  pre-push hook blocked the push.

  Each of the three new steps passes `--locked`. Without it, `cargo metadata`
  re-resolves and rewrites the lockfile, so the scan would report on a
  dependency set nobody committed. The cost is that a workspace version bump
  invalidates those lockfiles, which now fail the job instead of going
  stale; the release procedure records how to refresh them.

- **The pre-push hook no longer passes an `unsound` advisory.** `cargo audit`
  files an `unsound` advisory under `warnings` rather than `vulnerabilities`
  and exits zero for it by default, so the hook — which read only
  `vulnerabilities.count` — reported a lockfile carrying a use-after-free
  advisory as clean. The hook now passes `-D unsound -D yanked` and reads
  all three categories out of the report, matching the set `deny.toml`
  denies. A hook that passes where CI fails is worse than no hook.

  A yanked crate is reported separately from an advisory, because the
  remedies differ: an advisory can be waived in `deny.toml`, while a yanked
  crate has no advisory id to ignore and can only be fixed by updating the
  lockfile.

### Documentation

- **The "Write a server" guide described an API that does not exist.**
  (`site/src/content/docs/guides/write-a-server.md`) It showed
  `use protocol_droid::prelude::*`, a `#[server]` attribute on a *struct*,
  a `Dispatcher` *trait* a consumer implements, and a `Server::new(..)` /
  `serve(config)` pair — none of which is the crate's shape. The real API
  is `#[protocol_droid::server]` on an *impl block*, `Dispatcher` is a
  struct rather than a trait, and the entry points are
  `Server::builder(name)` and `serve_stdio` / `serve_http`. A reader
  following the guide would not have got a compiling program.

  The guide now also says what the attribute has to be attached to and
  why: an attribute macro only sees the item it is on, so a `#[server]`
  on a struct cannot see the `impl` beside it, and every tool in that
  `impl` would be invisible to it.

- **The quickstart imported a `prelude` module and described a runtime
  the library does not build.**
  (`site/src/content/docs/getting-started/quickstart.md`) There is no
  `protocol_droid::prelude`. The tip block also said `serve_stdio` builds
  a runtime; it is `async` and runs on whatever runtime the caller
  already has, which is what the `#[tokio::main]` in the same snippet is
  for.

## [0.5.3] — 2026-10-25

A patch for the `#[server]` macro, and a security fix that a patch is the
right shape for.

The macro fix is the reason this release exists: a consumer using
`#[server]` / `#[tool]` had to add `schemars` to their own `Cargo.toml` or
the generated code would not compile. The error pointed at the `#[server]`
attribute rather than at the macro, so the natural first reaction —
`use schemars;` — does not help.

The advisory is the reason the patch reaches the dependency graph at all.
`ctutils 0.4.3` has a non-constant-time mask generation, and it reaches
this crate through `hmac 0.13` → `digest 0.11.3` → `ctutils`. The fix is a
lockfile update, not an API change, so a patch is what it is.

### Changed

- **Dependency advisories on the repository are down from 28 to 1.** The
  remaining one is `esbuild` (low, `GHSA-g7r4-m6w7-qqqr`) in
  `site/pnpm-lock.yaml`. Dependabot reports the update as
  `security_update_not_possible` — latest resolvable `0.27.7`, lowest
  non-vulnerable `0.28.1` — but that is a resolution result rather than a
  proof that no fix exists, since `0.28.1` is published and vite's peer range
  admits it. A `pnpm.overrides` entry forcing `esbuild: 0.28.1` is the untried
  path. The advisory covers the `astro dev` server on Windows; the published
  site is static output and never runs it.

  [`docs/dev/repo-operations.md`](docs/dev/repo-operations.md#the-one-advisory-that-stays-open)
  records the analysis.

- **The documentation site is built in CI.** (`.github/workflows/site.yml`)
  Nothing built `site/` before, so a green PR on that directory said nothing
  about the site. Dependabot's astro 5 → 7 PR passed fourteen green Rust
  checks and did not build; the only reason it was caught before production
  was a local `pnpm build`.

  The new job installs with `--frozen-lockfile`, runs `astro check` (which
  the build does not do on its own), builds, and asserts the output has the
  expected shape. It is a required status check, so a broken site blocks the
  merge.

  Two details worth knowing. The workflow has no `paths:` filter, because a
  path-filtered workflow reports no check run when the filter does not match,
  and a required check that never reports blocks every merge; the filter is
  applied to the build steps instead, so the job always reports. And the node
  version is pinned to `22.23.4`, the floor astro 7 declares, rather than the
  newest release — proving the site builds on the oldest runtime it claims to
  support. `pnpm` is pinned the same way, through the `packageManager` field
  in `site/package.json`.

  Documented in
  [`docs/dev/repo-operations.md`](docs/dev/repo-operations.md#ci-builds-this-site).

### Fixed

- **The `#[server]` macro no longer needs the consumer to depend on
  `schemars`.** (`dbea59a3`, #63) A consumer of `protocol-droid` that used
  `#[server]` / `#[tool]` had to add `schemars` to its own `Cargo.toml` to
  make the generated code compile, and the error pointed at the `#[server]`
  attribute rather than at the macro.

  The generated argument struct derives `JsonSchema` through this crate's
  re-export, but the derive expands to unqualified `schemars::…` paths that
  resolve against the *consuming* crate's root. `schemars` 1.x honours the
  derive's `crate` attribute — it emits `use <path> as schemars;` inside the
  `const _` block it wraps the expansion in, shadowing the unresolved name
  for every path it expands to, including the `where`-clause bounds — so one
  attribute per generated struct fixes it.

  The regression test lives in `crates/protocol-droid-cli/tests/` because
  that crate is the workspace's one consumer of `protocol-droid` that does
  *not* depend on `schemars`. Every test inside `protocol-droid` is blind to
  this: that crate depends on `schemars` itself, so it is in the extern
  prelude of its own tests whatever the expansion does. The test also reads
  the generated `inputSchema` back out of the registry, so a redirect
  pointing at the wrong crate fails there rather than passing a compile
  check.

### Security

- **`ctutils` is fixed rather than waived.** (`RUSTSEC-2026-0385`, medium)
  `ctutils 0.4.3`'s `Choice` mask generation could compile to a branch on
  secret values, and `ctutils`' `u128` comparisons were not constant-time on
  32-bit targets. `ctutils 0.4.4` fixes it; this workspace takes `0.4.5`.

  This one is reachable, and it is worth being precise about where. The path
  is `protocol-droid` → `hmac 0.13` → `digest 0.11.3` → `ctutils`, and
  `ctutils` is pulled in by `digest`'s `mac` feature rather than by
  `hmac`'s own use of it — `digest/src/mac.rs` does `use ctutils::CtEq;` and
  calls `ct_eq(tag)` to compare a MAC tag. Our own HMAC comparison in
  `application/mcp/input_required.rs` is exactly that path:
  `StateKey::open` verifies a `requestState` MAC with `verify_slice`. A
  constant-time regression there is a real defect and not a theoretical one.

  0.5.2 shipped the vulnerable version in all four crates' `Cargo.lock`, and
  `protocol-droid-cli` publishes its lockfile, so the published binary
  carried it. A consumer who resolves fresh gets `0.4.5` from the caret
  requirement on `ctutils 0.4`; a consumer whose own lockfile still pins
  `0.4.3` needs `cargo update -p ctutils`.

- **All four committed lockfiles now carry the patched `ctutils` and the
  current `protocol-droid` version.** The three excluded from the workspace
  (`fuzz`, `interop_rmcp`, `interop_ts_sdk`) had drifted: the root lockfile
  moved to `ctutils 0.4.5` and the interop fixture's did not, so it kept the
  vulnerable `0.4.3` until the pre-push hook blocked the push. The other two
  were staler still, pinning `protocol-droid 0.1.0` against a workspace at
  0.5.2.

  All four are current now, and each records `ctutils 0.4.5`. The hook scans
  every committed lockfile, so this is the state it was already asking for;
  the drift was that nobody had run it since the advisory landed. The CI gap
  this exposes is recorded in `SECURITY.md` rather than closed here.

- **`RUSTSEC-2026-0387` on `crypto-bigint 0.5.5` is waived, with the
  argument written down.** (`deny.toml`) It is reached through
  `jsonwebtoken`'s `rust_crypto` backend → `p256`/`p384` → `ecdsa` →
  `elliptic-curve`, and there is no upgrade path: the fix sits behind
  `p256`/`p384 0.14`, which `jsonwebtoken 11.1.0`'s caret requirements
  (`^0.13.2` / `^0.13.0`) do not admit, and 11.1.0 is the latest release
  whose `master` carries the same pins.

  It is unreachable because the only path to `elliptic-curve` here is ECDSA
  *verification*. `ecdsa`'s `verify_prehashed` runs on the public key, the
  message hash and the signature's own `r` and `s` — no secret scalar
  reaches the affected operations. The signing path (`sign_prehashed`, which
  calls `k.invert()` on a secret scalar) is the reachable one and this crate
  has no path to it: `jsonwebtoken`'s `EllipticCurveKeyParameters` carries
  only `kty`, `crv`, `x` and `y`, so a JWK has no field in which to carry a
  private scalar.

  The waiver carries that argument in full, so the next person to read
  `deny.toml` does not have to re-derive it.

- **`enforce_admins` is on.** (`.github/branch-protection.json`) It was
  `false`, which meant a repository admin could push straight to `main` and
  bypass the pull-request requirement. Enabling Dependabot's alerts made this
  worth closing: an advisory is now reported against the repository, and the
  person who would fix it could also skip the review saying the fix is right.

  The release chain is unaffected — Auto Tag pushes a tag, and branch
  protection applies to branches, not tags.

- **`ip-address` in the interop fixture is fixed rather than suppressed.**
  (`GHSA-rxp7-6hxx-x8q5`, medium) Dependabot proposed this as #55 and it was
  closed in favour of an ignore rule, on the reasoning that a transitive bump
  churns a lockfile whose job is to hold the SDK at one version. That
  reasoning was wrong: the SDK's own declared range is `^10.2.0`, so 10.7.4
  was always permitted. The bump moves three lines, leaves
  `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` at `1.32.1`, and takes the fixture's
  `npm audit` from one moderate to zero. The ignore rule is removed.

  `npm install` does not do this on its own — it honours the lockfile, so
  10.7.3 stayed installed until the lockfile was updated deliberately. The
  `dependabot.yml` entry for that directory is kept for exactly this
  reason: without it there is no schedule watching a lockfile that only
  changes by hand.
