## [0.4.0] — 2026-10-19

A server can now require OAuth from public API alone, and publish the document
a client needs to find out how. Closes
[#33](https://github.com/greysquirr3l/protocol-droid/issues/33).

### Added

- **The RFC 9728 protected-resource metadata document is served.**
  (`e1767c9`) A client that receives a `401` reads the `WWW-Authenticate`
  challenge, follows it to the metadata document, and learns where to get a
  token. Until now the challenge could name a URL nothing was serving.
  `ResourceMetadata` gained the `Serialize` impl RFC 9728 §2 defines, with
  §3.2's omit-when-empty rule; `serve_protected_resource` returns a
  `GET`-only router for deployments that need the document on a different
  origin than the MCP endpoint.
- **The metadata document mounts itself.** (`31d82af`)
  `with_resource_metadata` mounts the route on the MCP router and points the
  `401` challenge at the same URL, both read from one value, so the two cannot
  drift apart. The route deliberately skips the authenticator — an escape route
  cannot require the credential it explains how to obtain — and still passes
  the same `Host` and rate-limit checks as every other route.

### Fixed

- **The default build did not compile.** (`0fd17f1`)
  `cargo check --workspace --all-targets` failed on default features because
  the `a2a_serving` bench imported `adapters::secondary::a2a` without
  `required-features = ["a2a"]`. CI missed it because it ran
  `cargo test --workspace`, which skips benches. The matrix now checks
  `--all-targets` per feature set.
- **Intra-doc links were broken and rustdoc was ungated.** (`ad7ce31`) Six
  unresolved links under lean features, and nothing in CI ran `cargo doc`, so
  they could not reach `main`. CI now gates on `--all-features`.
- **The `auth` module doc described T16 as future work.** (`7d8902d`) It had
  shipped; the doc still said it had not, which is how a reader concludes the
  resource-server half does not exist.

### Documented

- **Requiring a credential on a server.** (`db69cdc`, `2752b01`) The security
  guide documented the client OAuth flow in detail and the resource-server half
  not at all. It now covers `with_authenticator`, `with_policy`, the
  auto-mounted document, and the fail-closed contract that refuses to build a
  route table when an authenticator is wired without a policy. The snippet is
  compiled, not hand-written — an earlier draft cited four import paths that
  did not exist.
- **A chain test ties the `401` challenge to the served route.** (`db69cdc`)
  Both halves existed; nothing proved they named the same URL. The test fails
  on a wrong resource, a wrong path, and on config that names a document it
  does not serve.
- **An assembly test answers [#33](https://github.com/greysquirr3l/protocol-droid/issues/33)'s
  question.** (`2752b01`) The issue claimed a server could not require OAuth
  without assembling internals. It could, and can still — the test builds one
  from public API alone, which is what the claim needed.

### Previously unreleased fixes from `0.3.0`

- **The `0.3.0` binaries job could not produce a release.** (`ce3ed1d`) Three
  separate faults, each fatal on its own: the job had no `contents: write`, so
  it could not create the draft release it was uploading to; the musl targets
  had no C compiler for `ring`; and the Windows build ran under PowerShell,
  which cannot parse `set -euo pipefail`. `cargo --bin` was also given the
  target name with its `.exe`.
- **Two test assertions printed the very secrets they police.** (`6011212`) A
  panic message is a log line, and one test interpolated a full session id into
  its failure message while another named the offending credential in the
  assertion that exists to stop credentials reaching an error string — so the
  one circumstance in which the value reached a CI log was the one where the
  test caught it leaking. The second now reports which of the three went wrong
  without reprinting it; the first names the delta, which was the whole
  diagnosis anyway.
- **The docs site could not install.** (`9c79168`) pnpm 11 refuses to install
  while a dependency's build script is neither allowed nor denied, and both
  `esbuild` and `sharp` still held the placeholder value, which broke
  `pnpm build` and the deploy script. Both genuinely need their install step:
  `esbuild` fetches its platform binary, `sharp` its native module.

## [0.3.0] — 2026-10-19

Conformance is now green on every revision the pinned suite covers, on both
sides. The server matrix is 3/3, 55/55, 81/81 and 151/151 on `2025-03-26`,
`2025-06-18`, `2025-11-25` and `2026-07-28` (`2026-07-28` was 81/119). The
client matrix, newly run, is 2/2, 18/18 and 32/32 on `2025-06-18`,
`2025-11-25` and `2026-07-28`, OAuth included. Most of the gap was library
behaviour, not fixture work, and several of the fixes apply to every revision.

### Added

- **Runtime registration that announces itself.** (`927f9d0`) `Server::handle()` returns a
  clone-able `ServerHandle` that adds and removes tools, resources, templates
  and prompts while serving. Each change is published and then sent as
  `notifications/{tools,resources,prompts}/list_changed` to every session whose
  negotiated profile includes the matching `listChanged` — on stdio, on a
  Streamable HTTP session, and on a `2026-07-28` listen stream. Before this the
  server emitted no `list_changed` on any revision, and a tool added while
  serving was listed but could not be called.
- **`ServerHandle::notify_resource_updated`.** (`927f9d0`) `resources/subscribe` (and
  `resourceSubscriptions` on a listen stream) now record a real subscription,
  so the `resources.subscribe` capability the server advertises is honoured.
- **The `2026-07-28` stateless lifecycle over HTTP, in full** (`927f9d0`): per-request
  `_meta` validation, `MCP-Protocol-Version` / `Mcp-Method` / `Mcp-Name` and
  `Mcp-Param-*` checked against the body (`-32020`), `-32022` echoing the
  requested version, `-32021` with `requiredCapabilities`, `404` for removed and
  unknown methods, `subscriptions/listen`, and `serverInfo` in every result's
  `_meta`.
- **SEP-2322 multi round-trip requests.** (`927f9d0`) `InputRequired` builds an interim
  result; `RequestContext::input_response`, `request_state` and `seal_state`
  read and write the retry. `requestState` is HMAC-SHA256-sealed under a
  per-server key, so a tampered state is refused before any handler runs.
- **A stateless HTTP client.** (`927f9d0`) `StatelessHttpClient`, reached through
  `Client::connect_to` with an `http-stateless:` spec, sends the per-request
  `_meta` and headers and mirrors `x-mcp-header` arguments.
- **Sampling and elicitation over stdio.** (`927f9d0`) The serve loop keeps reading while
  a handler waits on the client, delivers the answer, and queues any request
  that arrives meanwhile so replies keep their order.
- **The `2026-07-28` lifecycle over stdio** (`a2cadea`): stateless requests,
  `subscriptions/listen` on the shared channel, cancellation of an in-flight
  request or a listen stream, and the same `-32022` / `-32021` data as HTTP.
- **OAuth client building blocks** (`a2cadea`): `WWW-Authenticate` parsing, discovery URL
  ordering, canonical resource URI, scope selection and step-up, metadata
  parsing with issuer validation, `client_secret_basic` / `_post` / public
  token authentication, and the `authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported`
  rule (an advertising server that omits `iss` is refused).
- **An OAuth 2.1 client that runs the whole flow.** (`687d90e`) `OAuthAuthorizer` handles a
  `401` or `403`: protected-resource metadata, authorization-server discovery,
  PKCE `S256` verification, client selection (held, pre-registered, metadata
  document, dynamic registration), scope selection and step-up, `resource`
  taken verbatim from the metadata, `iss` checks, and redemption. Pass it to
  `ConnectOptions::authorizing` and the Streamable HTTP and stateless clients
  retry with the token. It stops after three refusals. It passes every
  `auth/*` scenario of the client conformance suite on `2025-11-25` and
  `2026-07-28`.
- **Sign in from a browser.** (`dbde884`) `LoopbackBrowser` is a `UserAgent` that opens the
  authorization URL (web URLs only) and receives the redirect on a loopback port,
  with a timeout. `protocol-droid inspect <server> --oauth list` uses it; a client
  registered ahead of time is named by `PROTOCOL_DROID_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID` and
  `PROTOCOL_DROID_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET`, never by a flag.
- **`probe` recognises a legacy HTTP+SSE endpoint.** (`288ff83`) A URL that refuses every `POST`
  with a 4xx is retried as `sse:` (the 2025-03-26 backward-compatibility rule),
  and the result is reported only if that works.
- **Refresh tokens.** (`a89bb63`) `OAuthAuthorizer` keeps the refresh token a login returns and
  trades it for a new access token when the server says the token is no longer
  good, so an expired token no longer sends the user back through consent. A
  spent or revoked refresh token is forgotten and the full flow runs; a
  challenge for more scope skips the refresh. `TokenEndpoint::refresh` is a
  new defaulted method, so existing implementors still compile.
- **A `Server` over the legacy HTTP+SSE transport.** (`4f904b6`) `HttpBuilder::legacy_sse()`
  (or `legacy_sse_at(stream, message)`) mounts the `2024-11-05` routes beside
  Streamable HTTP on one listener. The same tools, resources and prompts answer
  on both, `list_changed` and progress go out on the session's stream, a tool
  can ask the client a question, and a client offering a later revision is
  answered with `2024-11-05`. `LegacyDispatcher::dispatch` is now async and
  carries per-session state (`LegacySession`, `LegacyDispatcher::open`).
- **The bridge forwards to a `2026-07-28` stateless upstream.** (`8598ad5`) `protocol-droid
  bridge --upstream http-stateless:http://host/mcp` lets a `2025-11-25` (or
  older) client use a stateless server: the upstream's revision is discovered
  once, and each forwarded request carries it and the bridge's capabilities in
  its own `_meta`. `TransportPeer` is the library piece, usable over any
  `ClientTransport`.
- **`conformance_reference_server --legacy-sse`** (`6332dce`) mounts the `2024-11-05` routes
  beside `/mcp`, as a runnable example of `HttpBuilder::legacy_sse()`; probe it
  with `protocol-droid probe sse:http://127.0.0.1:8080/sse`.
- **`Host` checking and rate limiting on the legacy routes.** (`4f904b6`) They had `Origin`
  and authentication but neither of these, so a rebound DNS name or a flood of
  `POST`s reached the dispatcher.
- **`a2a` implies `http`.** (`687d90e`) Building with `--features a2a` alone did not compile.
- **A comparative benchmark against `rmcp`.** (`dbf2cd6`) `interop_rmcp`'s `compare` binary
  drives both stdio servers with the same client; the two are within about 5 %
  of each other (`docs/benchmarks.md`).

### Changed

- **`LegacyDispatcher::dispatch` is async and carries per-session state.**
  (`4f904b6`) It gains an associated `Session` type and an `open` method, and the
  router's session store now holds a `LegacySession`. Anyone who implemented the
  trait must update; the crate's own implementors did.
- **A legacy HTTP+SSE session negotiates only `2024-11-05`.** (`4f904b6`) A client
  offering a later revision is answered with it, because it is the only revision
  that defines the transport.
- **The idempotency store keeps the last 4 096 finished results rather than
  refusing new work once full.** (`dbf2cd6`) A retry is replayed while it is within
  that window; an older one runs again. A store full of running calls still
  refuses. See *Fixed*.
- **Documentation.** (`67e076a`) The CLI reference is rewritten against the binary's real
  flags, and the guides cover OAuth sign-in, the legacy server, the stateless
  bridge and the security checks.

### Fixed

- **A server stopped answering `tools/call` after its 4 096th call.** (`dbf2cd6`) The
  idempotency store filled with finished results and refused every new request
  id from then on, so any long-lived session or server failed permanently. It
  now drops the oldest *finished* result to make room, never one still running.
- **The legacy HTTP+SSE client never matched a numeric reply id.** (`4f904b6`) It
  compared the awaited id as the string `"1"` against the number `1` on the
  wire, so any server that answered with a numeric id left every request waiting.
- **The bridge offered its upstream the oldest revision first** (`8598ad5`), so it
  negotiated `2024-11-05` with every server that still accepted it. It now offers
  the newest revision that has a handshake.
- **A finished tool result from a `2026-07-28` server could not reach an older
  client.** (`8598ad5`) `resultType: "complete"` was treated as a feature the older
  revision lacks. Older revisions say the same thing by omitting the field, so
  the bridge now forwards it; `input_required` is still refused.
- **`protocol-droid bridge --allow-downgrade` could not be used while serving.**
  (`8598ad5`) clap required `--check-result` beside it, so only the probe could
  receive the flag.
- **A `default-features = false` build warned about an unused import** in the
  client connector. (`687d90e`)

- **A numeric `progressToken` was echoed back as a string** (`927f9d0`) on every revision,
  so a client correlating by value never matched its progress.
- **stdio delivered no progress or log notifications.** (`927f9d0`) The peer's sink was a
  placeholder that refused every frame, and the progress token was never read.
- **`logging/setLevel` was accepted and ignored.** (`927f9d0`) It now filters; at
  `2026-07-28` a request without `logLevel` receives no log records.
- **Stateless requests shared one session id** (`927f9d0`), so two clients reusing a
  request id for the same tool were answered with each other's recorded result.
- **Listings wrote `"description": null`** (`927f9d0`) for an absent description, which no
  revision's schema admits.
- **Methods a revision removed were still answered** (`927f9d0`) (`ping`,
  `logging/setLevel` and `resources/(un)subscribe` at `2026-07-28`).
- **The HTTP client never sent `MCP-Protocol-Version`** (`927f9d0`) after negotiating
  `2025-06-18` or later.
- **`protocol-droid probe` reported `2026-07-28` as refused** (`927f9d0`) by servers that
  support it: its `server/discover` carried no `_meta`. A Streamable HTTP
  target's stateless revisions are now probed with the stateless client.
- **The Release workflow failed on every green push** that did not create a
  tag. It now reports "nothing to release" and skips (`d7fe867`).

## [0.2.0] — 2026-10-17

A minor bump, not a patch: `ServerBuilder::resource` and `::prompt` are renamed
to `resource_with` / `prompt_with`, and a bare `#[resource]` is now a compile
error. That breaks source for anyone who registered a listing-only resource,
so under semver it is `0.2.x` rather than `0.1.x`. All four crates ship at the
same version.

The five commits below are the whole of the delta since `v0.1.0`, and all of
them close gaps on the path a consuming project takes: what a tool can answer
with, what a server can serve, and who the server thinks is calling.

### Added

- **A `#[tool]` handler can answer with any content block** (`a359baf`). A
  handler whose return type is `ToolResult` now takes a path that lowers
  through the existing `WireToolResults` codec at the session's negotiated
  revision, rather than being shaped by the macro into a single text block.
  Images, audio blocks, and embedded resources become reachable from `#[tool]`
  for the first time. A block the negotiated revision cannot express is refused
  under `DegradePolicy::strict` rather than quietly dropped — audio is answered
  at `2025-03-26` and refused at `2024-11-05`.
- **`resources/read` and `prompts/get`** (`2fcb9d6`). Both methods were
  absent: the dispatcher answered seven methods and refused the rest, so a
  server could register resources, advertise them in `resources/list`, and then
  fail to hand one over. Registration is opt-in via `resource_with` alongside
  `resource`, and `prompt_with` alongside `prompt`.
  - `ResourceContents` and `GetPromptResult` land as pure IR with no
    serialisation of their own; assembly lives in `application/server/read.rs`
    because it depends on the negotiated revision.
  - A prompt's content block goes through the tool codec rather than a second
    copy of it, so `prompts/get` cannot drift from `tools/call` on a field a
    later revision adds.
  - Neither method is idempotency-keyed, unlike `tools/call`: a read has no side
    effect to protect, and a key would make two legitimate concurrent reads of
    one URI collide into `DuplicateInFlight`.

### Changed

- **A bare `#[resource]` or `#[prompt]` is now a compile error** (`51f78f7`).
  `ServerBuilder::resource` and `prompt` registered a listing with no way to
  serve it, and the dispatcher could not tell that apart from a URI the server
  never had — both answered `InvalidParams`. That breaks a promise on the wire
  rather than at the call site that built it. The listing-only methods are gone
  rather than deprecated:

  ```rust
  #[resource(reader = serve_it)]   // a reader must be named
  ```

  **Migrating from 0.1.x.** `ServerBuilder::resource` and `::prompt` become
  `resource_with` and `prompt_with`, taking the handler as a second argument:

  ```rust
  // 0.1.x
  Server::builder("app").build().resource(my_resource);
  // 0.2.0
  Server::builder("app").build().resource_with(my_resource, serve_it);
  ```

  The methods are renamed rather than the old pair deprecated, so the compiler
  names the replacement instead of leaving a listing that still does not serve.
  `resources/read` and `prompts/get` did not work in 0.1.x at all — the
  dispatcher answered `UnknownMethod` — so nothing that worked stops working.

  The reader is named rather than inferred from a convention: a convention works
  until a resource's contents are read by a helper three impls away, and then it
  registers the wrong method or silently registers nothing — both surface to a
  client as a resource that lists and will not open. Six compile-fail fixtures
  pin each error message.

### Fixed

- **The release workflow published crates in the wrong order.** The loop read
  `schema → protocol-droid → macros → cli`, but `protocol-droid` depends on
  `protocol-droid-macros`, so crates.io cannot resolve it until the macros
  crate is published. Publishing the macros *last* makes the library's own
  `cargo publish` fail with `no matching package named
  \`protocol-droid-macros\` found`. Both the dry-run and the real publish loop
  now order by the dependency graph: `schema → macros → protocol-droid → cli`.
  The same wrong order was documented in the release guide and is fixed there
  too. This would have failed at tag time, on the first real release, with
  nothing in CI to have caught it.
- **The library no longer hardcodes its sibling versions.** `protocol-droid`
  depended on `protocol-droid-macros` with a literal `version = "0.1.0"`, so
  bumping `[workspace.package]` produced a build failure rather than a version
  bump. The macro crate is now a proper `[workspace.dependencies]` entry and
  inherits, which means one list to bump instead of a pin that silently
  disagrees with it.

- **A handler now sees the authenticated principal on every transport**
  (`6a81010`, `2f91316`). `PeerSession` documented `with_auth` as the way a
  real principal arrives, and no transport in the tree ever called it — so a
  `#[tool]` handler's `ctx.peer().auth()` reported the anonymous default even
  when the request had authenticated successfully. This failed closed (anonymous
  is default-deny), but it left a consumer with no way to attribute an action to
  a caller on HTTP: no audit trail, no per-caller policy, no per-caller quota.
  - *Streamable HTTP* (`6a81010`): the principal is resolved per request and
    overlaid onto that request's own copy of the peer. The stored session keeps
    the anonymous default — session state outlives the credential that produced
    it, and a principal recorded there has the wrong lifetime for a token that
    can be refreshed, replaced, or withdrawn mid-session. The new
    `PeerSession::without_auth` makes that stored-peer shape explicit and is what
    a persisted handshake result stores.
  - *Legacy HTTP+SSE* (`2f91316`): `LegacyDispatcher::dispatch` now takes an
    `&AuthContext` as its first parameter, resolved per request. A legacy session
    is nothing but an event tail, so there is no session state for a principal
    to be pinned to anyway.
  - *stdio* (`2f91316`): `StdioBuilder::auth` lets the deployment declare the
    principal for the life of the connection. There is nothing on a pipe to
    authenticate, and the alternative was unreachable rather than merely
    awkward — a scope-gated tool is invisible to an anonymous session, so a
    stdio server registering a `Write`-scoped tool could never serve it.
- **`protocol-droid-cli` manifest parses again** (`2f91316`). It inherited
  `categories` from a `workspace.package` that does not define it. That is a
  hard parse failure, not a warning: any `cargo` command touching the workspace
  failed to load the manifest. Now `command-line-interface`, which exists as a
  crates.io slug, rather than `command-line-utilities`, which does not.

### Known gaps

- **Conformance matrix is below target on three revisions.** `tools-call-error`
  fails on `2025-06-18`, `2025-11-25`, and `2026-07-28`. The root-cause
  analysis and the six-step order of operations for closing the matrix are in
  [`docs/CONFORMANCE-GAPS.md`](docs/CONFORMANCE-GAPS.md); the short version is
  that the codecs and session engine round-trip every wire shape the suite
  checks, and the failing scenarios are asking the reference-server fixture for
  tools and prompts it does not yet register.

## [0.1.0]

Initial release. Workspace, vendored schemas at pinned commits, `ProtocolVersion`
and the feature catalogue, the canonical IR with six lift/lower codecs, the
single-pass JSON-RPC router and session engine, all four transports with both
server and client halves, OAuth 2.1, HTTP hardening, the A2A and ACP protocol
modules, and the `bridge` / `probe` / `inspect` / `record` / `replay` /
`conformance` CLI surface.

# Security Policy

## Supported versions

`protocol-droid` is published as four crates (`protocol-droid-schema`,
`protocol-droid`, `protocol-droid-macros`, `protocol-droid-cli`) on
crates.io. Security advisories are issued against the latest released
minor version; the previous minor receives advisories for **30 days**
after a new minor ships. The `main` branch is built and tested on
every push; advisories against `main` only are evaluated case by case
because the work to backport a fix is small but a backport is not
guaranteed to be free of merge conflicts on the older minor.

| Crate                    | Latest stable | Previous minor |
| ------------------------ | ------------- | -------------- |
| `protocol-droid-schema`  | `0.8`         | `0.7`          |
| `protocol-droid`         | `0.8`         | `0.7`          |
| `protocol-droid-macros`  | `0.8`         | `0.7`          |
| `protocol-droid-cli`     | `0.8`         | `0.7`          |

All four share one version — every member inherits `version` from
`[workspace.package]`, so there is no series in which the crates
disagree. The 0.x line means the semver contract is not yet stable, not
that the versions are unmaintained.

Published on crates.io: 0.3.0, 0.4.0, 0.4.1, 0.4.3, 0.5.0, 0.5.1 and
newer. 0.3.x and everything before it are past the 30-day window that
follows a minor and are not maintained.

The MSRV (1.98.1) and the supported Rust toolchain are pinned in
[`rust-toolchain.toml`](https://github.com/greysquirr3l/protocol-droid/blob/main/rust-toolchain.toml)
and in `[workspace.package].rust-version`; advisories on the
compilation surface (not the wire surface) are evaluated against the
MSRV, not the latest stable.

## Reporting a vulnerability

**Use [GitHub's private vulnerability reporting](https://github.com/greysquirr3l/protocol-droid/security/advisories/new)**
for the initial report. That channel encrypts the message in transit,
restricts the audience to the maintainer, and gives a unique URL to
track the conversation.

Please include:

1. The version(s) of the four crates that are affected, pinned
   exactly (e.g. `protocol-droid = "0.1.3"`).
2. A reproducer — a server fixture, a wire capture, an upstream peer
   that triggers the issue, or a unit-test-shaped snippet. The
   reproducer does not have to be public; the test that lands as the
   fix is enough.
3. The impact, in the words of the threat model below. "I can read
   other users' files" is more useful than "path traversal"; "the
   `X-Remote-User` header is trusted without validation" is more
   useful than "missing auth check".
4. Whether the report is embargoed. Default is no embargo; if a CVE
   or coordinated disclosure matters, name the date and the
   recipients.

Reports that arrive out of band — by email, by issue, by DM — are
accepted but the response is slower. A report of an active exploit
should also carry a phone number in the first message; an
"actively exploited" report that is only on a tracker is read in
working-hours order, not in incident order.

## What is in scope

Anything in the four crates' source that affects a consumer's trust
boundary, the wire surface, or a peer of the library:

- **JSON-RPC envelope routing** — wrong id routing, wrong method
  dispatch, frame framing errors that let a peer smuggle extra
  bytes through a `&RawValue` parse.
- **Wire codec behaviour** — a `tools/call` argument that the
  application refused but the codec accepted, or a result the
  application trusted but the codec lost a field on. The codec
  never silently drops a field; if it appears to, that is a bug.
- **Capability gating** — a `FeatureProfile::is_enabled` answer
  that lets a path run when the negotiated capabilities do not
  cover it. A `list_changed` notification sent to a peer that
  did not advertise `list_changed` is always a bug.
- **Token handling** — redaction failures at the tracing layer
  (the test is `tests/secret_logging.rs`), bearer-token leaks
  in error paths, PKCE verifier leakage, OAuth state
  non-entropy.
- **HTTP transport hardening** — `Origin` allowlist bypass,
  DNS-rebinding via `Host`-header mismatch, request-deadline
  or concurrency-ceiling bypass, missing or wrong rate-limit
  knob.
- **Filesystem-backed resources** — path canonicalisation
  failures, a `..` traversal that escapes the allowed root,
  symlink handling that lets a resource read outside its
  declared scope.
- **Fuzz harness regressions** — the harness in
  `crates/protocol-droid/fuzz/` runs nightly; a found input
  is itself a reproducer and is in scope.
- **Build / supply chain** — a `cargo deny` finding that
  bypasses the CI gate, a vendored schema that drifted from
  the manifest, a transitive dependency that drops a security
  patch.

## How a vulnerability gets found

A report is the best route and not the only one. Five things run without
anyone looking:

| Where | What it checks | Coverage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `supply chain` CI job | `cargo deny` against a freshly fetched advisory database | all four committed lockfiles |
| Dependabot alerts | advisory database against every manifest | root, `site/`, and the interop fixture |
| Secret scanning | credential patterns across the history and every push | whole repository |
| CodeQL | `security-and-quality` queries over the Rust source | every push to `main`, every pull request, and weekly |
| `pre-push` hook | `cargo audit` over every committed lockfile | all four, including the three outside the workspace |

Two gaps are worth stating plainly rather than leaving to be discovered:

**Every committed lockfile now gets a CI-side advisory watch.** Until the
`supply chain` job was extended, it scanned the root lockfile only.
`crates/protocol-droid/fuzz/`, `crates/protocol-droid/tests/interop_rmcp/`
and `crates/protocol-droid/tests/interop_ts_sdk/` are excluded from the
workspace, so `cargo deny` never saw their dependency graphs; the pre-push
hook covered them locally, which is a mitigation, not equivalent coverage.

The job now scans all four, one step per lockfile, and each of those
steps passes `--locked`. Without `--locked`, `cargo metadata` re-resolves
the graph and rewrites the lockfile on disk, so the scan would report on
a dependency set nobody committed — a different check, not a stricter
one. With `--locked`, the scan reports on the lockfile as committed, and
fails loudly when that lockfile is stale.

That gap was not theoretical. When `ctutils` was bumped to 0.4.5 for
RUSTSEC-2026-0385, the root `Cargo.lock` was updated and the interop
fixture's was not, so the fixture kept `ctutils 0.4.3` until the pre-push
hook blocked the push. The hook was the only thing that saw it, and the
lockfile it caught was stale on more than the advisory: it still pinned
`protocol-droid 0.1.0` against a workspace at 0.5.2.

The `interop_ts_sdk` fixture is the one case where a manifest *is* watched:
Dependabot's security updates reach it, and it is declared in
`dependabot.yml` so a transitive advisory gets a bump proposal rather than
sitting unnoticed. Note that `npm install` honours the committed lockfile,
so it will not self-heal — the lockfile has to be updated on purpose. The
other two are Rust, and are now covered by CI as well as by the hook.

**The site is built in CI, but the peer-range gap is still worth knowing.**
The `site` job installs with `--frozen-lockfile`, runs `astro check` and
`astro build`, and asserts the output has the expected shape, so a change
under `site/` that does not build fails the PR rather than passing every
check. It was not always so: Dependabot's astro 5 → 7 PR passed fourteen green
Rust checks without building, because starlight 0.30 pins `astro: ^5.0.0` and
`pnpm install` does not enforce peer ranges — the failure appears only at
build time. `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` does not change that; it
enforces the *lockfile*, not the peer ranges.

`deny.toml` is the single list of accepted advisories, and it is the same
list the `pre-push` hook reads. A waiver belongs there with a reason saying
why the advisory is unreachable from this code; there is no second place to
record one.

## What is out of scope

- **The consumer's deployment.** A consumer that disables TLS
  verification on its own `reqwest` client, that does not set
  `Content-Security-Policy` on its own HTTP server, that picks
  a token-storage adapter that is not `OsSecrets` and stores
  the token in a world-readable file — that is the consumer's
  deployment, not this library.
- **A2A peers that are not under the consumer's control.** A
  push-notification webhook URL that resolves to a private
  network is refused by the SSRF denylist at config time, and
  re-validated at delivery time. A URL that resolves to a
  public network the consumer did not intend to send to is a
  consumer-configuration problem.
- **A peer that has compromised the consumer's process.** The
  library's parsers are fuzzed against malicious input; a peer
  that already has code execution on the consumer's host is
  not in the threat model.
- **MCP revisions older than the lowest vendored one.** The
  library does not claim to speak revisions it does not have
  wire types for. A consumer who needs revision `X` and
  `X` is not in `crates/protocol-droid-schema/spec/` is not
  in scope.
- **The CLI's own configuration file format.** The CLI is a
  thin adapter; the configuration it parses is the consumer's
  to validate, and a bad config is the consumer's error, not
  a security issue.

## Response timeline

| Step                                        | Window          |
| ------------------------------------------- | --------------- |
| Initial acknowledgement                     | 7 days          |
| Triage and impact assessment                | 30 days         |
| Patch landed (or status update)             | 60 days         |
| Public advisory and CVE request (if needed) | 90 days         |
| Embargoed release at the consumer's request | by request      |

A "status update" in the 60-day row is a maintainer message in
the original advisory thread explaining what is blocking and
what the next step is — a patch that needs a contract change,
a reproducer that does not reproduce, a CVE that is still in
the CNA queue. The status update is what prevents a silent
60-day pause.

## Security model

The library is **default deny**:

- An `AuthContext` is a required parameter on every stateful
  port method. There is no path through the library that does
  not carry one.
- Authorization predicates are pure domain functions. The
  predicate that says "this user can see this resource" lives
  in `domain/`, not in an adapter; the adapter hands it the
  data and applies the answer.
- TLS verification is on by default. A `reqwest` client with
  certificate verification disabled is not constructed; the
  library has no path to do so.
- Path canonicalisation refuses a `..` traversal that escapes
  the allowed root with a typed error, not a panic.
- Tokens, Authorization headers, session ids in full, and
  elicitation responses are redacted at the tracing-layer
  boundary. The test that proves the redaction list is
  complete is `tests/secret_logging.rs`.

The full design, including what the library does *not* do
(token storage, rate limiting, CORS) and what the consumer is
responsible for, is in the
[Security model guide](https://greysquirr3l.github.io/protocol-droid/guides/security/)
on the docs site. The audit that backs the no-finding summary
in this policy is in
[`SECURITY-REVIEW.md`](https://github.com/greysquirr3l/protocol-droid/blob/main/SECURITY-REVIEW.md).

## Coordinated disclosure

A 90-day window is the default. A reporter who needs more time
(an embargoed CVE, a downstream rollout that takes longer than
the patch) names the date in the first message; the maintainer
confirms or counters. An embargo that runs past 180 days is
reviewed at 180 days; a longer embargo is honoured only if the
reporter and the maintainer agree in writing.

A patch lands **before** the advisory is public, and the
advisory text is shared with the reporter for review at least
48 hours before publication. The patch is credited in the
advisory, in the release notes, and in the git history; the
reporter's preferred attribution (name, handle, or anonymous)
is honoured.

## Past advisories

None. The repository's first release was tagged after the
SECURITY-REVIEW audit in October 2026, and no vulnerability
has been reported against a tagged release.

## Dependency advisories in the published graph

A dependency advisory is not an advisory against this crate, but it is
still something a consumer of a published version inherits, so it is
recorded here.

**RUSTSEC-2026-0385 — `ctutils` — affected every published version up
to and including 0.5.2. Fixed in 0.5.3.**

`ctutils 0.4.3`'s `Choice` mask generation could compile to a branch
on secret values, and its `u128` comparisons were not constant-time on
32-bit targets. Upstream fixed it in `ctutils 0.4.4`.

The path into this crate is `protocol-droid` → `hmac 0.13` → `digest
0.11.3` → `ctutils`, and `ctutils` is pulled in by `digest`'s `mac`
feature rather than by `hmac`'s own use of it: `digest/src/mac.rs` does
`use ctutils::CtEq;` and calls `ct_eq(tag)` to compare a MAC tag. The
reachable path is this crate's own HMAC comparison in
`application/mcp/input_required.rs`, where `StateKey::open` verifies a
`requestState` MAC with `verify_slice`. That is a real comparison over a
value derived from a server-held key, so the regression is a genuine
defect and not a theoretical one.

What a consumer needs to know:

- **A library consumer** resolves their own dependency graph, so a
  fresh resolve picks up a patched `ctutils` on its own. A consumer
  whose own lockfile still pins `ctutils 0.4.3` should run
  `cargo update -p ctutils`; the requirement is `^0.4`, so the patched
  version is already permitted.
- **A binary consumer** of `protocol-droid-cli` is the case that needs
  attention. A binary crate publishes its `Cargo.lock`, and `cargo
  install` honours it, so `cargo install protocol-droid-cli --version
  0.5.2` installed a binary built against `ctutils 0.4.3`. 0.5.3 ships
  the patched version, as does every release since.

The advisory was published on 2026-10-23, after 0.5.2 was tagged on
2026-10-22, so the fix could not have shipped in 0.5.2.

**RUSTSEC-2026-0387 — `crypto-bigint` — waived, not fixed.**

`crypto-bigint 0.5.5` has a constant-time regression in its `u128`
operations. It is reached through `jsonwebtoken`'s `rust_crypto`
backend → `p256`/`p384` → `ecdsa` → `elliptic-curve`, and no upgrade
path exists: the fix sits behind `p256`/`p384 0.14`, which
`jsonwebtoken 11.1.0`'s caret requirements do not admit.

It is unreachable from this code. The only path to `elliptic-curve` is
ECDSA *verification*, which runs on the public key, the message hash
and the signature's own `r` and `s` — no secret scalar reaches the
affected operations. The signing path is the reachable one and this
crate has no path to it: `jsonwebtoken`'s `EllipticCurveKeyParameters`
carries only `kty`, `crv`, `x` and `y`, so a JWK has no field in which
to carry a private scalar.

The waiver and its full reasoning live in
[`deny.toml`](https://github.com/greysquirr3l/protocol-droid/blob/main/deny.toml),
which is the single list of accepted advisories. It should be re-read
whenever `jsonwebtoken` or `rsa` changes, not waited on a schedule.

## Acknowledgements

The threat model and the no-finding summary draw on the
[OWASP Top 10:2025](https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/) and
[OWASP API Security Top 10:2023](https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0x11-t10/)
checklists. The MCP-spec-specific surface is read against the
official [Model Context Protocol specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/)
and the [conformance suite](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/conformance).

---

*This policy is reviewed at every minor release and at every
change to the wire-codec surface. A change to the supported-
versions table or to the response-timeline rows is a release
note, not a docs-only change.*

ECDSA *verification*, which runs on the public key, the message hash
and the signature's own `r` and `s` — no secret scalar reaches the
affected operations. The signing path is the reachable one and this
crate has no path to it: `jsonwebtoken`'s `EllipticCurveKeyParameters`

to carry a private scalar.

whenever `jsonwebtoken` or `rsa` changes, not waited on a schedule.

note, not a docs-only change.*

# Security Policy

## Supported versions

`protocol-droid` is published as four crates (`protocol-droid-schema`,
`protocol-droid`, `protocol-droid-macros`, `protocol-droid-cli`) on
crates.io. Security advisories are issued against the latest released
minor version; the previous minor receives advisories for **30 days**
after a new minor ships. The `main` branch is built and tested on
every push; advisories against `main` only are evaluated case by case
because the work to backport a fix is small but a backport is not
guaranteed to be free of merge conflicts on the older minor.

| Crate                    | Latest stable | Previous minor |
| ------------------------ | ------------- | -------------- |
| `protocol-droid-schema`  | `0.8`         | `0.7`          |
| `protocol-droid`         | `0.8`         | `0.7`          |
| `protocol-droid-macros`  | `0.8`         | `0.7`          |
| `protocol-droid-cli`     | `0.8`         | `0.7`          |

All four share one version — every member inherits `version` from
`[workspace.package]`, so there is no series in which the crates
disagree. The 0.x line means the semver contract is not yet stable, not
that the versions are unmaintained.

Published on crates.io: 0.3.0, 0.4.0, 0.4.1, 0.4.3, 0.5.0, 0.5.1 and
newer. 0.3.x and everything before it are past the 30-day window that
follows a minor and are not maintained.

The MSRV (1.98.1) and the supported Rust toolchain are pinned in
[`rust-toolchain.toml`](https://github.com/greysquirr3l/protocol-droid/blob/main/rust-toolchain.toml)
and in `[workspace.package].rust-version`; advisories on the
compilation surface (not the wire surface) are evaluated against the
MSRV, not the latest stable.

## Reporting a vulnerability

**Use [GitHub's private vulnerability reporting](https://github.com/greysquirr3l/protocol-droid/security/advisories/new)**
for the initial report. That channel encrypts the message in transit,
restricts the audience to the maintainer, and gives a unique URL to
track the conversation.

Please include:

1. The version(s) of the four crates that are affected, pinned
   exactly (e.g. `protocol-droid = "0.1.3"`).
2. A reproducer — a server fixture, a wire capture, an upstream peer
   that triggers the issue, or a unit-test-shaped snippet. The
   reproducer does not have to be public; the test that lands as the
   fix is enough.
3. The impact, in the words of the threat model below. "I can read
   other users' files" is more useful than "path traversal"; "the
   `X-Remote-User` header is trusted without validation" is more
   useful than "missing auth check".
4. Whether the report is embargoed. Default is no embargo; if a CVE
   or coordinated disclosure matters, name the date and the
   recipients.

Reports that arrive out of band — by email, by issue, by DM — are
accepted but the response is slower. A report of an active exploit
should also carry a phone number in the first message; an
"actively exploited" report that is only on a tracker is read in
working-hours order, not in incident order.

## What is in scope

Anything in the four crates' source that affects a consumer's trust
boundary, the wire surface, or a peer of the library:

- **JSON-RPC envelope routing** — wrong id routing, wrong method
  dispatch, frame framing errors that let a peer smuggle extra
  bytes through a `&RawValue` parse.
- **Wire codec behaviour** — a `tools/call` argument that the
  application refused but the codec accepted, or a result the
  application trusted but the codec lost a field on. The codec
  never silently drops a field; if it appears to, that is a bug.
- **Capability gating** — a `FeatureProfile::is_enabled` answer
  that lets a path run when the negotiated capabilities do not
  cover it. A `list_changed` notification sent to a peer that
  did not advertise `list_changed` is always a bug.
- **Token handling** — redaction failures at the tracing layer
  (the test is `tests/secret_logging.rs`), bearer-token leaks
  in error paths, PKCE verifier leakage, OAuth state
  non-entropy.
- **HTTP transport hardening** — `Origin` allowlist bypass,
  DNS-rebinding via `Host`-header mismatch, request-deadline
  or concurrency-ceiling bypass, missing or wrong rate-limit
  knob.
- **Filesystem-backed resources** — path canonicalisation
  failures, a `..` traversal that escapes the allowed root,
  symlink handling that lets a resource read outside its
  declared scope.
- **Fuzz harness regressions** — the harness in
  `crates/protocol-droid/fuzz/` runs nightly; a found input
  is itself a reproducer and is in scope.
- **Build / supply chain** — a `cargo deny` finding that
  bypasses the CI gate, a vendored schema that drifted from
  the manifest, a transitive dependency that drops a security
  patch.

## How a vulnerability gets found

A report is the best route and not the only one. Five things run without
anyone looking:

| Where | What it checks | Coverage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `supply chain` CI job | `cargo deny` against a freshly fetched advisory database | all four committed lockfiles |
| Dependabot alerts | advisory database against every manifest | root, `site/`, and the interop fixture |
| Secret scanning | credential patterns across the history and every push | whole repository |
| CodeQL | `security-and-quality` queries over the Rust source | every push to `main`, every pull request, and weekly |
| `pre-push` hook | `cargo audit` over every committed lockfile | all four, including the three outside the workspace |

Two gaps are worth stating plainly rather than leaving to be discovered:

**Every committed lockfile now gets a CI-side advisory watch.** Until the
`supply chain` job was extended, it scanned the root lockfile only.
`crates/protocol-droid/fuzz/`, `crates/protocol-droid/tests/interop_rmcp/`
and `crates/protocol-droid/tests/interop_ts_sdk/` are excluded from the
workspace, so `cargo deny` never saw their dependency graphs; the pre-push
hook covered them locally, which is a mitigation, not equivalent coverage.

The job now scans all four, one step per lockfile, and each of those
steps passes `--locked`. Without `--locked`, `cargo metadata` re-resolves
the graph and rewrites the lockfile on disk, so the scan would report on
a dependency set nobody committed — a different check, not a stricter
one. With `--locked`, the scan reports on the lockfile as committed, and
fails loudly when that lockfile is stale.

That gap was not theoretical. When `ctutils` was bumped to 0.4.5 for
RUSTSEC-2026-0385, the root `Cargo.lock` was updated and the interop
fixture's was not, so the fixture kept `ctutils 0.4.3` until the pre-push
hook blocked the push. The hook was the only thing that saw it, and the
lockfile it caught was stale on more than the advisory: it still pinned
`protocol-droid 0.1.0` against a workspace at 0.5.2.

The `interop_ts_sdk` fixture is the one case where a manifest *is* watched:
Dependabot's security updates reach it, and it is declared in
`dependabot.yml` so a transitive advisory gets a bump proposal rather than
sitting unnoticed. Note that `npm install` honours the committed lockfile,
so it will not self-heal — the lockfile has to be updated on purpose. The
other two are Rust, and are now covered by CI as well as by the hook.

**The site is built in CI, but the peer-range gap is still worth knowing.**
The `site` job installs with `--frozen-lockfile`, runs `astro check` and
`astro build`, and asserts the output has the expected shape, so a change
under `site/` that does not build fails the PR rather than passing every
check. It was not always so: Dependabot's astro 5 → 7 PR passed fourteen green

build time. `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` does not change that; it
enforces the *lockfile*, not the peer ranges.

list the `pre-push` hook reads. A waiver belongs there with a reason saying
why the advisory is unreachable from this code; there is no second place to
record one.

## What is out of scope

- **The consumer's deployment.** A consumer that disables TLS
  verification on its own `reqwest` client, that does not set
  `Content-Security-Policy` on its own HTTP server, that picks
  a token-storage adapter that is not `OsSecrets` and stores
  the token in a world-readable file — that is the consumer's
  deployment, not this library.
- **A2A peers that are not under the consumer's control.** A
  push-notification webhook URL that resolves to a private
  network is refused by the SSRF denylist at config time, and
  re-validated at delivery time. A URL that resolves to a
  public network the consumer did not intend to send to is a
  consumer-configuration problem.
- **A peer that has compromised the consumer's process.** The
  library's parsers are fuzzed against malicious input; a peer
  that already has code execution on the consumer's host is
  not in the threat model.
- **MCP revisions older than the lowest vendored one.** The
  library does not claim to speak revisions it does not have
  wire types for. A consumer who needs revision `X` and
  `X` is not in `crates/protocol-droid-schema/spec/` is not
  in scope.
- **The CLI's own configuration file format.** The CLI is a
  thin adapter; the configuration it parses is the consumer's
  to validate, and a bad config is the consumer's error, not
  a security issue.

## Response timeline

| Step                                        | Window          |
| ------------------------------------------- | --------------- |
| Initial acknowledgement                     | 7 days          |
| Triage and impact assessment                | 30 days         |
| Patch landed (or status update)             | 60 days         |
| Public advisory and CVE request (if needed) | 90 days         |
| Embargoed release at the consumer's request | by request      |

A "status update" in the 60-day row is a maintainer message in
the original advisory thread explaining what is blocking and
what the next step is — a patch that needs a contract change,
a reproducer that does not reproduce, a CVE that is still in
the CNA queue. The status update is what prevents a silent
60-day pause.

## Security model

The library is **default deny**:

- An `AuthContext` is a required parameter on every stateful
  port method. There is no path through the library that does
  not carry one.
- Authorization predicates are pure domain functions. The
  predicate that says "this user can see this resource" lives
  in `domain/`, not in an adapter; the adapter hands it the
  data and applies the answer.
- TLS verification is on by default. A `reqwest` client with
  certificate verification disabled is not constructed; the
  library has no path to do so.
- Path canonicalisation refuses a `..` traversal that escapes
  the allowed root with a typed error, not a panic.
- Tokens, Authorization headers, session ids in full, and
  elicitation responses are redacted at the tracing-layer
  boundary. The test that proves the redaction list is
  complete is `tests/secret_logging.rs`.

The full design, including what the library does *not* do

responsible for, is in the

A 90-day window is the default. A reporter who needs more time

confirms or counters. An embargo that runs past 180 days is
reviewed at 180 days; a longer embargo is honoured only if the
reporter and the maintainer agree in writing.

advisory text is shared with the reporter for review at least

advisory, in the release notes, and in the git history; the
reporter's preferred attribution (name, handle, or anonymous)

defect and not a theoretical one.

  version is already permitted.

ECDSA *verification*, which runs on the public key, the message hash
and the signature's own `r` and `s` — no secret scalar reaches the
affected operations. The signing path is the reachable one and this
crate has no path to it: `jsonwebtoken`'s `EllipticCurveKeyParameters`
carries only `kty`, `crv`, `x` and `y`, so a JWK has no field in which
to carry a private scalar.

whenever `jsonwebtoken` or `rsa` changes, not waited on a schedule.

note, not a docs-only change.*

restricts the audience to the maintainer, and gives a unique URL to
track the conversation.

1. The version(s) of the four crates that are affected, pinned

2. A reproducer — a server fixture, a wire capture, an upstream peer

   reproducer does not have to be public; the test that lands as the
   fix is enough.
3. The impact, in the words of the threat model below. "I can read
   other users' files" is more useful than "path traversal"; "the
   `X-Remote-User` header is trusted without validation" is more
   useful than "missing auth check".

   or coordinated disclosure matters, name the date and the
   recipients.

accepted but the response is slower. A report of an active exploit
should also carry a phone number in the first message; an
"actively exploited" report that is only on a tracker is read in
working-hours order, not in incident order.

Anything in the four crates' source that affects a consumer's trust
boundary, the wire surface, or a peer of the library:

- **JSON-RPC envelope routing** — wrong id routing, wrong method
  dispatch, frame framing errors that let a peer smuggle extra
  bytes through a `&RawValue` parse.
- **Wire codec behaviour** — a `tools/call` argument that the
  application refused but the codec accepted, or a result the
  application trusted but the codec lost a field on. The codec
  never silently drops a field; if it appears to, that is a bug.
- **Capability gating** — a `FeatureProfile::is_enabled` answer
  that lets a path run when the negotiated capabilities do not
  cover it. A `list_changed` notification sent to a peer that
  did not advertise `list_changed` is always a bug.
- **Token handling** — redaction failures at the tracing layer
  (the test is `tests/secret_logging.rs`), bearer-token leaks
  in error paths, PKCE verifier leakage, OAuth state
  non-entropy.
- **HTTP transport hardening** — `Origin` allowlist bypass,
  DNS-rebinding via `Host`-header mismatch, request-deadline
  or concurrency-ceiling bypass, missing or wrong rate-limit
  knob.
- **Resource exhaustion** — a session, queue or buffer that
  grows without bound because a peer opened it and left, or
  because the peer answers more slowly than it asks. A client
  that opens sessions and never closes them, or that `POST`s
  faster than the upstream answers, is the shape of this
  report; the bounded bridge inbox and the idle-session reaper
  are what keep the library on the right side of it.
- **Filesystem-backed resources** — path canonicalisation
  failures, a `..` traversal that escapes the allowed root,
  symlink handling that lets a resource read outside its
  declared scope.
- **Fuzz harness regressions** — the harness in
  `crates/protocol-droid/fuzz/` runs nightly; a found input
  is itself a reproducer and is in scope.
- **Build / supply chain** — a `cargo deny` finding that
  bypasses the CI gate, a vendored schema that drifted from
  the manifest, a transitive dependency that drops a security
  patch.

A report is the best route and not the only one. Five things run without
anyone looking:

| Where | What it checks | Coverage |
| --- | --- | --- |

| Dependabot alerts | advisory database against every manifest | root, `site/`, and the interop fixture |
| Secret scanning | credential patterns across the history and every push | whole repository |
| CodeQL | `security-and-quality` queries over the Rust source | every push to `main`, every pull request, and weekly |
| `pre-push` hook | `cargo audit` over every committed lockfile | all four, including the three outside the workspace |

`supply chain` job was extended, it scanned the root lockfile only.
`crates/protocol-droid/fuzz/`, `crates/protocol-droid/tests/interop_rmcp/`
and `crates/protocol-droid/tests/interop_ts_sdk/` are excluded from the
workspace, so `cargo deny` never saw their dependency graphs; the pre-push
hook covered them locally, which is a mitigation, not equivalent coverage.

steps passes `--locked`. Without `--locked`, `cargo metadata` re-resolves
the graph and rewrites the lockfile on disk, so the scan would report on
a dependency set nobody committed — a different check, not a stricter
one. With `--locked`, the scan reports on the lockfile as committed, and
fails loudly when that lockfile is stale.

RUSTSEC-2026-0385, the root `Cargo.lock` was updated and the interop
fixture's was not, so the fixture kept `ctutils 0.4.3` until the pre-push
hook blocked the push. The hook was the only thing that saw it, and the

  the token in a world-readable file — that is the consumer's
  deployment, not this library.

  push-notification webhook URL that resolves to a private
  network is refused by the SSRF denylist at config time, and
  re-validated at delivery time. A URL that resolves to a
  public network the consumer did not intend to send to is a
  consumer-configuration problem.

  library's parsers are fuzzed against malicious input; a peer
  that already has code execution on the consumer's host is
  not in the threat model.

  library does not claim to speak revisions it does not have
  wire types for. A consumer who needs revision `X` and
  `X` is not in `crates/protocol-droid-schema/spec/` is not
  in scope.
- **The CLI's own configuration file format.** The CLI is a
  thin adapter; the configuration it parses is the consumer's
  to validate, and a bad config is the consumer's error, not
  a security issue.

| Step                                        | Window          |
| ------------------------------------------- | --------------- |
| Initial acknowledgement                     | 7 days          |
| Triage and impact assessment                | 30 days         |
| Patch landed (or status update)             | 60 days         |
| Public advisory and CVE request (if needed) | 90 days         |
| Embargoed release at the consumer's request | by request      |

A "status update" in the 60-day row is a maintainer message in
the original advisory thread explaining what is blocking and
what the next step is — a patch that needs a contract change,
a reproducer that does not reproduce, a CVE that is still in

The library is **default deny**:

  port method. There is no path through the library that does
  not carry one.
- Authorization predicates are pure domain functions. The
  predicate that says "this user can see this resource" lives
  in `domain/`, not in an adapter; the adapter hands it the
  data and applies the answer.
- TLS verification is on by default. A `reqwest` client with
  certificate verification disabled is not constructed; the
  library has no path to do so.

  the allowed root with a typed error, not a panic.

  elicitation responses are redacted at the tracing-layer
  boundary. The test that proves the redaction list is
  complete is `tests/secret_logging.rs`.

reporter and the maintainer agree in writing.

[`rust-toolchain.toml`](https://github.com/greysquirr3l/protocol-droid/blob/main/rust-toolchain.toml)
and in `[workspace.package].rust-version`; advisories on the
compilation surface (not the wire surface) are evaluated against the
MSRV, not the latest stable.

## Reporting a vulnerability

**Use [GitHub's private vulnerability reporting](https://github.com/greysquirr3l/protocol-droid/security/advisories/new)**
for the initial report. That channel encrypts the message in transit,
restricts the audience to the maintainer, and gives a unique URL to
track the conversation.

Please include:

1. The version(s) of the four crates that are affected, pinned
   exactly (e.g. `protocol-droid = "0.1.3"`).
2. A reproducer — a server fixture, a wire capture, an upstream peer
   that triggers the issue, or a unit-test-shaped snippet. The
   reproducer does not have to be public; the test that lands as the
   fix is enough.
3. The impact, in the words of the threat model below. "I can read
   other users' files" is more useful than "path traversal"; "the
   `X-Remote-User` header is trusted without validation" is more
   useful than "missing auth check".
4. Whether the report is embargoed. Default is no embargo; if a CVE
   or coordinated disclosure matters, name the date and the
   recipients.

Reports that arrive out of band — by email, by issue, by DM — are
accepted but the response is slower. A report of an active exploit
should also carry a phone number in the first message; an
"actively exploited" report that is only on a tracker is read in
working-hours order, not in incident order.

## What is in scope

Anything in the four crates' source that affects a consumer's trust
boundary, the wire surface, or a peer of the library:

- **JSON-RPC envelope routing** — wrong id routing, wrong method
  dispatch, frame framing errors that let a peer smuggle extra
  bytes through a `&RawValue` parse.
- **Wire codec behaviour** — a `tools/call` argument that the
  application refused but the codec accepted, or a result the
  application trusted but the codec lost a field on. The codec
  never silently drops a field; if it appears to, that is a bug.
- **Capability gating** — a `FeatureProfile::is_enabled` answer
  that lets a path run when the negotiated capabilities do not
  cover it. A `list_changed` notification sent to a peer that
  did not advertise `list_changed` is always a bug.
- **Token handling** — redaction failures at the tracing layer
  (the test is `tests/secret_logging.rs`), bearer-token leaks
  in error paths, PKCE verifier leakage, OAuth state
  non-entropy.
- **HTTP transport hardening** — `Origin` allowlist bypass,
  DNS-rebinding via `Host`-header mismatch, request-deadline
  or concurrency-ceiling bypass, missing or wrong rate-limit
  knob.
- **Resource exhaustion** — a session, queue or buffer that
  grows without bound because a peer opened it and left, or
  because the peer answers more slowly than it asks. A client
  that opens sessions and never closes them, or that `POST`s
  faster than the upstream answers, is the shape of this
  report; the bounded bridge inbox and the idle-session reaper
  are what keep the library on the right side of it.
- **Filesystem-backed resources** — path canonicalisation
  failures, a `..` traversal that escapes the allowed root,
  symlink handling that lets a resource read outside its
  declared scope.
- **Fuzz harness regressions** — the harness in
  `crates/protocol-droid/fuzz/` runs nightly; a found input
  is itself a reproducer and is in scope.
- **Build / supply chain** — a `cargo deny` finding that
  bypasses the CI gate, a vendored schema that drifted from
  the manifest, a transitive dependency that drops a security
  patch.

## How a vulnerability gets found

A report is the best route and not the only one. Five things run without
anyone looking:

| Where | What it checks | Coverage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `supply chain` CI job | `cargo deny` against a freshly fetched advisory database | all four committed lockfiles |
| Dependabot alerts | advisory database against every manifest | root, `site/`, and the interop fixture |
| Secret scanning | credential patterns across the history and every push | whole repository |
| CodeQL | `security-and-quality` queries over the Rust source | every push to `main`, every pull request, and weekly |
| `pre-push` hook | `cargo audit` over every committed lockfile | all four, including the three outside the workspace |

Two gaps are worth stating plainly rather than leaving to be discovered:

**Every committed lockfile now gets a CI-side advisory watch.** Until the
`supply chain` job was extended, it scanned the root lockfile only.
`crates/protocol-droid/fuzz/`, `crates/protocol-droid/tests/interop_rmcp/`
and `crates/protocol-droid/tests/interop_ts_sdk/` are excluded from the
workspace, so `cargo deny` never saw their dependency graphs; the pre-push
hook covered them locally, which is a mitigation, not equivalent coverage.

The job now scans all four, one step per lockfile, and each of those
steps passes `--locked`. Without `--locked`, `cargo metadata` re-resolves
the graph and rewrites the lockfile on disk, so the scan would report on
a dependency set nobody committed — a different check, not a stricter
one. With `--locked`, the scan reports on the lockfile as committed, and
fails loudly when that lockfile is stale.

That gap was not theoretical. When `ctutils` was bumped to 0.4.5 for
RUSTSEC-2026-0385, the root `Cargo.lock` was updated and the interop
fixture's was not, so the fixture kept `ctutils 0.4.3` until the pre-push
hook blocked the push. The hook was the only thing that saw it, and the
lockfile it caught was stale on more than the advisory: it still pinned
`protocol-droid 0.1.0` against a workspace at 0.5.2.

The `interop_ts_sdk` fixture is the one case where a manifest *is* watched:
Dependabot's security updates reach it, and it is declared in
`dependabot.yml` so a transitive advisory gets a bump proposal rather than
sitting unnoticed. Note that `npm install` honours the committed lockfile,
so it will not self-heal — the lockfile has to be updated on purpose. The
other two are Rust, and are now covered by CI as well as by the hook.

**The site is built in CI, but the peer-range gap is still worth knowing.**
The `site` job installs with `--frozen-lockfile`, runs `astro check` and
`astro build`, and asserts the output has the expected shape, so a change
under `site/` that does not build fails the PR rather than passing every
check. It was not always so: Dependabot's astro 5 → 7 PR passed fourteen green
Rust checks without building, because starlight 0.30 pins `astro: ^5.0.0` and
`pnpm install` does not enforce peer ranges — the failure appears only at
build time. `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` does not change that; it
enforces the *lockfile*, not the peer ranges.

`deny.toml` is the single list of accepted advisories, and it is the same
list the `pre-push` hook reads. A waiver belongs there with a reason saying
why the advisory is unreachable from this code; there is no second place to
record one.

## What is out of scope

- **The consumer's deployment.** A consumer that disables TLS
  verification on its own `reqwest` client, that does not set
  `Content-Security-Policy` on its own HTTP server, that picks
  a token-storage adapter that is not `OsSecrets` and stores
  the token in a world-readable file — that is the consumer's
  deployment, not this library.
- **A2A peers that are not under the consumer's control.** A
  push-notification webhook URL that resolves to a private
  network is refused by the SSRF denylist at config time, and
  re-validated at delivery time. A URL that resolves to a
  public network the consumer did not intend to send to is a
  consumer-configuration problem.
- **A peer that has compromised the consumer's process.** The
  library's parsers are fuzzed against malicious input; a peer
  that already has code execution on the consumer's host is
  not in the threat model.
- **MCP revisions older than the lowest vendored one.** The
  library does not claim to speak revisions it does not have
  wire types for. A consumer who needs revision `X` and
  `X` is not in `crates/protocol-droid-schema/spec/` is not
  in scope.
- **The CLI's own configuration file format.** The CLI is a
  thin adapter; the configuration it parses is the consumer's
  to validate, and a bad config is the consumer's error, not
  a security issue.

## Response timeline

| Step                                        | Window          |
| ------------------------------------------- | --------------- |
| Initial acknowledgement                     | 7 days          |
| Triage and impact assessment                | 30 days         |
| Patch landed (or status update)             | 60 days         |
| Public advisory and CVE request (if needed) | 90 days         |
| Embargoed release at the consumer's request | by request      |

A "status update" in the 60-day row is a maintainer message in
the original advisory thread explaining what is blocking and
what the next step is — a patch that needs a contract change,
a reproducer that does not reproduce, a CVE that is still in
the CNA queue. The status update is what prevents a silent
60-day pause.

## Security model

The library is **default deny**:

- An `AuthContext` is a required parameter on every stateful
  port method. There is no path through the library that does
  not carry one.
- Authorization predicates are pure domain functions. The
  predicate that says "this user can see this resource" lives
  in `domain/`, not in an adapter; the adapter hands it the
  data and applies the answer.
- TLS verification is on by default. A `reqwest` client with
  certificate verification disabled is not constructed; the
  library has no path to do so.
- Path canonicalisation refuses a `..` traversal that escapes
  the allowed root with a typed error, not a panic.
- Tokens, Authorization headers, session ids in full, and
  elicitation responses are redacted at the tracing-layer
  boundary. The test that proves the redaction list is
  complete is `tests/secret_logging.rs`.

The full design, including what the library does *not* do
(token storage, rate limiting, CORS) and what the consumer is
responsible for, is in the
[Security model guide](https://greysquirr3l.github.io/protocol-droid/guides/security/)
on the docs site. The audit that backs the no-finding summary
in this policy is in
[`SECURITY-REVIEW.md`](https://github.com/greysquirr3l/protocol-droid/blob/main/SECURITY-REVIEW.md).

## Coordinated disclosure

A 90-day window is the default. A reporter who needs more time
(an embargoed CVE, a downstream rollout that takes longer than
the patch) names the date in the first message; the maintainer
confirms or counters. An embargo that runs past 180 days is
reviewed at 180 days; a longer embargo is honoured only if the
reporter and the maintainer agree in writing.

A patch lands **before** the advisory is public, and the
advisory text is shared with the reporter for review at least
48 hours before publication. The patch is credited in the
advisory, in the release notes, and in the git history; the
reporter's preferred attribution (name, handle, or anonymous)
is honoured.

## Past advisories

None. The repository's first release was tagged after the
SECURITY-REVIEW audit in October 2026, and no vulnerability
has been reported against a tagged release.

## Dependency advisories in the published graph

A dependency advisory is not an advisory against this crate, but it is
still something a consumer of a published version inherits, so it is
recorded here.

**RUSTSEC-2026-0385 — `ctutils` — affected every published version up
to and including 0.5.2. Fixed in 0.5.3.**

`ctutils 0.4.3`'s `Choice` mask generation could compile to a branch
on secret values, and its `u128` comparisons were not constant-time on
32-bit targets. Upstream fixed it in `ctutils 0.4.4`.

The path into this crate is `protocol-droid` → `hmac 0.13` → `digest
0.11.3` → `ctutils`, and `ctutils` is pulled in by `digest`'s `mac`
feature rather than by `hmac`'s own use of it: `digest/src/mac.rs` does
`use ctutils::CtEq;` and calls `ct_eq(tag)` to compare a MAC tag. The
reachable path is this crate's own HMAC comparison in
`application/mcp/input_required.rs`, where `StateKey::open` verifies a
`requestState` MAC with `verify_slice`. That is a real comparison over a
value derived from a server-held key, so the regression is a genuine
defect and not a theoretical one.

What a consumer needs to know:

- **A library consumer** resolves their own dependency graph, so a
  fresh resolve picks up a patched `ctutils` on its own. A consumer
  whose own lockfile still pins `ctutils 0.4.3` should run
  `cargo update -p ctutils`; the requirement is `^0.4`, so the patched
  version is already permitted.
- **A binary consumer** of `protocol-droid-cli` is the case that needs
  attention. A binary crate publishes its `Cargo.lock`, and `cargo
  install` honours it, so `cargo install protocol-droid-cli --version
  0.5.2` installed a binary built against `ctutils 0.4.3`. 0.5.3 ships
  the patched version, as does every release since.

The advisory was published on 2026-10-23, after 0.5.2 was tagged on
2026-10-22, so the fix could not have shipped in 0.5.2.

**RUSTSEC-2026-0387 — `crypto-bigint` — waived, not fixed.**

`crypto-bigint 0.5.5` has a constant-time regression in its `u128`
operations. It is reached through `jsonwebtoken`'s `rust_crypto`
backend → `p256`/`p384` → `ecdsa` → `elliptic-curve`, and no upgrade
path exists: the fix sits behind `p256`/`p384 0.14`, which
`jsonwebtoken 11.1.0`'s caret requirements do not admit.

It is unreachable from this code. The only path to `elliptic-curve` is
ECDSA *verification*, which runs on the public key, the message hash
and the signature's own `r` and `s` — no secret scalar reaches the
affected operations. The signing path is the reachable one and this
crate has no path to it: `jsonwebtoken`'s `EllipticCurveKeyParameters`
carries only `kty`, `crv`, `x` and `y`, so a JWK has no field in which
to carry a private scalar.

The waiver and its full reasoning live in
[`deny.toml`](https://github.com/greysquirr3l/protocol-droid/blob/main/deny.toml),
which is the single list of accepted advisories. It should be re-read
whenever `jsonwebtoken` or `rsa` changes, not waited on a schedule.

## Acknowledgements

The threat model and the no-finding summary draw on the
[OWASP Top 10:2025](https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/) and
[OWASP API Security Top 10:2023](https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0x11-t10/)
checklists. The MCP-spec-specific surface is read against the
official [Model Context Protocol specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/)
and the [conformance suite](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/conformance).

---

*This policy is reviewed at every minor release and at every
change to the wire-codec surface. A change to the supported-
versions table or to the response-timeline rows is a release
note, not a docs-only change.*

---
title: Security model
description: What protocol-droid does to keep a peer on the safe side of the trust boundary, what it does not, and where the consumer's responsibility begins.
---

The library's security model is *default deny*. The auth context
is a required parameter on every stateful port method, and the
authorization predicates are pure domain functions.

## What the library does

- **Token redaction at the tracing boundary.** Tokens,
  Authorization headers, session ids in full, and elicitation
  responses are redacted by the tracing layer. The redaction
  is tested in `tests/secret_logging.rs`.
- **TLS verification on by default.** A `reqwest` client that
  disables certificate verification is not constructed; the
  library has no path to do so.
- **Path canonicalisation for filesystem-backed resources.** A
  resource whose path traverses outside the allowed root is
  refused with a typed error.
- **Fail-secure on auth.** A `?` operator on a failed auth
  check is the default; an `?`-skipped check is not in the
  library.
- **Idle sessions are evicted.** An HTTP server sweeps a session
  that has been idle for 30 minutes, so a client that opens
  sessions and leaves cannot cost the server a map entry each
  time. A client whose session was evicted gets `404` on its next
  request and starts a new one.
- **A bridge session's inbox is bounded.** It holds 256 messages
  and answers `429` with `Retry-After` past that, so a client
  that `POST`s faster than the upstream answers cannot make the
  queue grow without limit.

## Protecting a server, and signing in to one

Both HTTP transports a server offers (Streamable HTTP and the legacy
HTTP+SSE routes) check the `Origin` header and the `Host` header
(the second catches a rebound DNS name, since `Origin` is absent from
every non-browser client), count requests against a per-subject rate
limit before authenticating, and put the same security headers on every
response, including the ones no handler wrote. A request with no
`Host` is refused.

### Requiring a credential on a server

Requiring OAuth is two builders, and the second one is the part that
is easy to leave off. An authenticator answers "is this token valid?";
a policy answers "does this endpoint need one?". The library treats an
authenticator without a policy as the silent fail-open it is, and
`into_router` refuses to build the route table rather than serve the
endpoint unprotected:

<!--
Mirrored from `crates/protocol-droid/examples/oauth_resource_server.rs`, which
is compiled by CI on every commit. Starlight does not expand mdbook's
`{{#include}}`, so this copy is duplicated — if the snippet and the example ever
disagree, the example is the one that is correct.
-->

```rust
use jsonwebtoken::Algorithm;
use protocol_droid::adapters::primary::transport::http::{
    AuthPolicy, HttpBuilder, OAuthAuthenticator, ServerConfig, SystemClock,
};
use protocol_droid::adapters::secondary::oauth::jwt::JwtSource;
use protocol_droid::application::oauth::NoScopes;
use protocol_droid::application::server::Server;
use protocol_droid::domain::ProtocolVersion;
use protocol_droid::domain::mcp::{ResourceMetadata, ResourceUri};
use protocol_droid::domain::registry::auth::{Scope, ScopeSet};

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    // Where tokens presented to this server are verified against. A real
    // deployment points this at its own JWKS; `IntrospectionSource` is the
    // opaque-token alternative.
    let source = JwtSource::new(
        Arc::from("https://login.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json"),
        vec![Algorithm::RS256],
    );

    // RFC 9728's protected-resource metadata: which resource this is, and who
    // may issue tokens for it. One value serves both purposes below, so the
    // document that is served and the challenge that points at it cannot name
    // different URLs.
    let metadata = ResourceMetadata::new(ResourceUri::new("https://mcp.example/mcp")?)
        .with_authorization_server("https://login.example.com")
        .with_scope("mcp:read");

    // Read before the metadata moves into the config. This is the exact string
    // a `401` carries in `WWW-Authenticate`, verbatim.
    match metadata.challenge() {
        Ok(challenge) => println!("a 401 would carry: {challenge}"),
        Err(error) => println!("no challenge: {error}"),
    }

    // Half one: what validates a token presented *to* this server. The audience
    // is bound to `metadata`, which is what stops a token minted for a
    // different resource being replayed here.
    let authenticator = Arc::new(OAuthAuthenticator::new(
        source,
        metadata.clone(),
        ProtocolVersion::V2025_06_18,
        NoScopes,
        SystemClock,
    ));

    // Half two: what says the endpoint needs one at all. These are separate
    // because "nothing is configured yet" and "this endpoint is deliberately
    // public" are different states, and conflating them is how a default
    // becomes a decision nobody made.
    //
    // Wiring an authenticator without a policy is the silent fail-open it looks
    // like, so `into_router` refuses to build the route table instead of
    // serving the endpoint unprotected.
    let policy = AuthPolicy::Require(ScopeSet::empty().with(Scope::Read));

    let config = ServerConfig::new()?.with_resource_metadata(metadata);

    // `Server` is what a `#[server]` declaration produces through
    // `.into_server()`; building one directly here keeps the example runnable
    // without a full tool declaration.
    let server = Server::builder("mcp").build();

    // `.serve().await` binds the address and starts listening. This example
    // stops short of that so it exits and prints instead of hanging.
    let _builder = HttpBuilder::new(server)
        .config(config)
        .with_authenticator(authenticator)
        .with_policy(policy);
```

Two details in that snippet are easy to trip over. `metadata` is cloned
rather than moved, because the authenticator needs the audience and the
config needs the publication URL, and it is deliberately not `Copy` — it
owns an `Arc<str>`. And `Algorithm` comes from `jsonwebtoken`, which is
a dependency of the OAuth feature rather than a type this crate
re-exports.

`with_resource_metadata` mounts the document on the MCP router and
points the `401` challenge at that same URL, both read from one value, so
the challenge cannot name a document that is not being served. The
document route deliberately skips the authenticator — the escape route
cannot require the credential it explains how to obtain — but it still
passes the same `Host` and rate-limit checks as every other route.

A single-issuer deployment should also name the issuer, which is off by
default because RFC 9728 publishes a *list* of trusted authorization
servers:

```rust
let authenticator = authenticator.with_expected_issuer("https://login.example.com");
```

On the client side, the OAuth flow:

- refuses a server whose metadata describes a different resource,
